items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Ā, tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Otir ā,
huri noa i t ō t ātou Whare, t ēnā koutou katoa. Me whakanui t ātou i t ēnei tahua-p ūtea.
Kua kite katoa tātou i te pai, me te hua mō ngā whānau katoa o Aotearoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings indeed to all of us thro ughout our House. We
must acknowledge this Budget.  We have all seen the value and benefit in it for all New
Zealand families.]
I am pleased and proud to be standing to sp eak in this Budget debate 2014-15. It is
the kind of Budget that is absolutely appos ite to its circumstan ces. We have had six
Budgets that have had to be delivered over the course of this Government, and each one
has been putting in place the building blocks for a stronger economy, a richer wealth of
society, more support for the families and children who need it the most, and investing
in the sustainability of our country and of our people long term. This Budget delivers all
that it should. We have come out from th e mess we inherited from the Opposition and
from the global financial crisis, deftly mana ged by the Minister of Finance. Each year
we have had the right amount of stimulus and the right amount of borrowing balanced
against the right amount of investment, because we understand, unlike those Opposition
benches, that money does not magically pour  through a hole in the sky. It comes from
investing in businesses and backing those companies to make greater investment
choices themselves to employ more people, to offer more jobs, to articulate what skills
they need, and to make sure that our education system delivers on that.

items.speaker: This Budget reflects our main priorities
items.text: strengthening our economy, getting more
growth out of it, and getting be tter public services of the kind that my colleague Steven
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18175
Joyce was just mentioning. We do not simply  fund departments to keep existing; we
fund them to deliver better services, and we  are getting better services from our very
experienced and capable Public Service. We  are also working in a more focused and
integrated way amongst Ministers across al l portfolios. Again, we understand, unlike
the Opposition, that people do not live their li ves in sectors; they live their lives. As a
result of that, you can see that at the heart of this Budget is a big heart for families and
children.
We are extending paid parental leave and the parental tax credit, while at the same
time investing more into early childhood education—$155 million, which caters for the
growth we are already having in early childhood e ducation, which itself is a sign of
growth in the economy as parents are going back to work and as more people are
finding jobs and seeking bett er and higher-quality early childhood provision for their
children. But, alongside this, at the heart of  this Budget is a significant health
investment: extending free doctors visits fo r those up to 13 years old and providing for
those prescriptions. We have been able to do this over time because we have built the
base to make that possible. Together, th at $500 million package at the heart of our
Budget shows how much this Government cares for, is concerned about, and is prepared
to make an investment in the families and chil dren of this country that we as a country
can afford to make.
I want to talk a bit more specifically about education. We have had some questions in
the House today about why youth unemploymen t, particularly in Pasifika and M āori
communities, is at the level that it is at. The answer is simple. Those young people, if
they do not have the skills they need, cannot get the jobs that are available. Eighty-four
thousand jobs have been created in the ec onomy in the past year. That means more
people are getting back to work, and, of that, nearly 11,000 are young Pasifika people.
We want to see more young people getting th e opportunities to get into work and to
make a life for themselves and for their familie s. But that has to be off the back of a
sustainable investment, which is education. That is why in our portfolio we have for the
first time gone over $10 billion. This Governme nt puts its money where its mouth is. It
knows that good-quality early  childhood education puts our young people on the best
learning trajectory possible.
We have a Better Public Services target of 98 percent of all new entrants in 2016
having participated in early childhood educa tion. We are at about 96 percent. Both the
Pasifika and M āori communities have increased their participation, and that is great
because it means they can move on into pr imary school with a stronger set of skills—
socialised, eager, and keen to participat e in their own learning. We see improvements
across primary schools as well as into sec ondary schools and on into secondary-tertiary
transitions, or at least on into training, into apprenticeships, into more academic courses,
and into employment.
That happens because we do this unsexy but necessary job of ensuring that five out
of five children get the best possible educat ion they can get. That means working away
at the system. It means, as I have alrea dy indicated, that we have nearly doubled the
investment into early childhood education. We have taken it from $800 million to $1.5
billion over the last six Budgets. At primar y and secondary schools we have increased
the investment by about 45 percent. The flag ship investment of $359 million, which the
Prime Minister announced in January, was the single biggest item in this year’s Budget.
That is directed at how we raise the quali ty of teaching and leading in our schools so
that we get more kids across the line and more  kids able to make choices for themselves
about the kinds of lives they will live.
In addition, we have recogni sed that our school s need day-to-day  support in their
operational funding—$85 million in this Budget.  That $85 million keeps pace with the
18176 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
projected cost of inflation, which is only one f actor but an important factor. In the last 6
years this Government has put over $600 millio n into providing that day-to-day support
for schools. We know how important it is th at schools are able—and this is all their
discretionary spending. That is in addition to all of the other investments that we make
into schools for professional l earning and development, for curriculum support, and for
the very strong investments we are making in properties. New schools are being built in
this country.
In Christchurch, of course, about 28 new schools will be built over the next 10 years,
and 115 schools in all will support a refresh of  the education network there—one of the
four priorities of this Government. We can  expect to see that becoming a leading
education network in New Zealand, but I thin k in Australasia as well, because of the
support we have given to that community and because those education leaders in
Christchurch have risen to the many, many challenges that they have had to face over
the last 3 or 4 years. That has been suppor ted in a wider sense by the investments that
my colleague the Hon Gerry Brownlee has made across Christchurch. Our Government
has not once resiled from its commitment to  ensuring that those communities will be
rebuilt, that they will continue to be a priority to us, and that we will put money in there
as it is required, and it will be invested wisely to sustain the growth of that community.
Education is one part of that story.
We are also putting investments in educat ion into the School High Health Needs
Fund, into Reading Together, and into Comp uters in Homes. These three programmes
together will support some of our most needy families. There is $3 million over the next
2 years for Computers in Homes. We expect to be able to help 1,500 more families. The
Computers in Homes programme does two main things. It helps families to become
acquainted with, and confident about, skills to engage in the digi tal world. They learn
how to use a computer, they learn how to access the internet, and they learn how to
design their own CVs, to Googl e jobs online, and to get th e information they need. At
the end of the programme they receive a computer and 12 months’ access to the
internet. But the second, equally important and powerful, contribution that Computers
in Homes makes is that it connects with th eir children, who are, more and more, being
exposed to the opportunities of  digital learning in our sc hools. This Government has
invested $700 million into making sure that our kids can participate in 21 st century
learning. Of that, we have inve sted in ultra-fast broadband  to the school gate and we
have ensured that the schools are wired to benefit from that connection.
My colleague the Hon Amy Adams has been relentless in ensuring that not only are
our contractors on time to ensure that this is happening in schools but, actually, they
sometimes get ahead of our timetable. Led by my colleague the Hon Nikki Kaye, we
have invested in the Network for Learning. Th is is a managed network that brings data
into schools—good quality, high speed, free, 24/7—to support the best possible 21 st
century learning, unlimited and uncapped. This is a $700 million investment, and we are
continuing to invest in that space, making su re that our properties  are modern learning
environments; that they are fresh, light, fl exible spaces; that they  are earthquake-proof;
and that we are dealing with leaky buildings . Minister Kaye has overseen a renewal of
that very important part of the education portfolio.
Our Government has prioritised five out of five learners, and this  Budget invests to
make sure that that becomes a reality ev ery day in classrooms and early childhood
centres up and down our country. We are back in black.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : Talofa lava, malo le
soifua. Fa‘afetai tele mo le avanoa i lau af ioga a le Speaker. It is evident that this
Government has reassessed its stance on the Pa sifika party vote, and has indicated in no
subtle manner how it hopes to win the hearts of the Pacific population. The decision to
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18177
put a Pacific face to the role of Minister pa ved the way for deliberate visits to church
services to appeal to the Pacific mass. Ev en Judith Collins managed to attend a Samoan
Catholic mass in South Auckland, in M āngere, at the Malaeola, accompanied by her
Asian and part-Samoan husband and followed by a Samoan entourage—an over-the-top
display. It was—[Interruption] Sorry, I hear somebody.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: This is the Budget debate.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : It is. It is coming. It was a
masquerade and artificial mana to somehow woo the hearts of the congregation.
The National Government clearly expects to  take Pasifika votes for granted. You
may fool a few, but it is not hard to see the underlying game played by National. As we
watch the game play unfold, there is no real hope given from Budget initiatives that yet
again are titled with empty promises of improvements and of a brighter future. The
strategy is clear—let us skim enough Pacific party votes to win th is election. Let us
make them feel good by attending their church es for the first time, in numbers, and in
the year of the election. Th e problem with this strategy is the undermining of Pacific
communities in their ability to see through the facade and recognise good policies that
give concrete results to all. Why is it th at Pasifika are always—always—on the extreme
spectrum of negative statistics yet the last to benefit from Government interventions?
The Minister of Pacific Island Affairs has made it clear that the Pacific language is
not a priority for this Government. He needs to tell the Prime Minister that language is a
very important aspect of learning. It is consid ered a very important part of the Pasifika
culture, and schools should be allowed to in corporate languages in to their curriculum.
New Zealand First will encourage Pasifika to  speak their languages.  The problem this
Government has is that it knows exactly what  the needs of Pasifika are, but it is
reluctant to follow through with any real commitment.
It is simple. Pasifika want to earn a stable and fair wage  through employment.
Pasifika have lost almost $90 a week in th eir overall weekly income since 2009, yet the
cost of living has gone up dramatically. La st year’s Budget saw a pathetic 3,000 trade
training initiatives introdu ced to appeal to young Pa sifika. A 2014 pre-Budget
announcement of $20 million for 6,000 more a pprenticeships for all New Zealanders
shows an increasing demand in priority trades. There needs to be a decrease in the
number of Pasifika “neet” youth. Those are the youth who are not in employment, not in
education, and not in training. You would thi nk that, with a surplus, more would be
invested to encourage trade training, particul arly in the area of rebuilding Christchurch
and housing construction in Auckland, which would benefit the New Zealand economy.
Housing affordability is now at its worst, a nd it is impossible for any of the Pasifika
people to access homeownership. It is now at  its all-time low of almost 19 percent.
Well, what can anyone expect with a 20 pe rcent deposit now required and the cost of
houses starting from $400,000 upwards? The 41 new special housing areas in Auckland
will not be effective for many. This Government  is out of touch in its belief that the
average family can afford over $400,000 for a new home.
Pasifika do not want handouts. They want th e opportunity to work hard in order to
earn a living to support their families. You may boast about a surplus, but I can tell
everyone listening to and watching this deba te right now that Pasifika communities are
not as excited. One can only hope that the $20 million to $25 million expected spend on
Pasifika futures will not end up in the same dubious business as Wh ānau Ora. Public
accountability is imperative in making sure that taxpayers’ money is not being spent on
or used to finance projects that deliver unsuccessful outcomes. Pasifika need worthy
projects that deliver jobs, affordable housing, education, and good health systems. It has
been said by many Pasifika orators of our time: “O le manu usu po, na te maua uma ia
anufe o le taeao.”—a bird that gets up early will inherit all the worms in the morning.
18178 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
When the Samoans translate that into orator y wisdom it is that early and well-prepared
hunters will catch all the goodness available. A Government with advanced strategies
will achieve its expected outcomes if there is genuine commitment for Pasifika, which
is not the case.
Bill English and Nick Smith rambled on and on last year about how the Warm Up

items.speaker: New Zealand
items.text: Healthy Homes programme was expected to insulate around 46,000
homes. Well, why do they not come to S outh Auckland and explain to the Pasifika
constituents why many of them are endlessl y on the waiting list or forever waiting on
the 0800 lines for somebody—anybody—to listen to  their housing concerns? Why does
the Minister not tell them why waiting for 4 months after speaking to an 0800 line robot
about urgent maintenance issues is sta ndard process under his Government? Why does
the Government not tell those affected by rheumatic fever, asthma, and meningococcal
disease that it is sorry but to  toughen up and to continue to live in an unhealthy, unsafe,
and overcrowded housing situation? Why doe s Tony Ryall not explain to them why
they have to basically prove that they ar e on their deathbed before anyone will address
their health issues?
No doubt you will try to cover these issues with the recent release of the $4.3 million
Matanikolo Project to provide 22 families with a better living situation. What a joke.
That is a complete joke.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to
interrupt the honourable member. I just wish  to advise members that courtesy is
contagious. There is far too much backgr ound chatter, and unl ess it relates to
parliamentary business I would urge members to take their private conversations outside
the Chamber.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : That is a wonderful comment.
Thank you very much.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member must
not comment.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : I know that 22 families down one
street alone are crying out for help. They  are crying out for improvements in their
quality of life and future prospects. Too many families will be crammed together on
small sites, and many of the special housing areas are in places where families are large.
Yes, indeed, you have targeted low-income households, but not for any other reason
than to ensure that they are left at that end of the spect rum. When you see the struggle
of living every day for these struggling families and the overwhelming amount of debt
that these families are unable to climb out of , there is no light. Why has it taken so long
for an initiative to expose the current dire s ituation of the loan sharks in this country
who have preyed upon the vulnerability of low-income families for far too long?
Pasifika are often the targets of these lo w-life lenders who car e only about profit
margins with no regard for the social impli cations. Dodgy loan sharks should be held to
account, and there should be a cap on interest rates.
Many of the community may still be excluded if they do not meet basic
requirements. Given the harsh reality of the current housing market situation, even with
this initiative, low-income Pasifika families will not be able to afford their own homes.
Pasifika parents are put in an uncomf ortable situation when schools recommend
compulsory school payments and donations. Th ere are also requirements for them to
buy laptops and modern technology. Does this Government understand the level of debt
a Pasifika student is left with after seeking the rewards of higher education?
New Zealand First will lift the minimum wage to $16.50 an hour, and the free
general practitioner visits should be implem ented immediately, not next year. Is the
election game plan worth playing out when it continues to put many in the back pocket?
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18179
National might demand the Pasifika vote. It  might demand the Pa sifika people’s vote,
but do not tell me that you honestly deserve it, because you do not. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker. It is a privilege to be able to sta nd in this Budget debate . I had an interesting
week last week. On Monday just gone I went  and spoke to Grey Power South Taranaki.
We had a really good discussion. Grey Power So uth Taranaki is a pretty feisty bunch of
people. They are always happy to take it to  you and ask you the hard questions when
you are there to speak to them. But the fact is that South Tarana ki and Wanganui over
the last few years are experiencing somethi ng they have not experienced before, and
certainly not under other Govern ments, and that is that th ey are experiencing a higher
level of GDP per capita than they ever ha ve before, and funnily enough, in Wanganui’s
case, a higher level of employment than is the national average. This is because both
areas within my electorate are built on the back of the export industry. What we know is
that under the previous Government there was not a single job grown in the export
sector for 10 years. Looking at where that  sits now, this Gove rnment is focused on
providing some certainty around financial policy and some certainty around people
investing in the economy, particularly in the export sector.
The economy of Taranaki, and South Ta ranaki as it comes into the Wanganui
electorate, is built on the back of dairy farming and the oil and gas industry. Those
people involved in oil and gas receive a higher level of remuneration than those
employed in similar jobs in other sectors. Th at is the nature of the industry, and it has
been very, very good for our part of the wo rld and very, very good for our country. In
respect of dairying, though, that, as people know, has been undergoing a purple patch
over the last few years in terms of reward for those who are involved in the industry not
only farm owners and operators but farm workers as well.
The big threat here comes from those prom ises we have already had from the other
side of the House in terms of a Labour-Greens Government. What we know is that there
will be a change to personal income  tax. It will go up under a Labour-Greens
Government. We also know that commercial tax rates will go up under a Labour-Greens
Government. We also know that there wi ll be changes to the labour sector—for
instance, the loss of the 90-day trial and the increase in minimum wages to $15, heading
towards $18 after that. We also know that th ere will be changes to ACC and changes to
the Resource Management Act. We also know  that there will be  the imposition of a
capital gains tax, and we know that there wi ll be increased charge s for carbon. So what
we know, then, is that electr icity prices will go up, as we ll, and the cost of doing
business in this critical export area of dairying is going to  become very, very heavily
taxed and levied. The average dairy farm, milking about 400 cows for 140,000
kilograms of milk solids, is expecting, th en, that it will pay well in excess of $2,000 per
week in excess taxes and levies, and the average drystock farm about $1,000.
This is a critical thing for our electora te. Those people whom we are working with
and whom we are speaking to have got their heads around th at very, very well indeed.
The response, for instance, at the Wanganui  riverside market wa s interesting, too.
Wanganui, as people will know, is  an area that has struggled in some aspects. Its
demographics are such that it has a hi gher than average older population. That
population does not keep in as  good health as ot her relative populations. It has a lesser
number of people who are well educated, and they are involved in less remunerative
work. So the gains that we have made from health care, for instance, are very, very near
to the hearts of those people in Wanganui. While many developed countries are freezing
or reducing health funding, National is sp ending more on health than any other
Government in New Zealand’s history—$1.8 b illion of extra investment over 4 years—
and taking health spending next year to a record $15.6 billion.
18180 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
It is interesting to note th at over the last few years of  the Labour Government the
Whanganui District Health Board struggled. It struggled to meet its targets, it failed in a
number of areas, and it was in  the media for all the wrong reasons. Yet over the last 6
years it has been in the media for all the right reasons. When you look at the measures
and when you look at the traffic light inde x of where those hospi tals are required to
perform, it is meeting all those targets and sits in about the top five of all district health
boards around the country, except for a coupl e of measures, which are mainly around
smoking cessation and others.
When we look at the education sector in Wanganui, we do very well with our schools
there, albeit after a lot of depopulation; th ere are more schools than  are required for the
population and there are a number of empty chairs. What we do know is that the schools
that operate within Wanganui do incredibly well. It is good to note, too, that the
Government is investing heavily in educatio n and recognising the expertise of teachers
and principals and their ability to share th eir expertise around the community in which
they work. As every electorate MP knows,  you may have many, many schools within
your electorate, and they operate at differe nt levels. You can walk into some schools
and they are absolutely humming; you walk in to other schools and it is like putting on a
big, wet duffel coat. To share that expertise around those schools in order to make sure
that every child has the opportuni ty for the best possible resu lts in their education is a
great thing.
I would like to talk a little bit about my  portfolios in respect of courts and youth
justice. Over the last few years we have inve sted in courts and invested in savings, and
we are seeing the results of that, which ar e fantastic. We have  invested in the
modernisation of courts, and I know that ac ross the House we have received support for
the investment we have made. Implementi ng the use of technology within our courts
has been a high priority for us, and we woul d like to one day achieve the status of a
paperless court. That is some  way off; nevertheless, it is an ambition that we hold dear.
It seems ridiculous to me that the way Ne w Zealanders interact with their banks, pay
their bills, book their hotels and air travel, a nd do a number of other things is all online,
but when we have to deal with  the courts, it has got to be a paper-based system. We are
moving very quickly in order to be able to change that. An example of that, for instance,
was the Environment Court’s 5-week hearin gs in relation to the Denniston Plateau,
where the whole of the court hearing was he ld on iPads. There wa s not any paper used
through that court process whatsoever.
But the big bugbear in courts is reducing waiting times and work on hand. So overall
in the last 12 months we have seen an 8.9 percent drop in the time it takes for a court
case to move through the Di strict Court system. That is a 16-day reduction. In the
criminal jurisdiction it is up to 18.3 percent, or a 23-day reduction in the average time of
work on hand. Disputes tribunals have sped up just over 21 percent, or 17 days quicker
than they were before. We are seeing th is reflected all the way through our court
system, and we have firmly between our teeth th e bit that is going to take us to an even
more efficient system. In collections, for instance, when we came into office, we
inherited a debt book of unpaid fines. It wa s $806 million when we came into office in
2008, and now it is down to $554 million. That is $554 million that is incredibly
frustrating because you cannot get your mitts  on it. It is like knowing there is $100
stuffed down the back of your couch, but you cannot quite get to it. We are doing
everything we can to ensure that we can get our mitts on it.
I want to finish off with a bit of a stor y around our youth justice results. When we
came into Government in 2008, we set abou t changing the way we were delivering
youth justice to our young people. We received a lot of stick for that. As the legislation
went through the Social Services Committee we  had a lot of stick about the initiatives
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18181
we were taking in the youth justice sector to extend the periods for supervision with
activity and supervision with residence, and to  bolt on to the back of that the ability to
have therapeutic treatments around drug and alcohol violence and abuse, and those sorts
of things. Probably the hottest one was ar ound the introduction of  military activity
camps. Just to bring Parliament up to speed in respect of our results there, in the first 12
months post - military activ ity camp, 79 percent are re ducing their frequency of
offending, 16 percent are not offending whatsoever, 81 percent are reducing the severity
of offending, and there is a 53 percent reductio n in violent offending. It is good to note
that the heat has now gone out of this de bate. Labour, the Greens, and all parties on the
Opposition side are fully in support of the yout h justice initiatives that we implemented
in 2008, because we are seeing the benefits of them. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I always enjoy the build -up in your introductions
to the next speaker, Mr Assistant Speaker Ro bertson. For all of the rhetoric in this
House in the aftermath of the Budget, I thi nk it is still importa nt to reflect that,
ultimately, Budgets should be about one thi ng. They should be about people. It is easy
to get distracted by all of the different de bate around appropriations and year-on-year
comparisons, but, underneath it all, people are ultimately what a Government’s Budget
should be about. At the end of the day th ere is no better measure as to whether a
Government is serving the needs of the count ry, the needs of the people in the country,
than whether the Budget is directed toward s the immediate needs that those people are
facing. If we were to distil dow n those needs, I think it is pretty simple to see through
all of the media coverage around people’s conc erns at the moment and the worries that
families have—and even when you are a politician and you doorknock, you know
immediately at the top of your mind what people are worrie d about in their day-to-day
lives.
That is what this Budget should have been about. The things that people are worried
about are really simple, basic needs. Firstl y, they are worried about whether they can
afford to live in a decent house—and not just  whether can they rent it but whether they
can ever aspire to live in their own home—a nd whether the home they are living in is
warm and dry and that their kids are well a nd safe inside it. Secondly, they are worried
about whether their kids are generally gett ing a good start—the best start—in life and
having all of the opportunities that they had as parents. No matter what, and no matter
how you paint parents from across the spectrum,  underneath it all, almost every single
parent, without doubt, wants better for their kids—without doubt. Thirdly, people, those
individuals we are talking to on the doorsteps,  are worried about whether they have the
kind of job that enables them not just to get some satisfaction from getting up in the
morning and going and doing that  job but to provide for th emselves—that is, whether
they can sustain themselves with the income and the wages that they are receiving in
that work, let alone provide for a family.
So, in that context, based on those three simple needs, how did this Budget perform?
Well, the Government has talked a lot about the needs of families. I think probably it
detected that there was a desire amongst people to see something for families in this
Budget. I think that as Labour members we di d a pretty good job of  raising the profile
of the needs of family members. We se t the bar with the Best Start policy. We
challenged the Government to do somethi ng also. But the challenge was based on
evidence. There are 285,000 children living in poverty in Ne w Zealand. That is roughly
27 percent. But if you break that down even further, for all of the Prime Minister’s
rhetoric about what he has done for Pasi fika people in New Zealand, one in three
Pasifika children is living in poverty. They are one of the major groups who are
suffering particularly at present in that re gard. We know also th at, of that group, 10
percent are living at what has been called the hardest end of poverty. That means they
18182 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
are living on even less than what the poverty line is established at, which is 60 percent
of median income. We also know that three out of five children living in poverty will
live there for a long time. They are most likel y to live there in thei r youngest years, so
under the age of somewhere around 4.
When we know all of that, what did this Budget do for that group? The Minister of
Finance talked about tackling the hardest end of poverty. He said that  last week in the
House before the Budget came out. He said that  that is what his Government was going
to do. But did it? I almost find that there is an irony in this—that the Government stated
that this is the very group that needed a targeted response, but the targeting happened
precisely around them, making sure that they  were the only ones,  almost, who were
excluded from the Government’s Budget m easures. The Government extended the
parental tax credit by an extra 2 weeks, so families get it for 10 weeks now, and it upped
the rate a bit to $220 a week. That is all good stuff—not quite as much as we would
have liked, but all good stuff. But the Governme nt then said the parental tax credit will
not go to anyone on an income-tested benefit,  yet the majority of families living in
poverty are those exact families. So, unfort unately, the notion of it being a “fudge-it
Budget” started right at that place for the families who needed it most. And what did the
Minister of Finance say those families would get? Well, they should celebrate because,
apparently, they got a CPI adjustment, and that is about it.
The Government has come back and said in  defence of itself that it has made free
health care for under-13-year-olds universal—s tarting next year, I should add. Well, I
would wager that probably what the G overnment did was go away and do a rough
calculation. Since National has come into Government we have had 40,000 preventable
hospitalisations for children. If you want to  save money for the taxpayer, one simple
thing to do would be to try to put a bit mo re money into primary health care and see
whether you can prevent those hospitalisations. It  is a simple measure. It is a simple act
to take. But, as Dr Nikki Turner has said, free doctors visits do not solve the root causes
of poverty, and therefore they will not reso lve poverty-related diseases. And what are
those poverty-related diseases? They are re spiratory illnesses,  bronchiectasis and
illnesses like that; more and more infectious skin diseases; and, of course, the one that
gets batted around the most, rheumatic fever.  All of those illnes ses come out of the
basis, usually, that we have children livin g in damp, cold, overcrowded houses. So if
you genuinely wanted to get to the root causes of those issues and therefore help those
at the hardest end of povert y, as the Government purports, then you would have been
dealing not only with the housing issue, whic h we know that this Budget did not, but
with the fact that, ultimately, parents want to be able to manage their own
circumstances. Where is their economic inde pendence? Where is the focus on ensuring
that they have the wages and the salaries requ ired to make sure that they are able to
ensure that their families are growing up in an environment that prevents those
illnesses?
But what else did the Government set out as its own measures for success in this
Budget? We had veneer—the facade, I guess—of wanting to support families, but next
was the surplus. The Government set up a goal that basically said that if it achieved
surplus, then it would have achieved every goal it needs to achieve as a Government—
end of. That is all that needs to be done with this Budget. And, yes, the Government got
there. But how did it do it? Well, by holding on to ACC levies at a higher rate than it
needed to, by cutting down spending for the Christchurch rebuild—which, by the way,
is meant to be our primary economic stimulus—and by reframing New Zealand
Transport Agency spend as loans. It is do ing that in the cont ext of having already
clocked up $56 billion in debt. We are paying $10 million a day in interest on the debt
this Government has accrued. What a shameful thing that is.
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18183
But what we have argued, and Labour is strongly putting forwar d as a counter, is a
plan for surplus that at the same time reso lves some of the systemic issues that the
Government chooses to ignore. On poverty, for instance, we need to act immediately.
We need immediate relief for those children living at the hardest end in their early
years. The Best Start package does not help for 10 weeks; it helps those families for 3
years, because we know that those are the most important years. The second thing is
immediate action on low wages. We will lift  the minimum wage and we will support a
living wage, but we will also recognise that we need to lift wages generally. We need a
high-wage economy, and you achieve that through investment in research and
development, through a monetary policy that supports exporters and our manufacturers,
and by just generally acknowledging that we ha ve to do things differently if we are
going to give our families the economic independence they deserve. On housing—
because it is, after all, about kids, about jobs, and about housing—the market has failed.
It is obvious. Everyone knows it; everyone has seen it. We are going to get stuck in. We
will ourselves, as the Government, build 100,000 affordable homes. We will introduce a
capital gains tax so that our tax system is fairer and we will move away from a housing
market that is dominated by speculators. We will say that if you want to own a home in
New Zealand, you need to be a resident here. That is fair enough. And we will make
sure that we have the social housing we need to support those who need it most.
Budgets should be about people. We know that New Zealanders want New Zealand
to be the fair and equal place they grew up w ith it being. We can return to that. We can
do it by making sure that every child has the very best start in life, that every family has
a warm, dry home, and that everyone has a job that keeps them supported and gives
them dignity. That is a Government you coul d believe in, and that  is what Labour will
deliver.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: The Prime Minister was right when he said
in question time that the Labour Party used to care. The Labour Party used to care about
a growing economy. The Labour Party used  to care about the welfare of New
Zealanders. The Labour Party used to care about those who were down on their luck and
needed help from the Government the mo st. But when we hear Labour Party MPs
questioning popular and necessary Budget initiativ es like free general practitioner visits
for those under 13, when we hear Labour MPs wanting to impose more costs on New
Zealanders wanting to buy homes, when you hear Labour MPs now  complaining about
the fact that New Zealanders are voting with their feet and are stay ing in this country,
you have to wonder why the Labour Party is in such dire straits right now. It is because
it simply does not get it any more.
The Labour Party simply does not get it  any more, but New Zealanders do. New
Zealanders get it right now because they understand that this economy is growing. They
understand that more childre n are getting an education in this economy. They
understand that more children are getting the health care they require and that more
operations are taking place. They understand  that crime is coming down and that the
law and order situation in this country is so  much better than it  ever was under Labour.
And they also understand that wages are rising  and that it is going to become even
easier to get into a home in future years. They know that it is working.
Jacinda Ardern was the last individual speaking from the other side. Jacinda Ardern
is the police spokesperson for the Labour Part y. I have heard her make comments about
the police budget in recent weeks. The fact of  the matter is that when it comes to the
police, our police are doing such a good job that crime is down 20 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You wait.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Those members do not like to hear it. They like to cackle from
the other side of the House, but crime is down 20 percent. We ha ve the lowest crime
18184 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
rate in 33 years. When Annette King was in  Government, crime actua lly started to rise
just a little bit in Labour’s last year. It actual ly started to rise in her last year when she
was the police Minister. Crime has now dr opped by 20 percent. Reoffending in this
country is coming down. Reoffending is down 12.5 percent in this country because of
the investment of time and effort that Mi nisters like Judith Collins and Anne Tolley
have put into the police and corrections budge ts. New Zealanders know that that is the
situation. They know that it is successful. They know that it is working.
Jacinda Ardern also talked about housi ng. I am glad she talked about housing,
because I live in the Botany electorate, wh ere some of the important special housing
areas that are going to get Auckland housing moving again are taking place. Nick Smith
just recently, a couple of weeks ago, announced  the largest of the special housing areas
in Flat Bush, near where I live. In the Fl at Bush special housing area, 4,500 houses are
going to be built—4,500. The pe ople living in that area ar e seeing housing taking off.
They are seeing the builders getting out there and working. They are seeing the
developers getting out ther e, subdividing the land, and in creasing the supply that we
desperately need in this country.
And then we hear the Labour Party talk ing about its 100,000 houses over 10 years.
Well, guess what! That is 10,000 a year. U nder National, we are already building
13,000 right here. Thirteen thousand houses a year are going to be built, under National,
under the housing accord and the special housing areas. The Labour Party’s big idea for
housing is 100,000 houses, 10,000 a year. That is fewer than are being proposed, and it
is happening under the special housing ar ea policy that this Government is
implementing. And that 13,000 is only in Auckland. The Labour Party’s plan is
supposedly for across the whole of the c ountry. Labour simply does not get it. Its
numbers are wrong, and it actually will not do anything under the policies it is
proposing. If it really cared about housing, it would get in and support Resource
Management Act reform, which this country desperately needs—Resource Management
Act reform that is being blocked by the lik es of the Labour Party and being blocked by
the likes of the Green Party. Those are policies that should be taking place.
If we look at a capital gains tax, those par ties believe that that is the grand panacea
for housing. Well, it is being done in Aust ralia right now, and gue ss what! It is not
working. Under Labour, housing costs went up by 96 percent. In the past 5 years they
have gone up by only 28 percent. Compare that  96 percent with 28 percent. If you want
to ask New Zealanders whom they believe on housing, just look at the statistics. They
know that the Labour Party has got it absolutely wrong.
I also want to talk about jobs, because j obs are what is going to get New Zealanders
wealthier. The jobs are what is going to ge t New Zealanders out of  welfare and on to a
better track for their lives. I listened a lit tle bit to Asenati Lole-Taylor and Jacinda
Ardern lamenting the fact th at there are individuals out there who do not have jobs,
lamenting the fact that there are individuals out there who are in difficult circumstances.
That is absolutely right.
There are people in this country who need a helping hand. There are people in this
country who need to get back on their feet. The only way they are going to get back on
their feet is if we have a gr owing economy, if we get more jobs for them, if we help get
them better educated, and if we ensure that law and order is sorted out in this country.
Those are the things we are doing. Those are th e things that are going  to get people out
of the poverty trap. The extra 170,000 jobs that will be created over the next 4 years will
get those people out of the poverty trap. The 84,000 jobs that were created in the past
year are helping to get New Zealanders out  of the poverty trap. Fifteen thousand New
Zealanders are coming off welfare right now. Fifteen hundred a week are coming off
welfare right now. In  the last year 30,000 fewer children ended up living in benefit-
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18185
dependent homes. Thirty thousand children are no longer living in benefit-dependent
homes. Those are the children who are going to  be the success of the future. Those are
the children whose parents have been able to get into work and who will be better off
because of it. For everyone else who is on welfare right now we should be doing
everything we possibly can to help them ge t a job, help them get better educated, and
ensure that they and their children are hea lthy—that is the way to a prosperous New
Zealand.
Those people on the other side might like to think that we over on this side are all
just rich Tories and everything like that. We ll, I have to say, I remember growing up in
South Auckland with a young mother and no father in a poor household. You know, the
best thing I was taught when I was growing up was to work hard, get educated, and do
what you can to get ahead in life. If every New Zealander who wants to get ahead in life
just worked hard, got educated, and put thei r best foot forward, with help from the
Government to get into jobs, that is the way New Zealanders get ahead in this country.
I am particularly proud of being a Nationa l member of Parliament when we are
seeing more kids getting educated. When we came into office, 67 percent of children
were getting National Certificate of Educationa l Achievement level 2; that is now at 77
percent.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Standards are dropping.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Standards are not dropping. Nati onal standards are ensuring that
we can actually measure how things are wo rking properly. Trevor  Mallard, the failure
of an education Minister, never cared about  properly measuring children. It took Anne
Tolley to sort that system out. It took Anne  Tolley to put in place a national standards
system so that New Zealanders actually know how their children are faring.
I am also proud of being part of a Governme nt that is investing properly in Auckland
transport. There is hundreds of millions of dollars of money being invested through this
Budget and in past Budgets into Auckland tr ansport. We are fast-tracking development
in Auckland transport over the next 10 year s. The Prime Minister last year announced
$10 billion worth of investment in Auckland tr ansport. That has been  reflected in this
Budget, and New Zealanders living in Auckland know that, as well.
ACC levies are coming down, more jobs are being created, more kids are getting
healthy, and more kids are getting an education—that is what this country wants. And if
you want to see how much New Ze alanders appreciate the fact that this country is in a
much better shape, just look at how they are voting with their feet. Under Labour, 3,000
New Zealanders a month were leaving for Australia; now it is only 350. Labour wants
to change the immigration system as it stands . It wants to change it completely. It is
actually a bit confused about it. But right now the statis tics are showing that New
Zealanders are voting with thei r feet. This country is in much better shape because of
the John Key - led Government, and I am proud to be a part of it.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. I welcome
the Government’s move to fund doctors visi ts for children under 13.  That is required
urgently. However, the detail of the implementation requires scrutiny. For under-6-year-
olds, parents will find that doctors visits are not truly free and still incur significant
charges. How many parents understand that Ne w Zealand’s children will have to wait
another 13 months before free doctors visits  come into effect? The legislation is
required immediately. How many children will suffer in the next 13 months because of
this delay? We all agree that there s hould be free medical care for children under 13,
and I call upon this Government to advance the legislation to come into effect before the
House rises on 31 July. I welcome the move to  extend paid parental leave to 18 weeks,
but, again, parents will have to wait nearly 2 years for the 18 weeks to apply.
18186 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
I turn to education. Sure, money has gone in, but most of it is being used to fix leaky
buildings and to create a re structuring—executive teachers, executive principals. Where
in this Budget is th e planning for 2020? Steven Joyce has been quoted as  saying that
ultra-fast broadband will revolutionise the way we trade, the way we operate, and the
way we communicate, and he is  right. But the reality is th at New Zealand is seriously
lagging behind the rest of the world on two fronts: planning and infrastructure. We need
ultra-fast broadband immediately. Where in the Budget is there money to upskill our
children, young people, and the existing workforce to provide us with the digital literacy
that is required?
We are fast moving into a world of predictive computi ng, wearable co mputing, and
quantum computing, where computers will  mimic and synthesise in seconds
information that currently takes months. Retail as we know it is changing dramatically.
We are moving from a world where the consum er goes to the market to one where the
market goes to the consumer. Thousands of jobs will be lost, but thousands more will be
created. Where is the identification of, and planning for, the skills and competencies of
children, young people, and the existing wo rkforce to operate and to face these
challenges? By 2020 we will have 3-D printers just like—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: He should have read it through first, out loud.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: —we used to have fax machines. They will be ubiquitous.
There is a word for you—sorry, Mr Assi stant Speaker; it was Mr Mallard I was
referring to. And manufacturi ng, as we know it today, will end. We need money in the
Budget so that New Zealand businesses can co mpete in the new world that is coming.
Our workforce needs these skills and competencies and so do we. So where is the plan?
I turn to housing. In the Budget the shame of  housing is Christchurch. It is a stain on
the soul of New Zealanders that the people of Christchurch are still suffering. Last week
I met a couple—a 70-year-old and a 74-year-old—who after 3 years are still living in
unhealthy conditions because of the bureaucra tic failure of the Earthquake Commission
and Southern Response. This couple had their first claim turned down because
inspectors were too lazy to lift the carpets, so a 70-year-old and a 74-year-old had to do
it themselves. Then they paid over $20,000 to  private engineers and found that the
concrete flooring slab had cracked and that  the waterproof membrane was breached,
promoting an osmotic effect and lifting th e water up into the house. How can these
people still be suffering after all this time? They are still fighting for fairness.
The truth is that there is a complete lack  of accountability in Christchurch. Who is
accountable for the bungling bureaucracy that ha s forced people in Christchurch to live
in squalid and unhealthy conditions for over 3 years? Who is the person responsible for
holding up the cheques to the people in need? Who is the person responsible for
ensuring that work done meets the required st andards? Who is responsible for Southern
Response’s low-ball settlement offers? Who is responsible for the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment guidelines that were supposed to provide uniformity for
reinstatement? These guidelines actually bre ach the Building Act because they provide
for a lower level of repair and reinstatemen t than that Act requires. The citizens of
Christchurch have been treated with contempt.
We need an urgent inquiry into building pr actices and into billing by contractors. I
know of jobs being overcharged. Here is an example: $200 worth of materials, $600
worth of labour, and finally the Earthquake  Commission being i nvoiced for over
$15,000. Added to that, the Government is saving money off the backs of suffering New
Zealanders, breaching trite law by operating to section 9 of schedule 3, and substituting
that section of the Earthquake Commission Act ahead of the primary definition, which
is to reinstate homes to as similar a conditi on as when new. Trite law requires that an
Act must be read in it s entirety, but the Earthquake  Commission is reading and
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18187
operating section 9 of schedule 3 in isolation.  In Christchurch we need accountability
and we need it now.
I turn now to Vote Parliamentary Service.  Recently, I have received information that
raises real questions about the use of parl iamentary funding by a party. I am writing to
the Speaker asking that the Parliamentary Service investigate these matters and report to
him. There was a clear precedent for this when in December 2001 the then general
manager, John O’Sullivan, reported to the Speaker on the Allian ce electorate liaison
unit. That report swept aside any uncertainty that might have existed and clearly stated
the rules. The leader of New Zealand First cannot claim to be ignorant—

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Vote Parliamentary Service—the New Zealand First Party is
using taxpayer-funded computer  software for party polit ical purposes such as
campaigning and fund-raising. The program, code-named Vanguard, is a constituent
relationships management system that stores  personal details of voters and is used for
mass mail-outs. Other political parties have these programs too—

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. This program has not been
launched. It is not part of—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is not a point  of order. I will
ask members that on points of order they be relevant to the matter. That is not a point of
order.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Other political parties have th ese programs, too, but they are
funded by the parties themselves and operated outside of Parliament. New Zealand First
paid tens of thousands of dollars out of th e leader’s budget to develop this software and
has its parliamentary staff working to run th e program for election year. This is a clear
breach of Parliamentary Service guidelines.
An internal party strategy document da ted 9 March 2014 states, under the heading
“Funds”: “Campaign fund request, first 2 weeks April—Self-funding after initial
distribution, followed by use of Vanguard a ppeals to focus groups.” A memo to the
party board by the president, Anne Marti n, dated 10 March 2014, stat es: “The director
of operations canvassed the use of Vanguard computer program. Suggest board advised
of its uses, including candidates’ college pr ogram as well.” This use of parliamentary
resources for fund-raising appeals and political campaigning is more than questionable,
especially from the New Zealand First Part y, which promised a fair go in the last
election. The public have a right to know wh at their money is being used for and
whether it is being used legally.
A company called Lone Star Market Research was registered on 1 August 2012. The
company’s sole director is New Zealand First’s director of operations in Parliament, and
is a member of the party’s campaign committee. The company was set up with the
intention of conducting political  activity for New Zealand Fi rst. New Zealand needs an
assurance from the Parliamentary Service and the leader of New Zealand First that Lone
Star Market Research has not received one  cent of taxpayer money, nor had the use of
parliamentary resources.

MPs and parties. Staff would seem to be in breach of the Parliamentary Service code of
conduct. I call upon the leader of that party to open his leader’s budget accounts to the
scrutiny of the Speaker first, and then to the public of New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: It gave me huge pleasure to return to
the Hawke’s Bay after the Budget was announced  last Thursday a nd to share it with
family, friends, and constituents. It was extr emely well received in the Hawke’s Bay.
People have seen, unlike the Opposition, how we have gone through a very difficult
recession over the last 6 years, and how th is Government has progressed through that
recession and has landed this economy in a superb position to go forward. They are
seeing the results of that now in terms of job growth, in terms of the economy going
forward in leaps and bounds, and, most part icularly, in terms of the turn-round in
immigration. If there is something that says that this country is going ahead, it is when
the migration statistics turn round and all of  sudden we see net positive migration back
to this country.
This will be my last Budget debate speech before I leave Parliament. I am extremely
proud to have been part of th is particular Budget. I am extremely proud to be a New
Zealander and extremely proud to be a member  of this House and of the National Party,
supporting this Budget, which was delivered  last Thursday. National came into
Government on the promise of delivering a br ighter future. We ha ve delivered that
brighter future through our actions over the past 5 years and through the outstanding
Budget of which I speak.
Do not take just my word for it. Intern ational commentators around the globe are
watching New Zealand become an economic pros perity story in the South Pacific. Take
Standard and Poor’s, for instance, which cu t New Zealand’s credit rating in 2011 after
the Canterbury earthquakes, and which ha s now said of this Budget that the
Government is on track to meet its targ eted operating surplus in 2015,  which would
improve the fiscal balance, consistent w ith its AA currency rating and stable outlook.
That is just one international commentator.
Secondly, Standard and Poor’s has also said that the Gove rnment is consolidating its
fiscal position, partly reflecting its ongoing efforts to reduce its cost base while
maintaining public services. I think that is what Kiwi s understand. Throughout the
nation, be it in Wanganui, Auckland, or Hawke’s Bay, we have got through this without
cutting the guts out of public services. We have actually c ontinued to deliver them, to
make increases, particularly in education a nd health, and the public has seen the results
of that, particularly in the Better Public Services area, wh ich Chester Borrows spoke of
earlier.
In education, on which Hekia Parata s poke—in early childhood education and in
every area of education we have seen lifts. It  is absolutely fantastic. We only have to
look across the Ditch to Australia and its comparative Budget to  see the chalk and
cheese of South Pacific Budgets. On th e one hand, we have New Zealand, which
forecasts a $300 million surplus in 2014-15, and as a result provides positive choices for
new spending, debt reduction, and/or, potentially, tax cuts in to the future. On the other
hand, we have Australia, which just a day ea rlier forecast a $30 billion Budget deficit,
massive expenditure cuts to its schools, hosp itals, pensions, and its foreign aid, together
with tax increases to arrest the deficit declin e. That is the recipe that the Opposition in
this House has delivered. That was the posi tion that we came into in 2008, with ever-
ongoing deficits forecast. The Australian situat ion is also the leg acy of a Labor-Green
Government and of uncontrolled spending. We saw it here when we came into office, as
I said previously.
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18191
Putting that aside, let us re turn to our Budget. It looks  ahead, building on the hard
work done by Kiwis, to 2 percent to 4 percent economic growth and a $372 million
surplus, growing to $1.3 billion in 2015-16 and $3.5 billion in 2017-18. That gives us
real choices—$1 billion of new spending in this Budget and $1.5 billion in 2015.
Government debt will peak at  26.4 percent, way below wher e it was originally forecast
in 2008 when we came in. We are seeing wage growth. The average an nual wage is up
$3,000 in the past 2 years and is expect ed to rise by $7,600 to $62,300 by 2018. That is
positive news. That is the economy going forward. We have also had forecasts of
170,000 new jobs over the next 4 years and ACC levy cuts of around $480 million. That
is significant. Consumer and business confidence  i s  a t  a n  a l l - t i m e  h i g h .  T h a t  i s  t o  b e
celebrated. But, as I said earlie r, of particular note is th e turn-round in migration. If
Chester Borrows and Dr Paul Hutchison refl ect on where we were at in the mid-2000s,
the emigration out of this country was dismal. Now we are seeing net positive
migration. That is a positive thing.
I am particularly proud that, as we have got choices, we are now delivering for
families, supporting children and families th rough this Budget. As the economy grows,
of course we can deliver more jobs and better wages for those families. In particular,
there has been a $500 million package of practical support for young families,
particularly for vulnerable ch ildren. That includes free general practitioner visits and
free prescriptions for all ch ildren under 13, 4 extra weeks of  paid parental leave,
increases to the parental tax credit, a nd an additional $155 million for early childhood
education. There we are seeing significant rises in M āori and Pacific Island children
attending early childhood education and improvi ng their results in school. We are also
seeing $33.4 million extra to support vulnerable children, which includes eight new
Children’s Teams to work with at-risk children.
This is a great Budget. It demonstrates a Minister of Finance at the top of his career. I
want to congratulate Bill English and his te am on their outstanding effort. Name for me
a Minister of Finance with a better track reco rd in the world at this  point in time. Name
for me a better Minister of Finance—I challenge you.
The success of this year’s Budget has resulted in some very interesting and
immediate political moves across the country and in the provinces. Firstly, we saw the
very hard-working Darien Fenton decide that  she was retiring. Then, interestingly, we
saw a range of Labour candidates announce that they would now not be standing for the
list in Hawke’s Bay. Both Stuart Nash and Anna Lorck have announced they will not be
seeking a place on Labour’s list.
This is very revealing, and it can be for one of only two reasons. Firstly, they have
read the tea leaves and they have realised th ey will be so far down on the list that they
will not have a bolter’s show of getting into Parliament through that door, or, secondly,
they have been following the polls, they have watched the Budget and where that has
landed, and they have realised that even with a good list position, the chance of them
getting into Parliament is remote. So they have decided to go for an all-out
constituency—not list—contest. So what we now have, if Labour did not already know,
are a couple of rogue candidates in the ba y. Goodbye, party vote; hello, personal vote.
Goodbye, party vote; hello, personal vote.
Here is what is going to  happen. Candidates will ha ve wildly different policy
positions and they will not put their leader’s photo on their billboards. That is for sure.
Consider those billboards, because this is where it gets really in teresting. Some of you
will recall that at the last election Stuart Na sh went all out for the electorate vote as
well. He thought Labour and its leader were  so bad that he would not put Phil Goff on
his election billboards. So he did not. Despite this strategy, he lost and was tossed out of
Parliament. What is the bet he will not put David Cunliffe on his billboards this year?
18192 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
He has got a track record in this space. And what about Anna Lorck? Will she have
David Cunliffe on her billboards? Well, with tweets like this one: “Can’t wait til Cunliff
turns up in HB… We haven’t forgotten he  sacked our DHB…he’s no leader he’s a
bully”—he’s no leader; he’s a bully. What a classic. She also refused to delete those
tweets when she was challenged.

items.speaker: So here is the wider question
items.text: will she put  David Cunliffe on her billboards, and how
many of those in the Opposition will? Will Tr evor Mallard put David Cunliffe on his
billboards? Just imagine if the hierarchy in  the Labour Party allows this to happen
around the country. Just imagine if it allows rogue candidates like Nash and Lorck to
prevail against the unity of the party. If it allows this to happen, Labour’s party vote will
implode. I predict an absolute whitewash.
This is a fantastic Budget. I am proud of what it has delivered for New Zealanders
around the country and for families. It is out standing progress for our country, and it is
fantastic to see the turn-round in migration. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: That was a very, very ironic speech
from a member, Chris Tremain, who is bai ling out of the National Party. He is not
willing to stand again in Napier because Stua rt Nash is going to beat him at the next
election. And what is he doing now? He is now helping Stu Nash win the seat for
Labour. That is what that member is doing. So I found that speech very interesting when
he wanted to name the Labour members who wanted to retire, forgetting that he was
doing that himself.
I actually have found it almost cringe-making to listen to John Key, Bill English, and
now Chris Tremain today crowing about how  much better New Zealand is doing than
Australia under a National Government. They did it on Budget day. Chris Tremain did
it today. Well, you know, they remind me of one of those cricket commentators we have
in New Zealand. We win one test out of  four, and suddenly we are the world
champions. The National Party members think that because for one year we have a
better record in some things than Australia, we are now doing far better than that
country.
Well, I say, before they get too cocky and ma ke us look like fools, let us have a look
at just a few facts. The unemployment rate in New Zealand, after 5 years of the National
Party, is now on a par with Australia. Th e Australian GDP per capita is around $48,000
in US dollars and New Zealand’s is 30 per cent below. That is today. The New Zealand
Government’s surplus was at 3.7 percent of GDP in 2007, and it went to a deficit of 5.1
percent in 2010, while the Australians had a surplus of 1.5 percent in 2007 and they
ended up with a deficit of 5 percent of GD P in 2010. In other words, the last Labour
Government left the National Party in a much  better state to handl e the global financial
crisis in New Zealand than any other country.
I have to say, have a look at the growth projections in the New Zealand Budget and
have a look at the growth projections in the Australian Budget. In 2015-16 the growth
projections in Australia pass New Zealand. In  2016-17 there is an even bigger projected
growth in Australia compared with New Zeal and, and in 2017-18 it is the same. I have
to say, one swallow does not make a summer, and one year when we might have beaten
Australia does not mean that we are now in a better position. I cringe when we go into
that sort of behaviour. The Aussies must be having a good old laugh over there as well.
One of the things that John Key has been sa ying about this Budget is that 12 percent
of households now pay 76 percent of all net ta x in New Zealand. Well, I need to tell the
members opposite that there is no such measure as net tax. What he is saying is totally
untrue because he ignores GST.  Forty percent of our tax take comes from GST. Who
pays most of the GST in New Zealand? Those on middle and low incomes. In fact,
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18193
those on low incomes spend almost all thei r money, and that means they pay GST on
everything that they buy.
I want to turn to the health budget and say now for some real f acts about the health
budget. Here are some truths abut what has been happening to  health funding under
Tony Ryall. I think it is now time to put as ide the political slogans that have been
posturing as a health policy and look at the impact of six Budgets under this Minister of
Health.
Did the members opposite realise, when th ey were clapping and cheering on Budget
day, that the health budget has been reduced in real terms by 2.3 percent in this Budget?
They are not my figures; they are Treasury’s own figures, and they are in the “blue
book”, if members want to go and look at them. If they take the time to read the shape
of health in the future under a National Govern ment if it is re-elected, they will see that
it does not look good at all—not my figures; Treasury’s figures. And they are not old
figures, either. They are the latest figures  and projections in the Budget document put
out by Treasury, which, we heard today fr om Mr Joyce—when he wanted to quote
Treasury—we should be listening to.
So let us have a look at what these figures  are. We have got 2.3 percent less in this
health budget—that is, in total expenditure—and we are going to have, when we look at
2015-16, 3.7 percent less. In 2016-17 it will be 3.6 percent less, and in 2017-18 it will
be 3.1 percent less in real terms.
I have to say that those figures are fr om the Budget projections in the National
Government’s own Budget. Did New Zeal anders know that? Did they know that
National has not only cut this year’s health  budget by 2.3 percent in  real terms but is
projecting a cut in the health budget out through the years? That is the truth. That truth
needs to be reported in the media. I am really  disappointed that a fact like that, which is
going to affect people’s health through th e services the Government provides—and
perhaps affect the way that people vote—is not being portrayed in the media.
Those are big cuts in health, when you c onsider that all but one Budget under Tony
Ryall has cut the health budget. We now know what is happening in health in terms of
the provision of services. Then, next year , should the National Party win, people are
going to say: “Oh my goodness! Oh, no! There’ s been a cut in health care. My, I’ve
heard that my mum can’t get an operation on her dodgy hip.”, or they will find that her
home help has been cut. Well, I have to say wake up, New Zealand. The National
Government has cut the health budget. If you vote for those members, they are going to
cut it every year in the foreseeable future.
In this Budget we did welcome the free docto rs visits for under-13-year-olds, but the
devil is in the detail. The questions I was as king today were not meant to criticise the
fact that there was free health care for under-13-year-olds. After all, after the Budgets of
the 1990s, when we had had affordable health  care and the subsidie s were taken away
by Ruth Richardson and the National Govern ment, I was the Minister of Health who
brought them back in. I am very committed to affordable primary health care. But what
this Government has not provided to our doctors is what the level is of that subsidy that
is going to be provided in order to give that service to children for free.
I have to tell you that the New Zealand Medi cal Association has said publicly that it
may have to cross-subsidise and charge adul ts more if the amount paid per child per
visit each year is insufficient. The question I would then ask is wh at impact that will
have on our old folk—those who are on a fixed income. Th ey live on the pension. They
have nothing else, and many of them are saying to us now: “Paying $45, $47, or $50 for
a doctor’s visit is already too much from our  pension.” If the asso ciation is going to
cross-subsidise for children, what is the im pact going to be on those people, who are
important people in our community?
18194 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
So it is up to the Government now to tell us  what the subsidy is that is going to be
provided. Will the $30 million per year over 3 years cover the cost? There is no doubt in
my mind that doctors are not just going to do it for free. There is no free ride here.
Somebody is going to have to pay for it.
Another feature of this Budget, as the Minister of Health said, is that there is going to
be another $100 million for elective surgery. We ll, I have to tell you that it is $100
million over 3 years—over 4 years; not 3, but over 4 years—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —$100 million over 4 years—is $25 million a year across
20 district health boards, and that is about  $1.25 million that each district health board
will receive. Do not expect to get your hip done any time soon. Then we come to public
health, which is $1.25 million per district health board each year—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: More.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —$1.25 million more—and $1.25 million will not pay for
many hips. As for public health under this Government, it has cut $16.2 million—

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —out of public health. Have a look at the figures, Anne
Tolley. Do not shake your head. That is what this Government has done, and then it has
the cheek to talk about obesity and stomach stapling.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to take a call on
this excellent Budget 2014, and what a coinci dence it is that Annette King has just
spoken about figures. She was the Minister of Health who presid ed over a doubling of
the health budget over 9 years, when there was a decrease in productivity and a decrease
in surgical operations. Under this Government , in just under 5 years there has been an
increase in surgical procedur es of 40,000 per year. It is al l very well for Mrs King to
talk about more money. Hea lth systems around the world ar e characterised by almost
infinite demand but finite resources. Mrs King would never have enough money to be
able to organise a health system properly, whereas under National over the last 5 years
we have seen huge gains in productivity a nd huge, tangible gains in immunisation and
surgical procedures; in radi ation therapy, which has become world standard; and in
public health.
But I just want to say that this Budget is a Budget worth celebrating, and from right
around the country we have heard commentators  say how excellent it has been. In the
electorate of Hunua, which I represent, just about every sector has been totally, totally
delighted by the Budget, whether it has been  the teachers, whether it has been the
farmers, whether it has been the business peopl e, or whether it has been the doctors and
the nurses. The business people of New Zealand have been very pleased by the National
Government because it has set a very clear agenda and it has kept to its promises. One
of its major objectives was to achieve a surplus, and that is indeed what it has done.
But it is quite extraordinary that Mr Park er, the finance spokesperson for the Labour
Opposition, is suggesting that Labour too would have achieved a surplus. Well, we all
know that Mr Parker and Mr Cunliffe are prisoners to the Greens and the unions—to the
Marxists and the socialists. They would spend more, they would borrow more, they
would tax more, and there is no way on eart h that they would ach ieve a surplus under
the current pressures that are facing them . The only way that the Greens and Labour
could generate a surplus would be if they were to bring out Russel Norman’s franking
machine—the money-printing machine—and away they would go. He was the
champion of quantitative easing, and what a shambles that would be.
It is a curious coincidence of biology that we  have just learnt that a little creature
called the Tasmanian devil has become an enda ngered species. But if one really thinks
about it, the Tasmanian devil would cause absolute chaos if  it was let loose in New
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18195
Zealand. In fact, I did get a de scription of it: “Its spine-chilling screeches, black colour,
and reputed bad temper, led the early European settlers to call this creature The Devil.”
But, really, the Greens and Labour are a huge  danger to the financial stability and
sustainability of New Zealand, and I am glad to report that the good people of Hunua
absolutely recognise that fact.
The doctors and the nurses around New Z ealand are very much welcoming this
Budget. Free access, or taxpayer-funded access—there is no such thing as free access—
for children is the best way to get early treatment and avoid hospitalisation. We have
people like Dr Nikki Turner fr om the Child Poverty Action Group, who is also head of
the Immunisation Advisory Centre and has been campaigning for this for years, and she
is delighted that the National Government  has delivered. We have got people like
Professor Innes Asher, a very distinguished  academic from Starship, who has written
many papers on the fact that if  children can be treated earl y for skin infections, often
they can afford lifesaving treatment, whic h goes on for months, for very, very serious
skin infections. This is a win-win. This is a win for the children and a win for the scarce
health dollar.
The farmers in Hunua have welcomed this Budget. They have welcomed it because
the taxation base is broad and reasonably lo w. Hopefully, it may go down even less, but
the clear signal is reward for effort. Inflation is 1.6 percent, economic growth is destined
to rise above 3.5 percent, and interest rates remain  relatively low. Th ere is significant
investment going into innovation and scie nce in the agricultural sector, and,
furthermore, there is an investment of  $40 million more into irrigation and water
storage. I must say that up in the area that I live in, in Hunua, the drought this year has
been worse than the drought last year, and yet we have the Labour Party and the Greens
opposed to more irrigation and opposed to water storage at a time when it is absolutely
crucial for the backbone of our economy—the farmers, the horticulturalists—to ensure
that they do have access to water.
The teachers in Hunua are also extremely pleased because they have seen an
investment of a further $858 million over 4 years, making a total of $10.1 billion, in
early childhood, primary, and secondary educati on. Indeed, there will always be people
like Annette King wanting more. But of particular interest to me and, I would say, the
Health Committee is taking an investment approach in the very early years to allow
children the maximum chance to achieve their fu ll potential, but also expecting them to
exercise individual responsibility as adults. It  was great to hear that there is a further
$155 million for early childhood education, which brings the total in New Zealand to
$1.5 billion on early childhood ed ucation. That is someth ing we would never have
dreamt of 10 years ago, but it will allow something like 98 percent of all children to be
able to receive that early childhood education.
There is no doubt that very early investment pays off, and the Health Committee has
indeed shown that in its latest inquiry, a nd that has been  backed up by international
experts such as the winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences Professor
James Heckman, who has shown beyond doubt that front-loading pays off hugely
compared with investment later on in li fe. There is no doubt that this National
Government, having put in place the Childre n’s Action Plan, the Vulnerable Children
Bill, and the newborn legislation—they are all part of the investment approach. The
$500 million package for families and children is far superior to the scattergun,
undirected half a billion dollar announcement that Mr Cunliffe made at the beginning of
the year. Much of that would have been  wasted. Personally, I would challenge any
Government anywhere in the world to keep focusing on the investment approach in the
