very early years, whether that  be through gold-standard serv ices in reproductive health,
education, maternity, or postnatal care, or in the area of nutrition.
18196 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
There was another great announcement by the Minister of Finance, which was that
the healthy New Zealand package to concen trate on exercise and good nutrition will be
rolled out around New Zealand. This 2014-15 B udget can only be described as a little
beaut.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker. Kia ora t ātou e te Whare. These are historic  times to be speaking to the 2014
Budget as a strong and independent M āori voice in the Parliame nt of this land. In 2
days’ time we celebrate 10 years to the da y since over 200 people gathered at Hoani
Waititi Marae in Auckland. At that time, representatives from Te Tai Tokerau, Ng āti
Whātua, T āmaki-makau-rau, Tainui, Raukawa, Wa iariki, Te Arawa in my area,
Mātaatua and Ngati Porou, Ng āti Kahungunu, Te Ātiawa, Ng āti Apa, Whanganui,
Raukawa ki te Tonga, and the New Zealand Māori Council journeyed across the country
to attend a hui to discuss the need for an independent M āori political voice. It was that
hui that mobilised over 200 M āori leaders to build on the momentum gained from the
hīkoi opposing Labour’s Foreshore and Seabed  Act 2004. This hui unanimously agreed
that the people are ready to act collectively to bring to the fore M āori interests of value
to all New Zealanders.
So began the journey of the Māori Party, a journey that has taken us through a 3-year
term in Opposition and two subsequent term s in a relationship with the Government.
Today I read a release from the La bour Party that talked about the M āori Party gains in
this year’s Budget, and it described them as being mere crumbs on the table—crumbs
on the table. If the $100 million of new money for M āori development that we achieved
in Budget 2014 was crumbs, then the money received in times of surplus when Labour
was in Government equates to a mere th ird of a crumb—a third of a crumb. I am
thinking of the days of plent y, in 2007, when, theoretically, M āori should have been at
the very best we have ever seen. Times we re good. In that memorable year, Dr Michael
Cullen announced a mere $35.6 million committed not just to M āori but also to Treaty-
related initiatives—$35 million. I say it was memorable because, of course, 2007 was
the year that Labour chose to vote against the United Nations Declaration on the Rights
of Indigenous People, citing opposition particul arly to article 3—t he right to self-
determination. That happened on 13 September.
One month later in the same year, 2007, on 15 October, more than 300 police carried
out the dawn raids on a dozen houses all ove r Aotearoa in response to what they
described as terrorist threats from the indige nous activists. So, yes, in the context of the
Tūhoe raids and the rejection of the Declar ation on the Rights of Indigenous People, I
guess that even a third of a crumb is memo rable. Comparing the two, then, we see $35
million in 2007 for Māori and the Treaty, as opposed to $100 million of new money this
year for the M āori Party initiatives. That  is how it stacks up. But, listen, there is a bit
more: $35 million in 2007 compared with $300 m illion across a whole range of votes in
2014—of both new votes and reprioritised f unding, which have tangible benefits for
whānau, hapū, and iwi. That is just a little bit over 10 percent of a crumb—10 percent of
a crumb.
That year was, if you like, a perfect st orm. There was a rare combination of
circumstances that came together to convince iwi M āori that the time had come for a
new direction. That direction came some  12 months later with the relationship
formalised between the M āori Party and the Government to form a coalition of the
willing to negotiate a more successful future  for all to enjoy. Budget 2014 reveals that
the Māori Party has pushed this Government hard on a number of matters, including a
commitment to establish the $30 million M āori Information and Communications
Development Fund in 2014-15, the establishment of a $5 million Te Mana o Te Wai
Fund, and the establishment of a centre of  research excellence for the funding of
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18197
mātauranga M āori research. We recognise the re levance and eff ectiveness of Wh ānau
Ora as a lead social and economic  transformation approach for M āori, Pasifika peoples,
and other New Zealanders, through the ongoing funding committed to Wh ānau Ora, the
work of three new commissioning agencies, and the establishment of a Treaty-based
partnership group comprising senior Minist ers and iwi leaders, to provide joint
direction, oversight, and promotion of Whānau Ora.
I will go on. We are following up on the recommendations of Te Paepae Motuhake—
the name of that report was Te Reo Mauriora—through to the Māori Language Strategy
and the proposed amendments to the M āori Language Act, which the Hon Dr Pita
Sharples hopes to introduce into this House pr ior to the House lifting for the 2014
election. I note the aim to secure funding to  invest in three economic development
initiatives that will address some of the outcomes sought in the M āori Economic

items.speaker: Development Strategy and Action Plan
items.text: He Kai Kei Āku Ringa. There is funding
secured for Māori radio and Te Māngai Pāho for iwi Māori economic development, and
$16 million for the M āori housing fund, to support the repairs and rebuilds of rural
houses and developing M āori social housing providers. There is $90 million to provide
free general practitioner visits and free prescriptions for all of our tamariki up to age 13.
And, most important and most ex citing of all, the Moving the M āori Nation national
fund is about investing in capacity-buildi ng and development and support for sporting
and cultural excellence. That is just a start.
Do we believe in the collec tive rights of indigenous pe ople? Well, hell yeah—hell
yeah. What is even more exciting about the 2014 Budget is that it shows the maturing of
the relationship between the Crown and iwi—a relationship that has been evident
through iwi leaders now being able to be  intimately associated with the policy
development process right across key portfolio s of the Government. We are particularly
proud of the Budget’s $5 million fund in respect  of the package to support children and
families as the absolute foundation of our na tion. That is what having influence is all
about.
If I can, in the last few minutes that are av ailable to me to talk  about the Budget, I
would like to just angle a little  bit of discussion across to one who is leaving the House
today, Mr Shane Jones. Te uri o roto o Te Aupōuri, Ngāi Takoto, Tararā anō hoki, tae rā
nō ki tana taha Wēra. Ko tētahi mea kāore i tino pai ki a au, ko te wero o te Māori nā i a
au, otir ā, te P āti M āori i ng ā tau kua hipa ake, noho kawa nei t ērā āhuatanga ki a au
ēngari, koinei te āhuatanga o t ēnei mea o te t ōrangapū. Wero atu, wero mai, tohe atu,
tohe mai, ka nui te mihi ki a ia. E mihi atu ana ki a ia i te mea, ka puta ia i te kuaha o te
Whare Pāremata i te r ā nei, koia t ērā. Mēnā kei te whakarongo a ia, ka nui te mihi ki a
ia. Koia tēnei i hara mai nā runga i te āhuatanga o te kāhui o te hunga i haere ki Te Kura
o Tīpene. Ko Mahara Okeroa t ērā, ko Hone Harawira t ērā, ko ahau, ko ētahi atu i hara
mai nō tērā o ngā kura. Ka mihi ki a ia m ō te āhuatanga o tana wer o, tana whakatakoto
kōrero ki roto i tēnei o ngā Whare Pāremata.
Ēhara i te mea, i rata tonu atu au ki āna k ōrero katoa ēngari, i puta n ā runga i te
āhuatanga ki t āna i kite ai, ki t āna i rongo nei, e kore taea te karo i t ērā āhuatanga. Ko
tōna ng ākau te mea i whakaputaina i roto i t ēnei Whare P āremata. He ng ākau M āori,
ēhara i te mea i rata mai Te Ao M āori ki a ia. Āe, he wā i hapa, he w ā i hē ēngari, ā, ko
tātau te tangata tērā. Ko ētahi, ē, arā noa atu ngā hē ēngari, i tōna mutunga mai, ko t āna
kawe i āna kōrero i roto i t ēnei Whare P āremata, i ētahi wā, ka āhua kawa tonu ki tana
taha, ki te Reipa.
Ā, kua kitea mai ai e ia i tētahi huarahi hei whāinga. Nō reira, e kore mutu wāku mihi
ki a ia, i a ia e puta nei i t ēnei Whare P āremata ahakoa, taku kore rata atu ki ētahi o
wana kōrero, he āhua kawa nei ki a au ēngari, koia t ērā i whakaputaina i runga i t āna i
kite ai, i t āna i whakapono ai, ā, otirā, o t ōna ngākau. Nō reira, k āti ake, ko ēnei ētahi
18198 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
paku kupu ki a koe, e te hoa, te hoa o Te Kura o T īpene, otir ā, te hoa o te Whare
Pāremata.
I t ōna mutunga ahakoa, ko koe t ērā, i t ērā taha, ko au ki t ēnei taha. He M āori an ō
hoki tāua i roto i t ēnei Whare P āremata. Me puta, m ā te w āhi ngaro koe e manaaki, e
tiaki i runga i t ō huarahi h ōu. Haere me ng ā manaakitanga o te w āhi ngaro. T ēnā
koutou, kia ora tātau katoa.
[I acknowledge the member of Te Aup ōuri, Ng āi Takoto, Dalmatian, and Welsh
descent. One thing I do not particularly like is that M āori person challenging me and
the M āori Party in years past; it is a situation I do not like but that is the nature of
politics. There are challenges and debates, and so I salute the member. I pay a tribute
to the member because he will be exiting through the doors of Parliament. If he is
listening, then I salute him. He was here al ongside other former students of St Stephens
School, such as Mahara Okeroa, Hone Harawira, me, and others. I congratulate him on
the way in which he presented his arguments in the House of Parliament.
I did not agree with everything he said, but it was based on what he saw and heard,
and who could argue against that. His spirit was expressed in Parliament. He has a
Māori spirit, even though M āoridom has not always liked hi m. Yes, he made mistakes
and was in the wrong but we are all human. Others have made many mistakes, but,
ultimately, his comments put him offside with the Labour Party.
He has discovered other pathways to  pursue, and so I offer my endless
congratulations to him as he departs from  Parliament. I did not agree with everything
he said, but it was based on his perspective and what he believed in his heart.
Therefore, these are short sentiments expre ssed to you, my frie nd from St Stephens
School, and, indeed, my friend in Parliament.
At the end of the day and although we are on opposite sides, we remain M āori in this
House of Parliament. Exit, and the unseen pl ace will care and protect you on your new
path. Farewell with the blessings of the pl ace unseen. Salutations to you collectively
and thank you all.]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call—5 minutes, Chris Auchinvole.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker, I will seek your
indulgence and perhaps get a bell at 4 minutes?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you. It is my great pleasure to speak in the Budget
debate 2014. We all listened very keenly to the Budget speech given by the Hon Bill
English. We have read Budget 2014 at a glance, and the numerous very positive media
reports about this ambitious, robust, yet quie tly confident Budget, carrying the stamp of
integrity of a Southland farmer. But to be  an effective politic ian, it is not enough to
simply listen to the sound of one’s own voice or, indeed, the voice of one’s leaders, to
read the good publicity, and to  pat ourselves on the back. No, we leave that to the
members on the other side, who stay in their own silos, not wishing, and not being quite
brave enough yet, to venture out of their little coffee clutches.
What we did over on this side of the Hous e is we went and asked the West Coast
community and the West Coast - Tasman area what they had taken from Budget 2014
and what was important to them. I spent last weekend going to places like Blackball and
going to the more remote parts of the West Co ast electorate, and this is what they said.

items.speaker: They said that the Budget was
items.text: “Steady as we go—a reliable set of hands on the
economy.”, “Ready to head into the next cy cle of economic growth, with an emphasis
on health, education, law and order.”, and “Good for young people, and great to have
such a commitment to broadband.” My colleag ues in the same corridor as me, Paul
Goldsmith and Paul Foster-Bell, would have varied ways of expressing the same thing,
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18199
with a different degree, perhaps, of el oquence of vocabulary,  but basically the
fundamental truths are there.
Let us look at some of thos e items as they have particular relevance to the Coast,
such as the recent redevelopment of Grey Base Hospital. Two weeks ago Minister Ryall
announced the business case for the new $67 million hospital bed facility in Greymouth.
It is currently in the final design phase, wh ere virtually the whole hospital will be new.
This is the biggest investment per he ad—the biggest investment per head—of
population in New Zealand’s history in health, and the Government is committed to
futureproofing the health serv ices on the West Coast. Let us look at some of the
facilities that are going to be made availabl e. There will be a bigger maternity unit than
currently exists, a new emergency department , a new intensive care unit, three state-of-
the-art operating theatres, and an integrated family health centre on the Greymouth
Public Hospital site, and we know how well thos e integrated family healthcare facilities
are working, because of our experience up in  Golden Bay. This is the highest health
spend ever, per head of population, and it includes a boost for cancer services and
elective surgery.
The Budget contains many other things that  are popular with the Coast people. The
social housing boost is also specifically good for the Tasman region. There is $30
million to help the community housing sector to provide more homes for high-needs
families. It is a family-friendly Budget.
Paid parental leave is under discussion and is going to be  lifted. I recognise that my
colleagues on the other side—because we disc ussed this at considerable length at the
select committee—wished to go further. My que stion to them now is which bits of this
package would Labour not want to do or woul d want to cut out. Would Labour want to
cut out the free doctors visits for children up to the age of 13? Would it want to cut the
paid parental leave extension that we are pr oviding? Would it want to reduce any of the
many aspects of this Budget that are doing so much to help families? I think not—I
think not. What we are doing is what Labour would normally do if it were being true to
its own measures.
This is a powerful Budget. I described it initially as having the drive and thrust of an
effective farmer. Over the past 9 years we have had droughts, financial deficits, and
natural and industrial disasters.  But with strategic choices, just as much pruning as was
bearable, and targeted policies—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. His time has expired.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: It is a great pleasure to share the spotlight with my
colleague to my left, Chris Auchinvole, who is such an articulate speaker, but I seem to
have taken 5 minutes off his time. I think th at is a reflection of my very caring whip,
who realised that I had suffered the flu and be en sick in bed for a little while, so he
thought he would be gentle with me. But I would have actually liked the full 10
minutes, because this is such a fantastic Budget and we have lots and lots to talk about.
As an adult who had been sick and who should really have gone to the doctor but
who had been relying on the traditional herb al medicine that my mother concocted, I
reflected back to when I was a young parent , a new parent. When my child was sick, I
was desperate to get to the doctor to make sure that my son was OK, even though it was
just a cold. As a young parent you worry about that. I reflect on the Budget that we have
delivered this year for families. There is $90 million in this year’s Budget to enable
general practitioners to offer free doctors vis its and prescriptions fr om 1 July next year
for children under the age of 13. What a fantastic thing we are doing for the families and
the young people and those people who are in need in this country. Budget 2014 is a
fantastically solid Budget. New Zealand is heading in the right direction with
18200 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
confidence. Over this past 6 years Nati onal’s good management of the economy has
meant that our books are back in surplus. Growth is at 4 percent. Wages are rising faster
than inflation and there is more money for families and businesses and for the most
vulnerable people.
If we can go back, let us have a look at  what we got back in 2008. In 2008 this
country was in a recession. It is now growing at about 4 percent—a fantastic record. In
Labour’s last 5 years there was a 50 per cent increase in  Government spending, which
helped push mortgage interest rates to almost 11 percent and crippled the internationally
competitive part of the economy. People co mplained about 11 percent, but if I
remember back to when I first bought a house , I think I paid about  20 percent for my
first house. People think the 6 percent we curr ently pay now is very expensive and very
high. National has got Government spending und er control and mortga ge interest rates
have come down.
Food prices went up 10.9 percent in the last year under Labour. They have gone up
only 1.5 percent under National. House prices went up 96 per cent over the 9 years that
Labour had the Treasury benches—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: —96 percent—and they have gone  up only 28 percent under this
National Government. People say that electricity pr ices are very high. Well, let me tell
you that under Labour they went up 72 percent—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: —72 percent, Mr Auchinvole—and under National they have gone
up only 20 percent.
This Government is committed to protecti ng children from abuse and neglect. We
have had a terrible record of that and I have spoken about that with previous bills in this
House. I have talked about the 22,000 cases of abuse and negl ect of our children a year.
More than 50 children have died in the past 5 years, which is an appalling statistic in
this country. I am very proud of the Vuln erable Children Bill, which is before the
House, and as chair of the Social Servi ces Committee I am pleased to see that the
operating funding for 2014-15 is going to be strengthened with $33.2 million. There is
$3.2 million for the implementation of the bi ll, making five Government departments
accountable for protecting and improving the lives of vulnerable children.
This National Government is delivering on the promises we make. We are growing
this country. We are making sure that thos e children, the most vulnerable children, are
getting a fair deal in this country. The Children’s Action Plan is well under way and the
new funding will see a further eight Child ren’s Teams being set up throughout the
country over the next financial year. We cu rrently have one in Rotorua and the other
one is in Whangarei. Through the new funding of $13.7 million for Child, Youth and
Family we want to make a difference to young people’s lives so that they do not have to
become a statistic, so that they do not have to end up on welfare, and so that we do not
have a generation of children who are depend ent on welfare. This is a great Budget and
I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā
koutou e ng ā rangatira huri rauna i t ō t ātou Whare. T ēnā koutou, t ēnā t ātou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings to y ou collectively the leaders throughout our
House. Acknowledgments to you and to us all.]
This Budget is a mockery. It is a mocker y of decency and common sense. It lacks
aroha, it lacks wairua, and it has no mana—no ma na at all. It is a Budget that has no
love for the citizenry of Aotearoa. It lack s compassion. I will give you an example. The
one commendable part of the Budget is th e free general practicio ner visits for our
tamariki from ages 7 to 13. It is gr eat on the face of it, but as for the wh ānau around the
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18201
motu, if their kids are sick right now, will th ey be able to take advantage of that? No.
Will they be able to take advantage of that next month? No. Will they be able to take
advantage of that in June, a year from now ? No. They are going to have to wait until
July 2015 before they can take their sick tamariki to the doctor.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I thought it was in this Budget.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: That is right, and the Governme nt put it in this Budget. This
is a “fudge-it Budget”, as we have said. We have heard about the Government shuffling
the figures, shifting things around, relabelli ng money. We have h eard from Te Ururoa
talking about this great big p ūtea that is coming to M āori. Look, I do feel aroha for Te
Ururoa, because he was very selective in this 10-year history of the M āori Party. He
failed to capture two very important even ts. The first was the walk-out from our
whanaunga Hone in the creation of the Mana  party. That was a very, very significant
event in the history of the party. But also he failed to mention the mountain of a man
from the south who actually took out the seat of Te Tai Tonga. Ēhara te Maunga Aoraki
i te maunga nekeneke. [ The mountain of Aoraki is not exactly one that moves about. ]
This mountain is not going to be moved. He was very selective—very, very selective—
in that history.
But getting back to this  Budget, we have the k ōrero, the famous proverb, of our
people: He aha te mea nui o te ao? He tangata , he tangata, he tangata. It is about people.
But if you look at the impact of this Governme nt and its policies ove r the past 6 years,
the situation for all our people is ge tting worse, and, in particular, for M āori. I want to
focus on inequality, because inequality in this  country at this time is getting worse. Let
us just roll by all of the ma in indicators and all the so cio-economic indicators. Our
people want a good job, they wa nt a secure job, and they wa nt to be able to work a
decent day’s mahi to be able to support their wh ānau, look after their kids, and get them
educated. It is not much that our people want.
But what do we see? M āori unemployment under this Government has grown from
8.6 percent in 2008 to 13.2 percent today. That is  an enormous increase. We have been
into double figures for the past 5 years. Is  that the great achi evement that the M āori
Party is so excited about and is celebrati ng, wanting to let the whole world know that
they have got so much p ūtea? There is 13.2 percent unemployment. That is an
indictment. And what does that mean? That means that M āori wh ānau, many of them
out there, have still got no j obs and are still struggling to ma ke ends meet. What is even
worse is that the M āori youth unemployment rate is far too high, as 21.9 percent—you
could say 22 percent—of our rangatahi are not in employment, e ducation, or training.
This is all happening under this Governme nt. We remember back to 2008-09, the Job
Summit, and the urgency that was applied to the M āori Job Summit. I was at that
summit, and the pressing urgency there was in terms of how we could save M āori jobs.

items.speaker: The proof is there
items.text: double-digit unemployment for the past 6 years. That is the record of
this Government.
I would like to move on to homeownership. That is a big moemoe ā for many
whānau. They want to be able to work hard to get that whare, get a house where they
run around, have their parties, and have their kids grow up. That is a distant dream for
many M āori wh ānau. If we look at the M āori homeownership rates, 28.2 percent of
Māori own or have an interest in their own home. If we flip that over, that means that 72
percent of all M āori around the motu do not own their own home. They either rent or
are staying with their own wh ānau to try to get by. Sevent y-two percent of our people
do not have the ability or the means to be able to get into  their own homes. We know
that the policies that have been applied in terms of loan-to-value ratios and other things
are making that aspiration even harder to get to. So homeownership is a complete
disaster.
18202 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
I want to move on to incomes. New Zeal anders are not earni ng enough, particularly
Māori. People around the motu will know that just under half of all Kiwis—just under
half of all Kiwis—have had no wage increase over the past year. They are actually
going backwards. By the time you factor in infl ation and the rise in the cost of various
necessities, they are actually worse off. So that is, again, an indictment. We have too
many young people in low-paid positions a nd in insecure work, and too many young
people who are graduating with no decent jobs to go on to.
We hear about this great ro ck star economy that we have . Sure, I am very proud that
when I go around the South Island, there are lots of great things happening if you go
into districts like Ashburton, Gore, and Mata ura. I was in my electorate office in
Invercargill the other day and the amba ssador for the Philippines was there. The
ambassador for the Philippines had travelled al l the way down to Invercargill to process
all of the visa documentation for the Filipi no community. It was great to see so many
whānau there, and I am sure they are making a wonderful contribution to those regions,
as they are in other districts around the South Island. But it got me to think why it is that
we are having to bring in so many wh ānau to do jobs when there is so much
unemployment here in our own country. The reason is that employers can get away with
it. They can get away with paying peanut rates for immigrant workers. They can get
away with just changing any terms and conditions at will. They can get away with those
things because this Government has allowed that to happen because it is looking after
its base, which is the farmers, the rural s ector. We know it has al ways been that way,
but there will be a change, and that is why we need a change in Government.
I know that Labour has the solutions. We do have the solutions. I do not like being
overly negative, but I do need to correct some things when they are raised in this House.
Labour does have a range of solutions. We  have our economic upgrade package. I
would line up David Parker and David Cunliffe  any day against any of the front bench
of the National Government . We have got the best policy—well-thought-through and
very responsible—and very prudent economic managers. We will implement that policy
when we get into office.
I just want to conclude by mentioning a sp eech that the Hon Dr Pita Sharples gave
last night, when he was speaking on the Budge t. Mr Sharples referred to some obscure
article that was written that gave the analogy that the M āori Party was the Road Runner
in stealth mode—that it was somehow quick, nimble, and able  to do great things. There
was an analogy to that cartoon.  There is only one animal in  stealth mode in the Road
Runner cartoon, and we all know who that is. That is Wile E. Coyote. We all know what
happens to him. He gets run over by a 10- tonne Tory National boulder. That is what
happens to Wile E. Coyote. On every s how he gets run over, mowed down, by the
National freight train. That is what has happened to the M āori Party, and that is what
this Government has done. This  is an atrocious Budget. I am looking forward to 20
September, when there will be hope, renewal, and a change of Government, and we will
be in power. Kia ora nō tātou.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Mr Speaker, might I
say just how honoured I am that you are in the Chair for my contribution to the debate
on this fantastic Budget. I see th at the gallery is full. That is great. We have got ex-MPs
here in the House who have all come along to hear my speech. I hope they stay for
Shane Jones. I hope they actually stick ar ound, because there is another show on the
road shortly. That is lovely. Shane Jones, I feel like I am, I do not know, the entrée
before the main, the soup before the steak  and chips, you know. Ye s, I am the little
entrée that sort of warms the crowd up fo r you, Shane Jones. I hope that you are getting
ready for your valedictory statement. Can I just say, because I do have the opportunity
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18203
to speak just before you, that, actually, you w ill genuinely be missed. It is a sad day for
some of us who have enjoyed you. But I get to talk about the Budget.
I am delighted that there might be a fe w more people who are listening in than
normally would. They get to hear about the fantastic work that we are doing for families
and for children in this Budget.  The list is long. I get to go  for a good few minutes here
to talk about just how great it is and the extent to which we have gone. The one thing I
think has not been picked up as much as it c ould have been is that more than $1 billion
in savings, if you like, have been made tha nks to a lower welfare spend than what was
projected in 2010. Shall we run through that again? More th an $1 billion—the forecast
is lower than what it was in 2010, and that is certainly due to an economy that is picking
up, but equally due to our welfare reforms. One hundred million dollars has gone into
the welfare reforms in this Budget. That will be $25 million a year over the next 4 years,
and you can already see the kinds of returns we get from that. In the last 12 months
alone since we introduced the reforms, the sa vings in the benefit spend have been about
$530 million. So it is absolutely significant. That support and spending on people earlier
are what make the biggest difference.
I am proud of this Budget. I am absolutely proud of the work that Bill English has
done, and I can tell you  that there has been many a nigh t when we have debated very
long into the night on what this Budget w ould look like and how we would respond to
some of the needs of families and children. Th e reality is that I loved that we were
debating the stuff that matters—the  stuff that really counts. Th e reality is that with data
analytics like those we have  now, not only do we hold more information on the most
vulnerable children and young people in this coun try than we ever have before but we
have access to it. That means we can target our funding to the children and families that
need it most. Unlike Labour, which would lik e to scatter the mone y across every child,
and the Greens, who would like to throw a b it to everyone, even those who do not need
it, and hope that it might actua lly hit those who are most vul nerable in this country, we
have gotten smarter, better, and far more sophisticated in how we target the most
vulnerable New Zealanders and get support to them earlier. For me, the significant
amount of $33 million in this Budget is to do exactly that.
One of the best examples I can give of data analytics and the difference it makes is
the changes we have made for teen parents. We have had a reduction in the number of
teen parents by 39 percent over the last 4 years. To give you the actual numbers, in 2008
there were 5,200 births to teen mums; la st year there were 3,300. We have 2,300 young
mums who are on a benefit at any one time.  We know their names and we know where
they live, and what we can do is we can wrap support around them early. What we
recognised was that the Government was not th e right place to do that. In fact, every bit
of evidence on the investment approach to ld us that keeping them away from the
Government for as long as we can will make the biggest difference. So every single one
of those young teen mums has wraparound suppor t from an adult. They now start by
having their money managed for them. Their re nt or board is paid up front. Their power
bill is paid. They get some money on a ca rd and some pocket money, but they can work
their way to independence—and can I say what an absolute difference that is making in
their lives.
If we were not targeting, if  we were not using data an alytics like we do, we would
continue to scatter and spray money around, hoping that it hits the very children and
young people who need it most. The reality is that  this Budget looks at us targeting it
even more to those who need it more. If you look into the details of the Budget, what
you will see is the money that is going into that  vulnerable children’s package. It lets us
have another eight Children’s Teams, and that  is important. We have the predictive risk
18204 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
model, which is actually controversial in itself. So whether you like it or not, we know a
lot.
We know whether a child’s parents have been  in jail, and whether the parents have
been in a State house for all of their lives. We know their benefit use. We know whether
or not there have been domestic violence incidents and whether the police visited the
week before. We know the vulnerability leve l. We know the risk factors. We know
where to put support and how to get it in earlier. The differe nce that that can make to
the harder and more complex end of what we  do is significant. Children’s Teams will
have that kind of information. They can then wrap one plan around a child with one lead
professional who can then actually follow through, and there is accountability the whole
way through, which makes the biggest difference.
I say that Labour forgets what actually happened. The reality for these kids is that if
we kept spending and if it was just about mo re money for every child, then we actually
would have seen a greater re duction in the number of abus e cases involving children in
the 2000s, when Labour was throwing money at it and scattering it around. We did not.
What we have seen for more than 10 year s is a steady increase in the number of
notifications and the number of substantiated cases of ab use and neglect. Unless we
target, unless we get in earlier and wrap support around them and know exactly what is
happening, we will continue to get the same so rts of results. This Budget steps up for
those very vulnerable young children who need us, and I am very proud of it.
The Budget also does more for Child, Youth and Family for therapeutic one-on-one
support. It ensures that, for those very hi gh-needs and complex-needs children, we are
actually able to put far more money into them. There are a few children who literally
cost us millions. There are some incredibly sad cases of young people who need 24/7,
one-on-one support—and even, in extreme cases, two-on-one support—to make sure
that they are actually safe themselves and that society is safe. So there are examples
where we have young people who literally have  a guard with them  and a therapeutic
placement person with them the whole time, and that is expensive. So we needed to step
up and make sure that we continue that and that we are actually backing the young
people who need it.
What we hear a lot, actually, is that  unemployment has gone up since National came
in. I was hearing just today that there are more Pacific people who are unemployed than
there were back when Labour was in. What the Labour members forget, of course, is
that for three consecutive quarters before  National came into Government in 2008
numbers had been going up under Labour, and it had done nothing. What they choose to
forget, of course, is that we  had a global financial crisis , which saw this Government
step up and help and support those who needed  it most at that very time. So, yes,
welfare numbers went up. Actually, in some  respects I am proud of that. That means
that we support those who need it most.
This is an outstanding Budget by a Minister  of Finance who is doing an outstanding
job. I am incredibly proud to stand up today and support it.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Can I thank all my parliamentary
colleagues for coming along to this contributio n in the Budget debate this afternoon. I
feel a little bit like the Parliamentary Rugby Team playing a curtain-raiser before an All
Blacks match. It might be a bit scrappy, but you know that it is going to be passionate. I
do want, however, of course, to note the si gnificance of today, because not only are we
going to hear from Shane Jones in his valedict ory speech but also I can say that this is
the first time this parliamentary term that Shane has arrived before time to a speech that
he is going to do in the House. I think that that is an absolutely fantastic thing.
It is my duty today to be the last speaker to talk about the Budget before we move on
to matters slightly brighter on the horizon. I think nothing highlight s the contradictions
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18205
and the mixed priorities in th is Government’s agenda than the education contribution in
this year’s Budget. Charter schools are get ting an extra $6,000 a year per student on top
of up to $40,000 a year per studen t that they are already getting, while State schools are
getting only $6,000 to $7,000 a year per student. How is that a leve l playing field? If
this Government genuinely ca red about raising student ach ievement for those students
who are not doing very well, it would not be putting money into charter schools; it
would be putting money into every State sc hool in the country. So why do we have
charter schools? Because of a dodgy cup of tea deal with a party of political ghosts—a
dodgy cup of tea deal with a party of political ghosts. It prised open the crypt and out
they popped, with the new-right playbook, and we ended up with charter schools in
New Zealand. We do not need charter schools . We need to be focused on making sure
that every school in New Zealand is a good school and every student gets the
opportunity to achieve their full potential.
While the Government is lavishing mone y on charter schools in its ideological
experiment cooked up with the party of political ghosts, schools and early childhood
education centres are barely getting enough f unding to keep up with their rising costs.
Schools are increasingly reliant on parental contributions and are not getting the funding
that they need. Bill English, who railed against the increasing costs of education to
parents when he was the Opposition’s spokesperson, has done absolutely nothing in 6
long years about that. Every ye ar the financial contribution parents make to their kids’
education has gone up under this National G overnment. Yet parents are struggling to
make ends meet, and this Government is doing nothing about that.
This Government has instead decided to pick  a war, pick a fight, with every teacher
in the country. Over the last few weeks we have sat in the Education and Science
Committee and listened to submitter after submitter after submitter say that this
Government does not value them, does not respect them, and does not even trust them
to have a say over how their own professional body operates. I think that is absolutely
disgraceful. Has the Government been listening? No, it has not. It has not listened at all.
But there is a better way. There is a better way, and it starts with making sure that
every child in New Zealand has the best pos sible start, through pa id parental leave,
through making sure their parents can make e nds meet through the Best Start payments,
and through providing high-quality and freely accessible early childhood education to
every child in the country. Thos e should be the priorities. T hose are not the priorities of
this National Government. We should have trust and respect—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The level of noise now coming from the Chamber is
completely unacceptable. I require Mr Hipkins to have a reasonably fair go.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That is all right, Mr Spea ker—I am pleased everybody is so
excited by my contribution in the Budget de bate today. We should have trust in, and
respect for, education professionals. The best  way forward for the education system in
New Zealand is one that is based on co llaboration, not one based on a Government
saying to teachers that they are not trusted, they are not respected, and they are not even
respected enough to have cont rol over their own professi onal body. It also means that
we should pay attention to the factors outside  the school gate that have an impact on
kids when they get into school. If kids’ pa rents do not have jobs, if they do not have
adequate income, and if they are not livi ng in quality, warm, dry, affordable houses,
then that is going to have an impact on kids’ readiness to learn when they get to school.
Where did we see reference to  that in this year’s Budge t? We did not. We did not.
The Government was silent on the major issues around housing a ffordability and job
creation. The Government simply fudged it. It did not do anything about those major
issues that New Zealanders are facing. If we want to get serious about making sure that
New Zealanders have the brighter future that John Key promised them but has
18206 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
absolutely failed to deliver, we should st art with children. We should start with making
sure they get the best possible start in life.  The Labour Party is absolutely committed to
that through increasing paid pa rental leave, through making su re that children’s parents
who need the financial support can get it through the Best Start payment, and by making
sure that early childhood education is available.
This Government does not care about the qu ality of early childhood education. It has
relaxed teacher quality requirements. It has relaxed the requirements for there to be fully
registered, qualified teachers in early childhood centres. I think that is absolutely
disgraceful. If we are going to increase participation in early childhood education, we
should be making sure that it is quality pa rticipation in early childhood education. That
is not something that this G overnment is delivering on. If we  really want to lift the
status of the profession, we could start by making sure that  we attract the very best
people into the teaching profession in the fi rst place, and yet the Government has done
absolutely nothing in this year’s Budget to  make teaching a more attractive career for
the best and brightest in our schools. We should definitely be focused on doing that.
Why should somebody consider teaching as a viable career when this Government
says that teachers cannot even be trusted to  have control over their own professional
body? We would not do that to lawyers, we would not do that to accountants, and we do
not do that for doctors. We do not do that  for almost any profession. In fact, the
National Party seems to care more about real  estate agents. It mounted a filibuster
against the regulation of the real estate industry because it thought that real estate agents
should be regulating themselves, and yet it will not allow teachers to do that. The
National Party cares more about real estate agents than it does about teachers.
This Budget has ignored the fundamental issues facing the education system. Instead,
it has sloshed money around into an ideologi cal experiment like charter schools, all
because of the dodgy cup of tea deal with the political ghosts from the ACT Party.
There may be one of them left in this Par liament now, but I can tell you what. One of
them is allowed to sit on this side of Par liament, but there will not be any left in this
Parliament after the coming election. Then we can finally put an end to the crazy
madness that is the new-right ideological ex periment of charter schools. Finally, I am
the final Labour speaker to speak before Sh ane Jones gets to deliver his valedictory
speech to the House today, so I would like to  take the opportunity, Matua Shane, on
behalf of the entire Labour caucus—and I know that I speak for all of us—to say that
you have made an enormous contribution to our team. You have had a big impact on
Parliament in a whole variety of ways. We  will certainly miss you and we wish you all
the very best for the future.
Debate interrupted.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, in accordance with a determination of the
Business Committee, I call on the Hon Shane Jones to make his valedictory speech.
Could I start by pointing out to the member that  I arrived at 5 o’clock to make sure that
I got a seat for this important event.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: He Reo M āori i te tuatahi. H ūtia te rito o te
harakeke, kei hea te kōmako, e kō? Māhau e ui mai ki a au, he aha kē te mea nui o te ao,
māku e k ī atu, he tangata, he tangata, he tangata. K āti, t ātou e Te Whare e hui nei, a
koutou kua whakamine mai nei ki te whakah ōnore i ahau i t ēnei rangi whakamutunga
ōku, tēnā koutou e ōku piri, tēnā koutou e ōku tūāhine, tēnā koutou e ōku tūākana. Tēnei
ahau te t ū i te aroaro ō tātou ngā kaitōrangapū, me te aroaro o te iti  me te rahi kua tat ū
iho ki konei.
21 May 2014 Valedictory Statements 18207
Kotahi anake te tangata m ō te āhuatanga ki te hunga kua whet ūrangitia, hei mihinga
māku, ko te toa o Hikurangi Maunga, a Parekura Horomia. Kia mihi atu ahau ki a
Parekura i mate i roto i te tau kotahi ka pahemo tata ake nei me ng ā rau mahara e iri nei
i te w ā pātū o tēnei Whare. R ātou ki a r ātou, tātou ki a t ātou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou,
tēnā tātou katoa.
[I will speak in M āori first. Pull out the centre shoot of the flax, where will the
bellbird sing, lass? You can ask me what is the most important thing in the world and I
will respond it is people, it is people, and it is people.  Well, to us assembled here in the
House, you who have gathered here to honour me on this final day for me, my close
ones, thank you my respected sister colle agues and elder statesmen. I stand before us
all fellow politicians and before the meek and the mighty that have arrived here.
In respect of those who have passed away, there one in particular whom I single out
and pay a tribute to. It is the champion of the mountain Hikurangi, Parekura Horomia.
I salute Parekura who died  recently, a year ago, and the many memorial tributes
adoring the walls of this House. Allow them to rest there among their own while we the
living remain here among our own, so gr eetings, acknowledgements and salutations to
us all.]
It is an emotional day. I have been on a media blackout. It has been akin to someone
suffering a bad experience after the recentl y outlawed synthetic drug episode. I have
lived, breathed, and I have put every bit of  my being whilst I was a politician—putting
myself either willingly or unwillingly—i n front of our people. The whakatauk ī, the
Māori proverb, I start this speech with is “He tangata, he tangata, he tangata.”—people.
It is with humility and honour that I stand in  the midst of my peers, under the gaze of
the public, people from business, people fr om the community, people from the north—
the last frontier of rugged individualism—and friend and foe. I mention that particular
expression because I see that Roger Douglas and Richard Prebble are in the House.
The notion that the people who should come to see me at my valedictory are Willie
Jackson, John Tamihere, Mr Prebble, Mr Douglas, and Ron Mark is a comment,
perhaps, on the nature of my politics as a me mber of this side of the House. There is
Willie Jackson, the M āori equivalent of Pam Corkery;  John Tamihere, Labour’s No. 1
exile; and the two gentlemen w ho belong to that generation of Labour politicians back
in the day. They are part of the legacy of the party that I belong to, that group of
reformers, including Sir Geoffrey Palmer  and including Mike Moore, and including
David Lange, who, in my time as a young man, was a hero in the political world.
After those reformists came Dr Michael Cullen, the godfather of the Labour Party,
and Helen Clark, the woman who, after a m eeting in Charles Waldegrave’s house with
Mike Williams, enticed me into politics. They honoured me with the opportunity to
enjoy the privilege of 9 years in this, the hi ghest marae, the highest  court, of the land.
And for that I owe those two individuals an inordinate debt of gratitude.
I thought that before I share some observat ions about some of my colleagues and the
ebb and flow of politics, I would talk a little  as to where I came from. I was born in a
little area near Kait āia, Awanui. My dad was one of 17. My dad’s mother was born in
1893. She visited upon me, along with my mother  and father, an enormous amount of
love and affection for the M āori language and respect for the Anglican Church—sorry,
Mum, I did not always hold up that part of th e bargain. I say that because they sent me
to St Stephen’s School, where I was for 5 y ears. I often think of the small group of
ladies from Mahurangi and Warkworth who sa ved their pennies to send a lad from the
gumfields of the north to St Stephen’s School.
I want to acknowledge the other boys from  St Stephen’s School who are in this
House today. Te Ururoa Flavell was my head  prefect. Hone Harawira and I come from
the same tribe. Our padre was Harry Taylor . I was the altar boy and Hone nicked the
18208 Valedictory Statements 21 May 2014
cross. The boys from St Stephen’s will be glad that one of their own has enjoyed 9 years
here, and to the end was himself—was his own man.
Beyond that I went to university, and I wa nt to acknowledge five people, Margaret
Clark, Rod Alley, Raj Vasil, and Dame Joan Metge, as well as Stephen Levine. They
were at Victoria University and took a great deal of interest in my time at university.
Then I went into activism. It may come as a surprise to members on the other side of
the House that at one time I too, along with Hone Harawira, was a proud activist. But it
is a rite of passage to be a M āori politician in the north a nd to have a burst of that
activism. In 1975 Winston Peters was leader of the Ng āti Wai Land Retention
Committee with Dame Whina Cooper. Dover Samuels was seeking to secure the land
and the Cavalli Islands, etc. He was a ma n who made a tremendous degree of progress
that, unfortunately, was not seen by his own hap ū. And that is often the way when you
pave the way. Of course, there was Hone  at the Waitangi Action Committee and me,
along with him, in the Kawariki group.
After that I went to a meeting where Geoffr ey Palmer was present, to deal with the
New Zealand Bill of Rights, in 1985—wheth er the Bill of Rights should contain a
provision to recognise the Treaty of Waitangi. I stood and argued against that. I said that
the Bill of Rights should not subsume the Treaty of Waitangi.
Geoffrey Palmer then enabled me to get a job where I followed Hekia Parata as the
director of the M āori secretariat in the Ministry for the Environment. That is when I
began working for Sir Geoffrey Palmer, who said to me: “Jones, Jones, read Liddell
Hart.” I went and consulted Liddell Hart. It is a book on th e history of the First World
War, where the members of the battalion ar e being gassed by their own troops, they are
being strafed by their own planes, they are being shot upon as a consequence of friendly
fire—adequate preparation for Labour Party po litics. His parting remark to me was:
“Jones, Jones, write, write, because when you write, you think. And you write so little.”
I was supported by Sir Paul Reeves, Dame Joan Metge, and Sir Geoffrey Palmer, and
was chosen by Royce Elliott to be the 1990 Harkness Fellow and I went away to
Harvard. It was an extraordinary experi ence for a young father with a young family.
While I was there, I sported an enormous red beard. I wandered around in a black coat,
etc., and I would sit with my son and we w ould be chatting away. And there is a great
Jewish community there, Mr Prime Minist er—Brookline. They would look at me and
they would come and speak to me in what  I presumed was Yiddish; I would reply to
them in Ngāpuhi. And as they spoke to me in their language, and as I replied further and
further in Ngāpuhi, a myth emerged: the Lost Tribe.
When I came back from Harvard University—an utter privilege for a boy from the
far north to be a Harkness Fellow and to study at Harvard Univ ersity—I gained the
attention of Jim Bolger, the then Prime Mini ster, and worked on the settlement of the
Sealord deal. Hekia Parata and I advised Mr Prebble, Koro W ētere, Roger Douglas,
David Lange, and Geoffrey Palmer about the se ttlement attempts in the late 1980s. That
was when I began my journey of trying to use the currency of settlements to advance the
interests of the tangata whenua.
As a consequence of Mr Bolger having confidence and faith in me, I became a
member of the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission. I rose to th e level of chairing
Sealord, the Māori Fisheries Commission and a host of other entities, and I participated
in selling Salmond Smith Biolab and deliver ing seafood assets back to the Chatham
Islands and our Māori people. And I became a pro-industry man. I, at that point, said as
much as possible that I would be a politicia n who exhausted every part of my being to
generate wealth, generate jobs, and ensure that those prepared to take risks to actually
generate an opportunity for the rest of us should not be condemned but should be
supported.
21 May 2014 Valedictory Statements 18209
I just want to share very br iefly the first time I came to Parliament. The first time I
came to Parliament was in 1980, on the day that  Matiu Rata resigned from the Labour
Party. I was in his office with R āpini Abraham, a leader of the R ātana Church, with the
tohunga of Ng āpuhi, Joe Toki, Taupuhi Eruera, Selwyn Muru, John Tahup ārae, Sonny
Keepa, and a host of other visitors. The second time I came to Parliament was to present
a Te Reo M āori submission to Mr Austin, a form er South Island member from the
National Party, who did not turn up, and it was received by Whetu Tirik ātene-Sullivan
in 1980. Then I came back with my uncle, Rev. M āori Marsden, Nik Tangaroa, and
George Brennan, and we comprise d, in 1980, the subcommittee of M āori policy in the
Māori Affairs Committee room, with Whetu Tirik ātene-Sullivan. So let no young pup
say that Shane Jones is a stranger to the legacy of the Labour Party.
Now I move on to another role, but before  I talk about this other role, let me
acknowledge some of the things  that have happened to me as a politician. Helen Clark
rang and asked me to support Ann Hartley one  day. We went to open a playcentre, a
young kiddies’ centre, and she said: “Sha ne, have you been doing much doorknocking
in 2005?”. I said: “Ah, I’m getting used to it .” She said: “The more you do it, the more
you’ll grow to like it.” I have had 9 years a nd I like it no more today than I did then. I
was a big-picture man.
Helen Clark sent me to th at hotbed of Labour activism, Dargaville. As I dodged the
brethrens, I eventually made it to Haruru Falls.  Haruru Falls is in the Bay of Islands. It
is near Waitangi. I went to the house. I was armed with the pamphlets with Helen’s
beatific face smiling off them. I approached the door—knock, knock. Through the misty
frosted glass I saw a figure coming to the door. The door sprang open and in front of me
was a voter of my age—a woman, semi-cla d. The most troublesome thing was she had
an imposing arrangement coming out of the top of her head in the form of a beehive.
Whilst I had eagerness for the beehive—no, no, no. The most bizarre thing is that she
went on to say: “You’re a bit late, aren ’t you, mate?”. I retreated back, not quite
knowing what to say, because on our side of the House, you are prepared to say: “Hi,
we’re here to talk to you about inclusivene ss, equity, gender equal ity, and a bicultural
Aotearoa.” All I could say was: “Ah, ah, He len Clark from the Labour Party sent me
here.” She said: “Oh, don’t worry about it. Th e other MP’s already been here.” I knew
then, with scientific clarity, that John Carter had that seat for life.
Dr Cullen blessed me by enabling me to be  the chair of the Finance and Expenditure
Committee, and a number of members on that side of the House were on that committee
when I was the chair, as indeed was Hone Harawira. The first duty that I undertook of
an international character on that committee was to lead a delegation to Rarotonga to
advise them on transparency. The dele gation comprised Doug Woolerton, Murray
McCully, and Hone Harawira—a tall order. The only problem with that delegation was
that while I was there, unfortunately, I fe ll off a motorbike. Despite parliamentary
ambitions about transparency, I did everythi ng I could to hide that accident from
Heather Simpson and Helen Clark. Hone Harawira immediately reported it to New
Zealand Herald’s Ruth Berry. By the time I got back  to New Zealand, there were 25
messages from Heather Simpson and Helen Clark. If you do not believe me, I am
willing to lift the leg of my trou, but for f ear of sparking unintended consequences in
my own caucus, I will resist it.
When I was a Minister, I was a colourful but hard-working character. My colleagues
will tell you that I never agreed with Helen that we should have a shower head policy.
But when you are a member of the team and junior, as I was, you deliver the policy of
the day. As you recall, we were going to regul ate the amount of water, have a certain
covering for hot-water heaters, and, as the wate r sort of dribbled into a bucket, then you
could work out whether it was 8 minutes, 8 seconds, or whatever it was. I knew I was in
18210 Valedictory Statements 21 May 2014
a dire situation when the only person who came  to my rescue was Jeanette Fitzsimons.
In those days the Greens were my fans.
One other thing that I want to refer to wa s that while I was the Minister for Building
and Construction, I freed the building profe ssion and I freed the community and the
economy from the wretchedness of the Building Act, so that you can now build a 10 -
square metre shed without a building permit. I was not to know that the current Minister
would regard that as the housing policy for South Auckland.
You do make decisions in the broad glare of publicity and you think: “Hmm, would I
do it again?”. And I must not walk away from  what was a visceral experience in terms
of when I was the Associate Minister of Im migration. I want to ask, how come a lot of
the Chinese fellows who get to know politicians have got the name “Liu”? Kia ora,
Maurice. In my case, the media spelled the name of the man as “L-i-u”. The political
alphabet of the Labour Party sp elled his name as “L - uh, oh!”, and that is where my
political reputation ended up for a period of time.
I do not want to dwell on too much more because time does not allow it, but if I can
acknowledge to the media that  whenever I was in the gu n, I fronted up. I want to
acknowledge Annette King. Phil Goff was out of the country when John Key, in a fit of
enthusiasm, decided that all credit card rece ipts should be made available to the public.
If there was ever a motivation to get the CIA on to the Prime Minister, God knows, that
was it. Our deputy leader trusted me to go forward with one adviser, John Harvey, and
front up to that issue. It did not cover me with a great deal of glory, but please know
this: I never ever ran, and I was prepared to front up to the media, whether it was good
or bad. If I could say something to Kelvin  Davis as he comes in, because, Prime
Minister, Parliament is now dishing out credit cards—I understand they are called
purchase cards. Kelvin, know this from me: cash is king, brother—cash is king.
I should acknowledge Phil Goff, David Shearer , and my mihi to David Cunliffe. We
had our leadership contest, which was probably the most liberating thing that I
personally did as a member of the Labour Party.  I had the ability to be paid and wander
around for 6 weeks saying whatever I liked ab out whomever I liked in my own party,
and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Bu t I have to accept that there are more people coming to
my do at the Back Bencher from the Labour Party than bloody well voted for me during
that contest.
Winston Peters was a person who did stretc h his hand out and assist me when the
Auditor-General’s investigation took place. There has been a lot of idle jotting and
scribbling about me and Winston Peters, largely driven by troublemakers from the other
side of the House. Winston and I are comrades  in arms in terms of the Tai Tokerau and
coming from the north. The notion that upon that political pew two halos could be
situated would invite an unw anted comparison to a double-yolk egg. But I will tell you
what, though. Had that happened, there would have been a great c ontest in terms of
Shakespearean quotes, but I w ould never have beaten Wins ton in that quote from

items.speaker: Richard III
items.text: “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!”.
To move away from a wee bit of levit y. As my senior colleagues would know, you
have fantastic opportunities when you are a Minister to rub s houlders with power
brokers and incredibly infl uential people around the worl d. One night, Helen invited a
number of us to dine with Condoleezza Rice. We  were treated to an inordinately clever
exposition and account of where affairs of the world, in terms of the military and
economy, were. I went from there in my self-d rive car back to Ta i Tokerau, and within
8 hours I picked up a hitchhiker. So here I am  going from meeting with one of the most
powerful women in the world, I am in the car, and I pick up a hitchhiker—a young
Māori lad of a similar age to my boy. As he sat in that car and we went down the road, I
said to him in M āori “Kapia te wini he makariri  rawa.”, which means “Close the
21 May 2014 Valedictory Statements 18211
window; it is too cold.” He said: “Oh, matua,  I want to leave the window open.” I said:
“Why is that, son?”. He said: “It makes me f eel free, and I have just come out of a 3½
year lag from the Ngāwhā prison.” If there was ever an inci dent within a short period of
time that made me feel humble as a M āori parliamentarian and a junior Minister, that
was it—to go from that level of power and in fluence, and still to have the confidence to
relate to one of my own rangatahi on the other side of the tracks, so to speak.
I want to acknowledge the me dia. I know that my colleagues have regarded me as
something of a headline hussy. Well, co me on, laugh—it is not as bad as bloody
“gelding”. Give us a break! I made a decisi on that if I was not going to be a champion
doorknocker, and if I was not going to be the best pamphlet distributor, then I was going
to ensure that the ideas that I was paid to represent and pa id to broadcast were done in
such a way that we used the services of the media.
It was Ruth Berry who reported my motorbike crash. It was Claire Trevett, I think,
who isolated that somewhat colourful re mark about a de-knackerised horse, thus
drawing attention to the fact  that I had de-knackerised a major part of my potential
support in the party in the leadership race.  It was Paddy Gower who showed us, when
he gushes enthusiastically every evening, giving  us the news, that we heard it all in the
urinal that particular week. There is also Duncan Garner. But, in particular, there are the
senior people. I want to acknowledge  Audrey Young—on age, knowledge—Tracy
Watkins, John Armstrong, and Vernon Small, even if Vernon Small was the only person
in Parliament who understood the Attorney-G eneral when he was railing against the
split infinitive.
In the time left I will say th at I sat School Certificate in 1975. I was a lad of 15 years
at St Stephen’s School when my teacher wa s Tony Ross. He introduced us to what has
stayed with me—a love of literature. He intr oduced us to a taonga from our side of Te
Ao Māori, from Hone Tūwhare. The poem is:
Where are the men of mettle?
are there old scores
left to settle?
when will the canoes leap
to the stab and kick
the sea-wet flourish
of pointed paddles?
will the sun play again
to the skip of muscles
on curved backs bared
to the rain’s lash
the seas punch?
to War! to War!
That was the cry to come to battle. That was the cry to take up arms that motivated
me and my generation to fight for our language, to fight for our rights, to fight to ensure
that Māori were not only an inclus ive but an indelible  part of Aotearoa. I am proud to
have fought for the bicultural narrative th at underpins our nation State. I acknowledge
that there is enormous change happening to  our ethnic make-up, but I implore us as
parliamentarians: do not untether our waka from that essentia l narrative entered into in
the Treaty of Waitangi.
I wanted to be a champion fo r industry. I have been well supported by fisheries and
by forestry folk, and that has enabled me to bring their ideas forward.
18212 Valedictory Statements 21 May 2014
I am a firm believer in trade. I admired, as  a junior Minister, Phil Goff and the China
free-trade deal. I will totally resist any sugge stion that my country will grow richer by
turning our back upon the essential importance of international trad e. But industry has
to lead, as well. If I have been disappointe d, it is because I have felt that those in
industry are lions in the boardroom but lamb s in public. They mistakenly think that
when a void emerges, it will not be occupied by those with clay feet. They mistakenly
think that climate change, for example, is the political province of lotus-eaters. They
make that error and imperil their long-term profitability.
So although I have sought to be an advoc ate for business culture, I shed not one
doubt about taking on Countdown, because that was about respect and fairness. But that
part of my career is now over. That falls now  to my colleagues from both sides of the
House to, yes, show that we can recollect and value our past but accept that the greatest
duty we have is the responsibility to the future, and the future belongs, in a political
sense, to those whom I am leaving behind.
To my staff, Tracy Dalton in the north; Julia Buck, who has been with me since
2005; young Ben Appleton, who is soon to go on an army trip  to Malaysia; and John
and Chrissie Pānapa, I salute you. You have enabled me to do my mahi down here and
keep the home fires burning.
To my children and wh ānau who are here today, I hope this speech represents the
end of one chapter and the ope ning of a new opportunity. I ha ve with me this evening
my mother. I have with me this evening also that person whom I affectionately call my
beauty queen, Dorothy Pumipī.
Although there may be an element of aw kwardness to name people, you have to
respect those who help you pick yourself up when things do not work out. So to all of
those who have shown me love and to those who feel I may have dashed your
aspirations by not being quite the person you wanted me to be, please sing me the
waiata “Please, release me. Let me go.” I salute you. You have honoured me by turning
out today. Please come and enjoy the oysters, the clams, and the fish, etc., over at the
Back Bencher. This is me. I am out. Kia ora tātou katoa.
Waiata
Sitting suspended from 6.05 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
Debate resumed on the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The most significant part of
Budget 2014 is that we are in the black. I am wearing a black tie to mark that, because it
is hugely significant. It is great news a nd a mark of respect for John Key and Bill
English in bringing down a balanced Bu dget in such difficult circumstances—
something that is the envy of  developed countries around th e world. Let me talk about
how significant it is. I still remember, and I have brought it down to the House with me,
the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update of October 2008. This is when Labour had
control of the Treasury benches and the offi cials’ advice. Labour said—and let me list
the figures to remind the House of where we  have come from—that we would have a
decade of deficits. In fact, I checked that.

items.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: A decade—10 years—of ever-increasing deficits. For the
financial year that we are debating, Labour  said that the Government would be
spending, in 2014-15, $5 billion more than wh at it would be receiving. But it gets
worse. It said that debt would now be at $80 billion, and, even worse, it said that on a
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18213
business-as-usual basis, carrying on with La bour’s policies, by 2020 that debt would be
$130 billion. That is a Greek level of debt. That is a bankruptcy level of debt. That is the
sort of dire state that New Zealand was in in 2008.
It is not like the intervening 5 years have been easy. The global fi nancial crisis that
bit in 2009 was the biggest ec onomic downturn since the Great Depression. In fact, Bill
English has had the toughest job of any Minister of Finance, 25 of them, in terms of the
global economic circumstances, and then throw on top of that New Zealand’s worst ever
natural disaster: the earthquakes in Christch urch. Add those circumstances together and
you would say that it was a near miracle that we are in the black for 2014-15. I
acknowledge that it is a small number, $360 milli on, but what is so encouraging is that
we are going to have choices in the next 3 years, with surpluses of $1 billion, $2 billion,
and $3 billion out into future years. That is an outstanding tribute.
Just to get the numbers clear, debt today is $20 billion less than the pre-election
forecast from 2008, and in 2020, when the pr ojections would have us wallowing in
$120 billion of debt, those debt levels will be  back to 20 percent of GDP, with the New
Zealand Government’s finances better than th ose of pretty much anywhere else in the
world. That is an extraordinary achievement, for which Bill English deserves huge
credit.
Listening to contributions from members opposite, they sort of say that getting to
surplus would have been easy. Well, where have  they been for 5 years? Let us go back
to 2009 and 2010. Labour members, including Mr  Cunliffe, were demanding that there
be a greater stimulus package and that the Government borrow more and spend more. In
every single area in which this Government has done the hard yards to get us in the
black, members opposite have screamed and whined and opposed and sniped. Let us
give a little example. One of  the things where saving was done was around the issue of
night classes. Do you know what it meant in  my area? I can remember a constituent in
my area who was earning over $150,000 strongly  objecting that he was now going to
have to pay for his own Pilates classes. We ll, sorry, get a grip. Is  balancing the books
more important, or is it the Government paying for well-off people’s Pilates classes?
But it is not just there. Whether it is in  terms of conservation, whether it is foreign
affairs, whether it is defence, or whethe r it has been primary industries, across the
board, members opposite have opposed every attempt to get this country in the black,
and now they have the gall to come to this House and say that getting to surplus would
have been easy. It was not. It has been ha rd yards. If New Zealand wants to know what
it would be like with a Labour-Green G overnment, just look across the Tasman.
Australia just last week tabled a Budget with a $50 billion deficit. It is putting up taxes.
It is cutting core services. It has got enor mous difficulty on its hands as a consequence
of the very policies that members opposite advocate for New Zealand, and we say: “Not
on your nelly! Let us keep New Zealand on course and in the black.”
In this Budget are provisions, extra steps,  around the issue of affordable housing. I
was listening to the Budget debate and th ere was a contribution from a Green member.
It was so extraordinary that I have to quote it. They said this: “What has the cost of
building materials got to do with affordable housing?”. I am sorry but I am one of those
practical engineering types. I have got news for the Greens. Houses are made of things
like wood and concrete and plasterboard. If  they are expensive,  that makes houses
expensive. If we, as a Government, can make steps so that those things might be more
affordable, we actually make houses more affordable.
I saw a policy announcement from parties oppos ite that said that they were going to
grant every first-home buyer an extra $2,000, and that was going to make houses more
affordable. Firstly, where does the $2,000 that the Government gives away come from?
It actually comes from homeowners, from people who are trying to pay the mortgage. It
18214 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
is just a money-go-round. It is actually not ma king things more affordable. But I say
this: every country that has tried to provide grants and to simply feed the demand side
of housing actually does not get there. You need to address the fundamentals. You need
to go after the issues of land supply, wh ich we are going after at pace. Members
opposite opposed every step this Government took last year with the Housing Accords
and Special Housing Areas Bill to free up th e process so that we might get more
sections available so that houses are more affordable.
Tomorrow we are going to be debati ng the Government’s changes around
development contributions. They have gone up more than any other item over the last
10 years. Members opposite are opposing reductions in those development contributions
and somehow pretend that they are about a ddressing the issues of housing affordability.
There is no magic bullet to that challenging issue. We need to do the things that the
Productivity Commission said we should do. Bu t do you know what I find particularly
galling? In every year from 2003 to 2008 house prices went up by more than 10 percent.
One year they went up by 19 percent. Wh at did members opposite do? Absolutely
diddly-squat. Absolutely nothing. House pri ces went up by 96 percent over that entire
period, and there is not a bill or reform  in any area that would have made any
difference.
Reflect on our 5 years. Actually, house pric es in New Zealand for the first 3 years
during that global financial crisis period went down. In fact, I had questions from
members opposite asking what the Government  is doing about the risk of house prices
dropping. The worst year was last year. House pr ices last year increased nationally by 9
percent. We have introduced over six different reforms to get on top of that issue and to
make a real difference, and those are the real long-term answers to the issues of housing
affordability.
I have one last point on that question,  and it is that the worst thing for
homeownership and housing affordability is th e issue of interest rates. The Budget
documents and the Treasury advice is abso lutely clear that if you spend like drunken
soldiers, you will drive interest rates up. Treasury has very clearly put in a spending cap
of $1.5 billion, which we are following, an d every utterance I hear from members
opposite is that they would exceed that, drive up interest rates, and rob New Zealanders
of their hopes and dreams of housing affordability.
This is an awesome Budget. It is a good Budget in the black, making progress for
New Zealand, and it should be commended to the House.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: That was an interesting contribution from Nick Smith.
There are a couple of initiatives, like the free doctors visits and prescriptions for
children under 13, that the Green Party supports, but this Budget is not a prudent Budget
because it is about debt. It is about fiscal  debt, social debt, and environmental debt.
When National came into power, the Govern ment debt was $14 billion. How much is it
now? It is $61 billion. Th at is $13,500 for every New Zealander—an increase of
$11,000 for every person in New Zealand since 2008. So John Key’s Government may
achieve a small surplus, but it has been pr ofligate in its borrowi ng, and it is burdening
present and future generations with the cost of repaying that debt. That debt means that
we have $1 billion in intere st costs every year, and that is $1 billion that we cannot
spend on health, on education, or on the enviro nment, like conservation. There is also a
major problem in the Government’s spending priorities, because it is skewing some of
the spending in the natural resource area to wards ripping off the environment. In this
Budget, National found an extra $40 million to subsidise more irrigation and more
pollution of our rivers and lakes, but it c ould not find a single dollar more to properly
protect our wild landscapes and our species like the mōhua, the kākā, and our threatened
native bats.
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18215
Those species are faced this year with a pl ague of rats and stoats, and yet National
could not find a single dollar extra to avoi d that threat. We ha d the Minister of
Conservation trumpeting the Department of  Conservation’s programme to increase
predator control over another 600,000 hectares to tackle the mast year. That is the heavy
seeding in our beech forests, which is followed by an increase in rat and mice numbers,
and then an increase in stoats, which then turn  on our birds. Yet is there a dollar in this
Budget to help control those rats and stoats—that pest plague? No. There is $40 million
for more subsidies for water pollution, but not  a single dollar mo re—in fact, there has
been a cut of nearly $5 million—in the fundi ng for the Department of Conservation’s
Natural Heritage Management System, whic h is the programme where we get pest
control done and where we get work done for our threatened species. It is the
department that is going to have to scrimp and save. It is going to have to reduce its
other work in order to tackle this predator  plague. There is not a single dollar extra for
conservation.
If this had been a Green Budget, we woul d have had a Government that looked after
all New Zealanders, not just the top 2 percen t. We would not have had the tax cuts for
the wealthy that have deprived the Governme nt of billions of do llars of revenue. We
would have invested in conservation to pr otect our public lands because we know that
investing in conservation protects our “100% Pure New Zealand” image. It protects that
$13 billion worth of brand that  is so essential to the marketing of our primary produce
and to bringing tourists here. It is an essent ial investment too because it helps to sustain
ecosystem services like clean air and water; it helps to sustain our quality of life and the
places where we can go kayaking, where we  can go tramping, and where we can go
walking; and it is spending that creates extra jobs in the regions. A Green Budget would
invest in protecting those wild landscapes.
Instead, in this Budget the Government is spending on very risky ventures. By
putting an extra $40 million into the Cr own Irrigation Fund, the Government is
signalling to the people of Hawke’s Bay a nd the Hawke’s Bay Regional Investment Co.
that it is likely to be spending on that very  grandiose dam scheme at Ruataniwha. It is
doing that despite the fa ct that there are no obvious priv ate investors for that scheme—
