TrustPower has pulled out, Ng āi Tahu has pulled out—and there is a very low
likelihood of getting good commercial returns.  So what is the Hawke’s Bay Regional
Investment Co. doing? It is looking to the Crown Irrigatio n Fund for a big handout to
subsidise that scheme and plug the giant hole in its funding.
So the Green Party knows that if we ar e going to have a pros perous economy, we
need to have an environment that we invest in, not one that we rip off through subsidies.
Our initiatives, like the Green Investment  Bank that was announced last week, would
seek to change the direction of our econom y to put it on a much more sustainable
footing in order to capture a slice of that trillion-dollar global market in renewables. A
Green Budget would be about having a more sustainable course for our future, not about
investing in industries that pollute and destroy our environment.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry, I was not informed that this was a split call—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: It’s a split call.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: It is a split call? Well, in that regard, you have 5 minutes,
Julie Anne Genter. It is helpful if members al ert the Speaker first, and then I can give a
warning bell. It would be preferable if that happened.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: The Budget is about choices. In the Green Party
we are very conscious that resources are lim ited, and so we have to make choices about
how we spend our money. Despite what th e National Party might say about us, we
believe in living within our means. One can tell what someone values by what they
18216 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
prioritise in their spending. The Green Party values our pristine natural environment, we
value people, and we value democracy. We wo uld make very different choices to this
Government in our Budget. A Green Budget would be one that builds an economy that
serves people and protects the planet, and th at enriches the lives of New Zealanders for
generations to come.
I stood to be an MP for the Green Party b ecause I love New Zealand. I want to help
look after our precious places and all of our people, and we can do that. We have so
many opportunities right now, in 2014, to cr eate a clean, green economy that works for
everyone, not just those who are already at the top. Unfortunately, this National
Government does not believe that we can have  a healthy environmen t and have jobs. It
consistently says that we ar e against jobs because we want  to protect the environment.
Nothing could be further from the truth. Our economy exists to serve us—it exists to
serve people—and it cannot exist without a healthy environment. Our economic success
is underpinned by the health of our environment.
I know that New Zealanders l ove our rivers and streams an d that they want them to
be clean enough to swim in, as they once were. Unfortunately, this Budget does not do
much to clean up our rivers. On the contrary, it earmarks $80 million to subsidise
irrigation schemes, which will make pollution in rivers worse. National is choosing to
prioritise big projects—like th e Ruataniwha Dam, a project that does not even stack up
economically in the short term, let alone environmentally in the long term—and the
National Government is consistently choosi ng to prioritise a few people who stand to
gain in the short term, even when it will leave New Zealand’s economy and
environment worse off, when it will leav e New Zealand’s rivers more polluted, and
when only a few people will benefit.
Another example of short-term thinking by th is National Government is the decision
to prioritise billions of dollars in the transport budget on a few motorway projects that
will serve only 5 percent of vehicle trips. It sounds crazy, and it is. It is going ahead
with these projects that do not stack up economically in the short term or
environmentally in the long term. Of cour se there are some people who will benefit
from these new duplicate highways. There are a few people who drive on those roads
who will say, once they have been  built, that they are better off. That is true, but we do
not see the opportunity cost, and there is a massive opportunity cost to spending billions
on just a few highways like the P ūhoi to Warkworth “Holiday Highway”; Transmission
Gully, which we are taking out a private loan to f und—even though the Government
claims to have returned to surplus, it is actu ally getting us into more debt for some very
dodgy projects—and the Waikato Expressway.
That opportunity cost is that we will not see the improvements to safety and
maintenance of these existing roads sooner. We will not see the improvements to train
and bus services that could have helped millions of New Zealanders get to work and get
to school more affordably and more quickly, whether they travel by public transport or
by car. The best way to free up the roads at peak time is to make it easier for some
people, not everyone, to leave the car at hom e. We will not see the transformational and
very low-cost benefits of making it safer for kids to walk and cycle to school. The
Green Party has a very smart, practical alte rnative to the Government’s programme that
will improve our existing roads and give New Zealanders more choices.
Housing has been raised as a major issue. I want to make just a couple of comments
about housing and how the National Govern ment is missing a huge opportunity to
address both the demand side and the supply side  of housing. It claims that there is no
demand problem, that there is no impact from foreign capital coming into our real estate
market. Well, that would make  New Zealand an absolute exception on the world scene,
because it is affecting property prices in cities across the world. Secondly, it says it is
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18217
entirely a supply issue and that freeing up new land on the fringe is going to create
affordable housing, but it will also bring with it enormous transport costs. It would be
wiser to enable cities to address the s upply problem through targeted building, and
increase the opportunities for people to live where they want to live where land values
are highest.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: On the day of Shane Jones’
valedictory, the Greens have just given us  two speeches to show exactly why he is
leaving a potential Labour-Greens Government. That is an  absolute prime example of a
party over there with policies that are anti -growth, anti-jobs, under the guise of some
nice, green environmental wording, but is actually so far to the left, so devolutionary of
our aspirations for our country, that I do not know where to start.
We note that in the Greens’ version of the Budget, if th ey did it, there would be
printing presses involved because that is how they would find the money. They would
get a printing press out and print money. Th ey are against water storage and irrigation
schemes across the country, not just in the example of the Ruataniwha Dam, which the
previous speaker, Julie Anne Genter, was ta lking about there. They  are against oil and
gas exploration around our country. They liv e in this conspiracy land. How do they
solve the housing problem and its issues? Well, I remember Metiria Turei talking about
crashing down the equity that people have in  their existing homes. They want to do a
Green Investment Bank. Where is the capital  for this bank coming from? From the
printing press, from domestic savings—the re is a wee problem there—or from the
offshore savings from evil foreign lenders to New Zealand? Where is it coming from?
They have the audacity to ta lk about bringing tourists he re and then are anti fossil
fuels. How are the tourists goi ng to get here, I do wonder? Th ey talk about jobs in the
regions, such as Hawke’s Bay. They rally against free-trade agreements for an exporting
region such as Hawke’s Bay, a country such as New Zealand, and yet they talk about
jobs in the regions. They were talking about water standards. Where were they
supporting the previous Labour Government  to help modernise New Zealand’s
freshwater standards, to br ing in minimum standards? Where were they when we
needed standards around oil exploration off our shores?
I do note my colleague Mr Shane Jones’ valedictory tonight. What an excellent
speech and what an entertainer, and I am qui te sure, just quietly, that some of the
members opposite are probably going: “Oh, ma ybe we made the wrong decision.” On a
personal note, I will miss Mr Jones. I do count him as a parliamentary friend. I do
acknowledge that we had a coup le of great times together, particularly on our US trip
together as part of the New Zealand – US A Friendship Group, the Parliamentary Rugby
Team, and particularly on the Finance and Expenditure Committee. We had a lot of fun.
Actually, Mr Jones is not the only person shunning Labour. He is not the only person
leaving Mr Cunliffe and Labour, because up in  the Wairarapa, Tukituki, and Napier all
three of the Labour candidates there are actual ly refusing to go on the Labour list. They
are refusing to go on the Labour list. Why?  How can that be? Which of Labour’s
policies must they not want to be a party to ? Perhaps it goes way back to Mr Cunliffe’s
sacking of the Hawke’s Bay District Health Board. Perhaps it goes back to Labour’s
banning Facebook policy. Perhaps it goes back to its policy of banning friends and
families of migrants to New Zealand. Perhaps it is just something to do with the man
ban. Perhaps those three candidates who are choosing not to go on the Labour list, and
who are therefore choosing not to campaign for Labour Party policies, do not want to
have anything to do with the Greens. That is fair enough. Perhaps they do not want to
have anything to do with Hone Harawira in  a potential Governme nt. Perhaps they do
not want to be part of policy that is essentially anti-job, anti-growth, anti - New
Zealand, although it might make a few nice headlines.
18218 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
It is the party vote th at decides the Government. It is the party vote. It is the party
vote. It is the party vote. How and why ca ndidates from the major Opposition party in
New Zealand are choosing not to follow Labour  Party policy on the party list, I cannot
understand. But I have seen this  before, and I have seen the results of it before. As a
candidate for the Nats in 2002, I know that our  organisation was not in the best shape.
There were a few issues, and individual candi dates tried not to be on the list and ran
localised campaigns. And do you remember the result? Worst result National has ever
had. I am quite sure that Labour is well on that  way and we are seeing that play out in
the regions with its candidates.
This was an excellent Budget. It is a continuation of the excellent and prudent
management of our economy. A surplus ha s been reached. After the Pre-election
Economic and Fiscal Update of 2008—just 6 years after that—there is a surplus of $382
million, which is apparently a trifling am ount according to the Opposition parties.
Actually, it is quite a significant amount, I would suggest. What does that surplus mean?
It means lower interest rates for longer—lower interest rates for longer—because of a
National Government and Bill English’s Budget discipline over the last 6 years. How do
we get to that surplus? What does it m ean? It means more oxygen in the economy for
the real job-makers out there. The size of  Government to the economy is now about 30
percent and heading lower, and better public services are being delivered all the time
across crime, health, education—you name it—even though times have been tight. That
is how you do things better. That is how you deliver better outcomes.
It is curious that Mr Parker, the Labour  finance spokesman, says Labour would have
got to surplus anyway. How would it have done that with the decade of deficits forecast
in 2008 with its existing policies, and then with voting against every single measure of
reform and cost-saving and budget leading up to this surplus? How could Labour have
got to surplus if it voted against all those things and with the various policies it seems to
be rolling out now? It is quite curious. Anothe r curious thing is that Mr Cunliffe in his
speech talked about Labour charging and targeting full employment—fair enough, an
aspirational goal. But then not long after that he said: “We are targeting 4 percent
unemployment.”, not full employment—zero—but 4 percent. Contradictory—what is he
up to? I do not know. The surp lus is very good for our fa milies, our country, and our
exports.
Just to talk quickly about my broadcas ting portfolio, I note that the Opposition
spokesman spoke and actually did not even mention broadcasting. I was quite surprised
about that. A very good announcement toda y was that over 500,000 hours of Television
New Zealand archives will be transferred from Television New Zealand to the Ministry
for Culture and Heritage and the Department of Internal Affairs to be made accessible to
New Zealanders online. That is Nati onal’s ongoing commitment to public sector
broadcasting—the preservation of what we have already and making accessible stuff
that has already been paid for and is owned by the taxpayer. That is actually what a
better public service is. We continue to allow Radio New Zeala nd and Television New
Zealand to seize the opportunities in fron t of them in the challenging digital
environment. The speech from the Chief Executive Officer of Radio New Zealand, Paul
Thompson, the other day should be widely read  by MPs in the House, and particularly
by Opposition spokespeople for broadcasting. It shows the ability of our publicly
owned, public sector broadcasters to begin to adapt to this very challenging and new but
exciting environment.
Where is Labour’s position on this? Labour’s position—and probably the Greens’
position; probably the Greens’ position woul d be worse—is that Labour wants to
control what you watch, when you watch, and how you watch. That is what it would do.
It is stuck in the New Zealand Broadcas ting Corporation one model. Labour members
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18219
talk about building a new channel, for goodness’ sake, when the entire world is moving
away from traditional channels  because it is about content,  content, content. We should
be blind as to how it is delivered, as long as  it is produced, got out there, and Kiwis can
access it.
How would Labour pay for this new channel?  Well, it is putting a levy, apparently,
on information and communications technolo gy providers—i.e., internet companies.
Internet providers in New Zealand will be  taxed. Labour goes back to its natural
position of: “If it is moving, we should tax it. ” Let us ban Facebook, as part of that, and
tax the internet within New Zealand to pay for the traditional mode of broadcasting to
build this new Labour channel it is talki ng about. It is absolute madness—absolute
madness. Labour is very much in a New Z ealand Broadcasting Corporation time warp.
National is digital, looking forward, work ing forward, futureproofed, and looking to
help New Zealand - owned organisations, Government and otherwise, seize the
opportunity to tell New Zealand’s stories across the world. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am advised that this is a split call—Louisa Wall.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: That is correct. I would like to take the
opportunity to mihi to the Hon Shane Jones and acknowledge that he gave his
valedictory speech tonight, and that many of my colleagues are over at the Back
Bencher, enjoying his hospitality. Many of us enjoyed what he had to say, and in fact I
want to pick up on something that Shane quoted in his speech. It was: “H ūtia te rito o te
harakeke, kei hea te kōmako, e kō?” [Pull out the centre shoot of the flax, where will the
bellbird sing, lass?]
What does that actually mean? At the heart of the flax-bush the bellbird sings. Where
will the bellbird be if the flax-bush ceases to be? What the intention of that whakatau āki
is all about is to en sure that we as wh ānau, as hap ū, as communities, and as society
support those who are the most vulnerable. Actually, the rito, which is in the heart of the
harakeke, is the most vulnerable. I make no apologies for the Labour Party being very
clear about what our priorities are, and would be if we were the Government. I
particularly want to commend my colleague Jacinda Ardern  and her Best Start policy,
which is all about making sure every New Z ealand child has the best possible start in
life, which begins with a $60 per week payment for every child, and particularly for
those children who are the most vulner able. They are the 285,000 children who are
living in poverty. They are the 170,000 children who are be neficiaries’ children, who
received nothing from this Government in the Budget. The Prime Minister reiterated
that today.
I would like to focus on two commentat ors post-Budget, one of whom is the
Associate Professor Mike O’Brien, who is the social security spokesperson for the Child
Poverty Action Group. His assessment of the Budge t was very clear. He said that only
one Budget item would directly  “affect poverty” and that was extending free doctors
visits and prescriptions to al l children under the age of 13. Th at is the only measure in
National’s Budget that is going to directly affect children who live in poverty. But he
had a caveat on that assessment, and I am su re the National members of the House will
find this interesting. This was within the c ontext of Northland. He said that there are
geographical issues for poor people living in isolated rural commun ities, so extending
free visits is of no use if you could not access them because of distance or an inability to
afford to get there. The only addition I would make, within the context of South
Auckland, is that those free doctors visi ts mean nothing if you do not have enough
general practitioners for our children to visit.
Dr Paul Hutchison is in the House toni ght, and he will know that Counties Manukau
District Health Board and the Counties Manuka u area is the lowest -provided region in
terms of general practitioners. We are over 10 0 general practitioners short. So within
18220 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
that context you can extend free visits, but  the reality is that if those general
practitioners do not exist in our communities, then again those families do not have
access to what we would consider the basics. Those basics are primary-care basics that
ensure that our children, particularly, are strong, they are healthy, and they are ready
and active and have the ability to go to school to learn.
I also want to pick up on a comment from this article in the Northern Advocate. It is
from a man called Hua Poraka from Dargavi lle. His assessment of National’s Budget
was pretty easy. His assessment was that Na tional does not care. National does not care
about the children in Northland. National do es not care about the children in South
Auckland. If National thinks that this B udget is going to reduce poverty, is going to
address the issues of child poverty, then it is greatly mist aken. The only other thing I
want to highlight is that Go rdon Campbell was very clear that  this is the “let them eat
crumbs Budget”. That was his assessment. I say that for some kids living in poverty it is
actually the “let them eat air Budget”. What  you have given children, and particularly
beneficiaries’ children, is fresh air. You have given th em nothing. You are not helping
them out of their circumstances. You are not providing a hand up or a way to a better
life. You have actually ignored them. Th at was the other assessment of Gordon
Campbell—that this Government has ignore d beneficiaries’ children, because guess
what? National does not care. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: I am pleased to take the other half of this call on
the Budget. What I was looking for in this Budget  was its vision. What  vision does it
reflect of contemporary New Zealand soci ety and contemporary issues facing our
people? I was asking myself the question: does it put people first? If it did, then I would
take the Budget seriously. People, after all, are the most important. If we do not put our
people first, if we do not de velop them well, if we do not give them the opportunities,
then we all pay for it in the end. We pay huge amounts of money to correct those
problems that are created when we do not put  our people first. Th at was not the vision
of this particular Budget. Its vision was somewhere else. Its vision was of a divisive
society. It was not a vision of treating our most vulnerable well.
Then I asked, well, what does it do—this is one of the most serious questions facing
New Zealand society today—about one of th e most serious problems? This is the
problem of inequality. [ Interruption] I say to the Hon Todd McClay that this is a
problem that is facing New Zealand soci ety. I do not think anybody in this House
doubts that inequality is awful and that it ought  to be addressed, particularly when that
inequality has very serious impacts on our children. And yet we know that the Budget
did not address those inequali ties. The Budget really began to say: “Well, do you know
what we’re going to do? We’re going to select  a small group of the most vulnerable and
we’re going to target some services towards them.”
I know that Paul Hutchison will soon talk about targeting, but when there is such a
big group, Mr Hutchison—285,000 children who are living in povert y—where is the
morality, and where is the ethics of addres sing 30,000 of them? Where is the morality?
How do you work that out, Mr Hutchison? In a sense, it is condemning the other quarter
of a million children to poverty. What that does, Mr Hutchison, is  it simply creates
another generation for the welfar e system to cope with, for the health system to cope
with, and for the justice system to cope  with. We create bigger problems down the
track, Mr Hutchison. And yet we know that for children, that moment of their lives, that
0 to 3 years, is what sets them up on thei r development trajectory for the rest of their
lives. That is what does it. Every piece of sc ience we know says that that is where we
should target. So everybody in this group ought to be targeted.
But when it is 285,000 children, Mr Hutchison, and we are targeting 30,000 children,
what is this silly game we are playing? It  really is condemning the most vulnerable to
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18221
even more miserable lives. There is plenty of evidence to show that we have not applied
the kind of morality, the decency, for creati ng a society where all boats are lifted. Here
we are wanting to advantage a small group of  those children, and that is where this
Budget fails abysmally. Our alternative idea s around children in Be st Start begin to
address, very systematically, each step, each segment of what it takes to lift all those
boats and to give those people a better start in life.
This is my last Budget speech and it is a brief one. I make it with some sadness
because I came into Parliament after a lif e of working with the most vulnerable,
working with children and families for 45 years. I say with some sadness that we now
see a period here when we ar e not addressing the most vulne rable. Much of what Nick
Smith said was really just discounting 9 years of very positive development. There were
9 years of economic management that gave this Government the headroom to manage
the headwinds that came. If it was not for th at, it would have been in dire trouble. But
Government members do not have the decency to acknowledge that. It was all designed
simply to create the Crosby/Textor - type spin that throws t hose figures around. But
their own performance is really immoral. It is immoral when looked at from the
perspective of putting children and families first. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: This is a very good Budget—New
Zealand is heading in the ri ght direction—and it is a confident Budget for a confident
country. That statement sums up the difference between this side of  the House and that
side of the House—a confident Budget for a confident nation.
I want to be charitable, after listening to th e last two speakers. Rajen Prasad said that
this will be his last Budget, so I will re sist the opportunity, the challenge, or the
temptation to do anything but wish him we ll in his many, many years ahead. But can I
say that we need to be optimistic in this House. We need to focus on the good things
that happen in New Zealand. We need to be fair and reasonable, and when we are in
Opposition we do not just have to oppose abso lutely everything. What must it be like,
after 6 years in Opposition, to feel that ever ything is wrong with this country and that
the members opposite are right all of the time? Well, let us wait and see.
For two elections in a row New Zealande rs have had a choice, and those New
Zealanders decided that they did want a brig hter future, and they did want to choose a
New Zealand that was heading in  the right direction. What they  have been saying to us
through the media, on the airwaves, as they ca ll the radio stations, a nd in our electorate
seats is that this is a confident Budget for a confident nation. And when the members
opposite stop talking and listen to New Zealanders they will  actually see what it is that
New Zealanders are interested in.
Let us contrast—not just our speeches a nd how aspirational we are compared with
members opposite—the Budget delivered by Bi ll English in New Zealand last week
with the one that was delivered in Australia  the very same week. But before we do, let
us remember 3 or 4 years ago when these ve ry members who have been quite vocal in
this House were saying: “Why aren’t you, th e National Government, more like they are
in Australia?”. They asked why we were not more like—and they used the term—the
Lucky Country, Australia, where all of thos e New Zealanders were going. Well, guess
what? They were leaving under the Labour G overnment and, yes, when we inherited
such a mess from the Labour Government af ter 9 years, they continued to go. But we
have not heard now, have we, or last week from the Labour Opposition: “Why aren’t
you more like Australia?”.
Can I say to New Zealanders that when th ey face the choice on 20 September of this
year of who will govern them, if they choose a Green-Labour Government coalition,
then they will get the wish that the Labour Party has aske d for: they will be much more
like Australia in this country than we are to day. The reason for that is that in Australia
18222 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
people are facing very difficult times. In Australia the Government has made cuts. It has
cut its welfare, it has cut its Public Service, and it has increased taxes. It has got a
special deficit tax. After all of those change s, and all of those cuts, the costs going up
when people go to the doctor, across the board, it is going to have a NZ$32 billion
deficit in this next year—a NZ$32 billion deficit.
That may be all right for members opposite in the Labour Party and the Greens.
Maybe they think that that is OK, but I am not  sure that is the feeling in Australia right
now. How come we are not hear ing from them now about why we are not more like the
Lucky Country? Compare that with the job that Bill English has done and the hard work
that New Zealanders have done over this last 5 years on what we must recognise as
being a very difficult time for New Zealanders—a deep recession.
As one of the members opposite always says, it has been the worst this and the worst
that, over 50 years. Well, there was a very  steep recession, a global financial crisis, a
challenge in Christchurch because of the earthquakes, and we have a modest surplus
coming to New Zealand—$372 million. It is a very  modest surplus, but that is so much
better than the deficits that were forecast by Treasury when we took over the
Government benches, and so very different from what is happening in Australia.
There is a forecast of a growth rate of  between 2 and 4 percent over the next 4
years—one of the first countries in the West ern World not only to get back to surplus
but to have sustainable levels of growth, which will help grow the economy and grow
incomes for New Zealanders. It is such a great difference between our two countries.
This was a Budget focused on growth, jobs, and prosperity. But it was not just about
the economy. There was much more to it than this, and I think this is what hurts the

items.speaker: Opposition the most
items.text: we are helping childre n and helping families. There is a $500
million investment in children and families in New Zealand. There are free general
practitioner visits and free pr escriptions for all children unde r the age of 13. I think that
is an excellent policy, and I congratulate  Bill English and Tony Ryall on making this
possible. Without the hard work, the de dication, and the caution around Government
spending over the last 5 years, it would not have been possible to do this with a Budget
surplus. There are free general practitioner vi sits and free prescriptions for every child
in New Zealand under the age of 13. There is 4 weeks’ ex tra paid parental leave,
extended to caregivers and othe r parents. That will be welcomed by parents and the
other caregivers of children in New Zealand.
There is an increase in th e parental tax credit of $70 a week, bringing it to $220 per
week. There is $155 million extra going into early childhood education. More money is
being spent on early childhood education every year under this Government than in any
year before, and, guess what, the taxpayers —mums and dads, and their children—are
starting to see a return on this investment  in children: $155 million extra in early
childhood education. Members opposite reject that, and do not support it.
There is $33 million extra to support vulnerable children—$33 million extra to
support vulnerable children—t o create eight new Children’s Teams. I won the seat in
my electorate of Rotorua 6 years ago. I was re -elected 3 years ago, and I will work very
hard for every single vote there this year. We had a Children’s Team delivered to us 2
years ago. It empowers the community and all of those groups to come together to focus
on those vulnerable children, to put them first, and to make their lives better. Already
we are starting to see the community grow ing, coming together, and working through
that. So we have that in Rotorua already. It  started a few years ago. We have worked
hard, it is starting to work well, and now we are able to use those things that we have
learnt and that were demonstr ated and roll them out to ei ght other parts of the country,
at a cost of $33 million. Members opposite woul d say it was a cost; on this side of the
House we see it as an investment of $33 millio n into vulnerable children, to make their
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18223
lives better. Well done to Tony Ryall and the re st of the team for excellent work around
helping children and around families.
The other thing I wanted to talk about—because if one listened to only the
Opposition one would think that there was no work done here at all—is health. What
more have we done in health? All of those statistics, all of that extra money I mentioned
that we spent around families, we get to do that and we also can run a modest surplus
this year—so different from Australia. “Better, sooner, more convenient care”—there
has never been a time when th at statement was truer. Ther e is $110 million extra for
elective surgery. That is knees and hips—knees  and hips for New Zealanders. They are
getting operations.
When I became the member of Parliament  for Rotorua 6 year s ago, a number of
complaints in the community were that pe ople were not getting th eir operations. They
were not being treated by hos pitals, they were being put on waiting lists, and then they
were receiving letters saying th ey had been knocked off the waiting list. The Labour
Government at the time said they were doing a great job, not by delivering operations
but by knocking people off waiting lists. Well, now there are more operations every
year in Rotorua and in other parts of the country than ever before.
There is $112 million for disability support, $96 million for increased home-based
support care, $90 million for free general prac titioner visits, $40 million in additional
support for the elderly, $33 million for faster  cancer treatment, $20 million to help fight
rheumatic fever, and $6 million for cochlear implants for children.
This is the Budget of a caring Government —a Government that has worked hard
over 5 years to move New Zealand out of re cession, to get us back  on track, to back
New Zealanders, and to get us back to a mode st surplus, which will grow in the years
ahead. This is a Government that has worked  hard with New Zealanders to deliver for
New Zealanders, and I think it could not be a better Budget, coming into an election.
I say this to you that if the members opposite want to revert and be like Australia or
other countries, then they should keep making the pledges they are making in the
Labour Party and the Green Party about how  they can just spend money on anything
they want, with no accountability. The public saw that over 9 years. They did not like it.
They rejected it. We will make a case as a confident Government. We have got a
confident Budget for a confident country. Th is will be a very good year to go to an
election. This is a caring Budget. It is a caring country. It is a caring Government. I
commend this Budget to the House.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: The Budget provides the opportunity for the
Government to outline its priorities and to talk about what its plan and its vision are. We
saw that last Thursday, and it is fair to say that, like for many New Zealanders, for this
side of the House it was pretty underwhelming. But let us imagine.
Let us imagine that every New Zealander woke up and they were in a home that was
warm and dry, and they could afford that home. Imagine what th at would be like.
Imagine that they had the security of knowi ng that the community they were living in
was one they could put roots down in and pa rticipate in. Being part of a community—
imagine that. Imagine that the children in  the house went to the local school and
remained there until it was time to move to the next stage in their world-class education.
Imagine what that would be like.
Imagine there was enough room in the hous e, in the home, and that that was a
healthy place where no one was at risk of getting Third World diseases. Imagine that
increasing numbers of New Zealanders were  able to own their own homes. That is
right—own their own homes. It was not that long ago that that was the Kiwi dream.
Imagine that all adults who were in jobs were earning a fair day’s pay for a fair day’s
work. Remember that? That used to be part of the Kiwi dream, too—a fair day’s pay for
18224 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
a fair day’s work. Imagine that they worked  hard, that they could get ahead, and that
they could improve their family’s standard of living.
Imagine that all of the children living in th is country had enough to eat. Imagine that
all of the children in this country had the opportunity to develop to their full potential
and to get ahead, irrespective of their backgrounds and their families’ economic
situations. Imagine that Budget 2014 had give n New Zealanders hope that that was the
sort of society we live in. But it is not.
Once upon a time, that was New Zealand, but  not any more—not under this National
Government. Now we know that New Zealan d is becoming less equal. These are the
real figures in this Budget, the things th at underline this Budget. There are 285,000
children living in poverty—a national disgrace. The cost of the tax cuts that National
gave to the rich is $1.2 billion, and now we cannot fund h ealth and education
sufficiently to keep up with cost incr eases and population growth. There are 42,000
more people unemployed now than when Nati onal came into office, and 46 percent of
our people did not get a pay increase last ye ar. Those are the sorts of figures underlying
the Budget, and those are the figures that impact on people and on families, and in the
end that is what matters.
We need Budgets and an economy that de livers for people—all people, not just
some. Those are the sorts of pr iorities and the sorts of plan s that could have been in
Budget 2014, but not, of course, under a National Government.
We also know that fairer societies are mo re successful societies. There is a body of
evidence now that shows that we all benef it from people having a fair go, and from all
kids having a great start in life and getting ahead. We all benefit from that. The social
costs of not doing that—imprisonment, mental health issues, and all of those things; the
opposite side of that—the information about that  is there. It is i rresponsible to ignore
that sort of information. Kiwis are worried about this.
A recent poll showed that 75 percent of New Zealanders believe that New Zealand is
becoming less equal, and Bill English in the House the other day just sort of dismissed
that, saying: “They’re wrong. Obviously, they’r e wrong.” Well, that is actually not the
reality out there on the doorsteps. When I ta lk to people, they are concerned about
inequality. They are not just the people doing  it tough themselves. Lots of decent New
Zealanders who are doing OK are worried about other people. That is the sort of society
we still have in this country.
The Government ignores all of that, and recent statistics, including the census. The
Government tried to dispute the census figur es, as well. Every time any information is
put out in this House, the Government ducks and dives. It disputes  the figures and says
they are not reputable. Even the New Zeal and census showed that there are now two

items.speaker: Aucklands
items.text: an Auckland for the rich and an Auckland for the rest. The Government
says the census is wrong, as well. Well, tell that to  the people in M āngere and Ōtāhuhu
whose incomes have actually dropped by 19 percent. Tell them that the census is wrong.
In the Maungakiekie electorate in Auckland, where I work, we have got the richest
and poorest Aucklanders living in one electo rate. Housing is one of the big issues.
Housing is a real indicator in the inequality  argument. I talk to people about a range of
different housing issues, such as the difficulty that peopl e are facing getting
maintenance done on their State houses because the Government is extracting more
money from Housing New Zealand. People have  contacted me about the fact that there
are State houses sitting empty while there are people desperately needing a home. There
are people being evicted as a result of reviewable tenancies, and elderly people worried
that they are going to be evicted. There are people who just have no sense any more that
they will ever be able to afford to buy a home.
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18225
Access to affordable housing is vital. It is vital for people because they need shelter,
but it is much more than that . It is about a home, it is a bout being part of a community,
and it is about good health a nd educational outcomes. So I know that this will be a
really significant issue in this election and I know that across the other side of the House
people know that, as well. You know—so rry, Mr Deputy Speaker. The Government
knows—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: But he knows.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: —including the Deputy Speak er—that there is a real
vulnerability on the housing issue because it is so clear.
Members opposite are so out of touch on this  issue. I still cannot  believe that the
member of Parliament for Maungakiekie, th e Hon Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, felt that a
deposit of $130,000—that is right, $130,000—is not out of reach for most people. Well,
that is just ridiculous. It is just ridiculous, on the sorts of wages that people are earning,
to save $130,000. That is so out of touch.
On the poverty issue, it is really intere sting to see how much members opposite want
to deny the issue of poverty a nd want to dispute what is  going on with wages. Low
wages in this country are a disgrace. Peopl e work hard and they cannot get ahead.
Forty-six percent of them did not get a pay increase last year. Well, prices certainly
continued to go up last year. So this Budget did not deliver on those issues.
Throughout New Zealand we see interg enerational inequality—young people
burdened with student debt, who have no sens e of ever being able to afford to buy a
home. We see inequality faced by wome n—single-income families, beneficiary
families, and working families headed by women; M āori and Pacific women. The
lowest-paid people in this country are Pa sifika women, earning little more than the
minimum wage, doing important work lik e aged care. That Government opposite
intervened in the court case where they are tr ying to get wage justice. This is what is
going on out there.
Labour offers a different vision. Labour offers a vision where wages will be
sufficient for people to have a decent standard of living, an d where there is a plan for
economic development with decent jobs and decent wages. If you look at the Budget,
where was any information or any ideas a bout developing our econom y to provide that
sort of work? There is an absence of any thinking. There is a lack of ambition about
moving forward, lifting the sta ndards in this country, and lifting the sort of economic
performance that we have in this country.
So we want to make sure that there are decent jobs and enough jobs. Let us aspire to
full employment. Let us aspire to lifting wa ges. Labour will lift wa ges. Labour will lift
the minimum wage. Labour will promote the liv ing wage. Labour will have fair labour
laws where workers will be able to negotiate  a decent pay increase, unlike the sorts of
attacks that they will face under National if it is returned in the election. So people, have
hope, and change the Government.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am advised this is a split call—5 minutes, Scott
Simpson.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is interesting to follow that
member, Carol Beaumont, who is a relativel y recent retread arrival in the Labour
caucus, on the same night that Shane Jones should give his vale dictory speech. Shane
Jones is leaving the Labour Party caucus for a brighter future, a more optimistic future,
and a more inspirational and aspirational fu ture than could ever be provided by the
Labour Party caucus. It was no good that member Carol Beaumont coming to this
House tonight and speaking in the Budget deba te and actually doing nothing more than
reading her Labour list ranking speech—snarky, whiney, negative, and offering no
hope, no vision, no inspiration, and no aspiration for hard-working New Zealanders.
18226 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
So here we stand. The nati on is just 121 days out from  a general election—121 days
out from the election. There are only 18 House sitting days before this, the 50 th
Parliament of New Zealand, ri ses. Last week we had Bill  English, the very competent
Minister of Finance in this John Key - led National Government administration, present
his sixth Budget to the nation, and what a good Budget it was. We are back in black—
back in black—with a modest but very wo rkable surplus of $372 million. Four months
out from the election, who could ever have thought that that was possible without the
hard work, dedication, and fiscal prudence of Bill English and this National team? Back
in 2008, when John Key, Bill E nglish, and the National team were first elected, the
country was in crisis. It was in  turmoil. It was on the bri nk of financial disaster, and it
was the careful, prudent management of Bill English and John Key that saw us return to
an even keel and got us back on the right track.
Last weekend I had many conversations with hard-working Kiwi people, Kiwi
voters, and Kiwi cons tituents in the Coromandel electorate, which I have the great
pleasure to represent. What th ey were telling me was that  this was a very good Budget.
The feedback was excellent. That is quite unusual for a Budget because often people are
not engaged with a Budget. Often people just let it wash over them, but this time people
did get the message. They understand that this  is a caring National Government that has
Kiwi families at the very heart of its policies—that we care, that we understand, and that
we know it has been tough for so many New Z ealanders over these last 6 years. We
have now got away from the profligate spen ding of the Labour Government, where the
answer to everything was simply to throw more money at it.
I am proud to rise in support of Bill Engl ish’s Budget, which is clearly and very
definitely focused on families at the heart of  everything it contains. It is decent, hard-
working New Zealand families that are the focus of the Budget, and they deserve it so to
be. We had the worst global financial crisis since the 1930s. That is just one of the
measures that Bill English and this team have  had to contend with. Then, of course, we
had Christchurch to contend with. We ha ve done, I think, a very  good job. I think New
Zealanders, in 121 days, will realise that as well.
I want to just mention one pa rticular aspect of the Budget that is very near and dear
to my heart, and near and dear to the hearts of all people in the Coromandel—that is, the
$26.5 million that has been allocated to furthe r the fight against kauri dieback disease.
One-third of New Zealand’s remnant kauri stand in my electorate, so it was a disaster of
epic proportions when, a couple of months  ago, the announcement came that kauri
dieback had been found in the Coromandel. This new $26.5 million of investment by
the Government into fighting kauri dieback will mean that over 100 kilometres of new
tracks can be laid, 5 kilometres of new boa rdwalks can be constructed, and an extra 300
hygiene stations can be created.
This Budget is a good Budget. In 121 days New Zealanders will be faced with a stark
decision. That will be a decision to stick with  John Key, Bill English, and this National
Government on the course of solid fiscal management that they have embarked upon
and are getting real results with, or to put  it all at risk with  a Labour-Greens-Mana
coalition. I know which way New Zealanders are going to vote in 121 days. I commend
this Budget to the House.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: I would like to thank my distinguished
colleague from the Coromandel, Scott Simpson, for yielding in this split call. It is an
enormous pleasure, an honour, and a privileg e to rise and speak in favour of this
Government’s sixth Budget delivered by our ve ry prudent Minister of Finance, the Hon
Bill English. When looking through the depart mental estimates, it is fantastic to see
such a large amount of invest ment going into the things that really matter to New
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18227
Zealand and the areas that make a real di fference in people’s liv es—not just the pet
projects and reckless expenditure that the side opposite seems to prefer.
I have been knocking on doors in the Wellingt on Central electorate over the last
weekend, and I have to say that the feedb ack on this Budget has been overwhelmingly
positive. The $500 million package for children and families in particular has been
popular among the voters in Wellington. That is  expanding the eligibility and duration
for paid parental leave, addi ng to the parental tax credit, and giving further access to
early childhood education. The free doctors vi sits and free prescriptions for children
under the age of 13 especially have been extremely popular.
Another area of investment that is of direct relevance to the good people of the
capital is the Government’s support of the film-making industry. The newly restructured
Screen Production Grant offers an incentive of a 30 percent grant to attract international
productions, with an additional 5 percent ava ilable for productions that offer significant
economic benefits. A 40 percent grant is available for local Ne w Zealand productions,
and the range of productions that now qualif y for this grant has been considerably
expanded. This has been very well received also. Gisella Carr, the Chief Executive of
Film New Zealand, said that “the increase d incentive is very welcome, as is the
Government’s recognition that attracting film and television production into New
Zealand has significant wider benefits for New Zealand, in cluding most recently in our
tourism sector.” With three more Avatar films to be fully realised in Wellington,
pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into th e local economy, I think the proof is in
the pudding with this particular policy.
We have also heard that business owners  are breathing a sigh of relief that the
Government has remained prudent in this Budget. The Wellington Employers’ Chamber
of Commerce Chief Executive Raewyn Bleakley has said that a “restrained Budget is
exactly what this country needs to cement-in the economic gains of the past few years,”.
She went on to comment that the Budget doe s not appear to be a “vote-winning lolly
scramble”. That is a very positive thing, and it will build on the platform of a return to
strong and sustainable growth, adding that “T he prospect of more  jobs, higher wages,
and even tax cuts further down the track wi ll be welcomed across the economy.” Also,
the managing director of Xero, a fine Wellington -based firm, said that the initiatives in
the Budget that have specifically delivered  for business were most welcome, outlining
the research and development tax credits and the hand back of considerable ACC
levies—half a billion dollars’ worth—as most welcome initiatives.
To me it is also good news that this G overnment’s sensible management of the
economy has given the private sector the c onfidence to go forward and make sensible
investment decisions, and I, for one, especially welcome the news this week that we
have heard a 2,500 - seating cap acity convention centre and a 5-star hotel are being
considered for Wellington by private entrepreneurs and investors. This is something that
will happen only when a Government provides  an environment conducive to the private
sector taking these opportunities and risks.
I also welcome the investment this B udget makes in boosti ng trade, supporting
exporters, defending the realm, and helpi ng our Pacific neighbours with their aid
programmes. Today we heard in media reports  the Hon Shane Jones say that he has no
regrets about leaving an incompetent and de bilitated muddle that is today’s Labour
Party and coming over here to join the Government waka. There was nothing in the Hon
Shane Jones’ very eloquent valedictory speech that suggested that that is anything but
the truth. I want to say to the Hon Shane J ones, as someone who left the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs and Trade to enter Parliament, to someone who is making the journey in
the opposite direction: “Welcome aboard, Jonesy .” I am sure the member will find this
waka to be more seaworthy, to  be a lot quicker across the water, and to have a much
18228 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
more competent captain, and with nowhere as many drips and leaks as his former
vessel.
We on this side of the Hous e look forward to working wi th the most talented and
sensible member of the Opposition. T ākina te hoe kia rite—let  us wield the paddles
together. In doing so, let us achieve great things for economic development at home and
in our wider region. I absolutely unreservedly commend this Budget to the House and to
the people of New Zealand.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on behalf of
New Zealand First. It would be very easy to be lulled into a false sense of security
listening to some of the speeches from that side of the House and seeing the generous
dollop of money that was put into the health  area in the latest Budget. In New Zealand
First we particularly liked some of the heal th initiatives that received funding. We liked
the free health care for all ch ildren aged under 13. That has been one of our policies for
many, many years, so we were pleased to s ee it come into fruition. We also liked the
fact that children are going to get two cochle ar implants. We all need two ears to hear,
rather than one. So there were some very positive initiatives in health.
However, once again, this Government has neglected the very important area of aged
care in its Budget. We all know that the need  is increasing at a steady rate, and that
when people go into a rest home their needs ar e far greater than they ever have been,
because they stay at home for as long as th ey possibly can. We like them to do that, too.
But there was absolutely nothing that actually  looks at funding for aged-care services
and employees. The Budget was totally silent on anything and everything that actually
applies to this particular group. No strate gy was visible, apart from ignoring the
problem. I was looking for “faster, better, soon er” action in this particular area, and I
know that the Minister of Revenue, the Hon Todd McClay, was talking about that
previously.

items.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: See, we do listen on this side of the House.
Working in a rest home is not an easy job; rather, the reverse. I would say that most
of us here in this House coul d not and would not wa nt to work in this particular area.
Fortunately, there are people who can and w ho do and who like to work in this area,
caring for our seniors. Aged-care workers provide a great servi ce while battling and
scrimping to survive on the minimum wage , which has been completely overlooked by
this Government. One can earn more money in a supermarket packing shelves than what
one can earn in the rest home industry. Thes e hard workers have a very demanding job
looking after our elderly, whether it is in a rest home or even in the person’s own home.
We rely on these people to carry out this  job, yet the Government basically ignores
them as if they do not matter. We all know  that costs are risi ng right throughout New
Zealand society. Pressure is building, and ag ed-care workers need to get a bigger slice
of the pie than they get now. These people have been to our Health Committee. Of
course, we have got all parties represented on the select committee, including
Government members, but, really, we are not listening to what these workers are saying.
There were, as I said earlier,  a number of good health  care initiatives in the Budget, but
the failure to address the distri ct health board funding at the levels required to maintain
the service in this particular sector is di sappointing, and it is going to result in increased
pressure on staff across the whole sector.
The bottom line—and we all know it—is that  our country is facing an ageing
population, and we need the facilities and th e workers to help cope with this. The
number of aged-care facilities, the number of beds, and the number of staff are all going
to need to increase to cope with the demand that we have upon us. The 2010 Grant
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18229
Thornton aged residential care services re view predicted that by 2026 between 12,000
and 20,000 new residents would require aged residential care—not a little number.
The Government clearly needs to quantif y the impending demand for elderly care.
But what do we see? Basically, this has been trivialised because the valuable occupation
of aged care is being ignored. Aged-care st aff carry out a whole range of tasks—some
of them are seriously unpleas ant—and they are woefully underpaid for them. The fact
that a person can receive a better wage stac king shelves at the supermarket shows just
how much value the Government places on this  particular sector. It is absolutely
disgraceful. The Government must set appr opriate staffing levels  and remuneration for
aged-care workers to acknowledge  their vital work and ensure  the safety and care of
those people working in the se ctor. The subsidy paid for the elderly in care should also
increase. New Zealand First believes that it needs to increase, as recommended in a
2008 report, and then be adjusted to meet the annual rate of inflation. That is only fair.
So what do we have? The Government is primarily to blame for the low wages and
pay inequalities in the aged residential ca re sector. New Zealand First took action in
2005 to improve workers’ wages after a PricewaterhouseCoopers report showed that the
sector was seriously underfunded by about 20 pe rcent—a percentage that has only ever
increased over the years. As part of New Zealand First’s confidence and supply
agreement with the Labour Government  in 2005 we boosted funding by $850 million
over two Budgets. Post-2008 National took its eye off the ball, and it did not inflation-
adjust the increase we worked so hard to ge t. That has led to the situation today where
Government workers are paid about 16 perc ent more than private providers doing
similar work in residential aged-care facilities and in home-based community support.
This Government needed to front up to ensure fair, uniform funding for the aged-care
sector, which provides a valuable yet totall y unappreciated servic e. And did it? No, it
did not. The Government needed to include money in the Budget to ensure that our
older age group is adequately cared for and liv ing in conditions that we would be happy
to live in ourselves or for our parents or our grandparents to live in. People have sent me
photos that show that some of the facilities are disgraceful.  A student flat would be far
better than some of the conditions that elderly residents are living in. By paying the staff
a minimum wage, reducing bed numbers, and not  keeping standards at a premium, we
are never going to see any improvement in th is area. The Government is going to be
completely caught out if it does not address adequate f unding of this area now. The
Budget was totally lacking in this area, and the silence was absolutely deafening.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
Minister, Simon—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: You’d better give me my last name, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: —Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I know there are
other Simons in the House, but that was th e most pregnant pause I have ever heard.
What is it? “Politeness is contagious”, a nd I thought you had forgotten my name there.
But enough about that.
Look, it is great to follow Barbara Stewart.  She is a great woma n. I know that if it
was up to her, New Zealand First would be supporting National after the election,
should it be in a position to do so. I know that she has been tr ying to seek peace
between Brendan Horan and Winston Peters, and she is disgusted by the nastiness going
on between them right now. I know, as I say, that she is a good person with a good heart
who, if she was not a member of Parliament  for New Zealand First, would be voting
National.
What a great Budget we have seen in the last few days, a Budget where Bill English
and the Prime Minister came to this House an d laid it all out for New Zealanders. How
18230 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
well received—I agree with Scott Simpson—that Budget was. We are now managing a
growing economy. After Rajen Prasad’s party le ft us with a decade of deficits, through
good stewardship day after day we are now back  in black, and that means that we are
able to put families at the heart of this Budget.  All of the things that Rajen Prasad did in
the Families Commission, all of those things, pale in comparison with the way that we
are now, through responsible stewardship, able to show families a dividend of growth.
The contrast between the Rt Hon John Ke y and his speech to  this House on the
Budget and that of David Cunliffe and the Labour Party—boy, I tell you what. You saw
in David Cunliffe a gentleman who was not sure whether to say: “Well, we’re unhappy
because you’ve stolen our two or three good id eas.”, or “Actually, this is terrible and
not left wing enough.” He could not work out  which was his position. I understand that,
because this is a Budget for our times that  New Zealanders are very, very happy with.
They are glad to see us back in surplus and putting families at the heart of the Budget.
I said that Mr Cunliffe was unhappy becau se we have stolen Labour’s ideas. Well,
actually, no. Paid parental leave—let us look  at that. We have always said—I am not
sure what Rajen Prasad is doing; I will come back to him—that paid parental leave is
something that, when circumstances permit, we want to do something about, and now
we are in a position to do that. But, unlik e the Labour Party and unlike the Green Party,
it is a considered, responsible package, whic h reaches more people who deserve it. As I
said in my speech on Budget night, we have done the hard policy work to come up with
that thoughtful package.
I know, in terms of stealing id eas, that now that Rajen Pr asad and Darien Fenton are
leaving this place—and maybe you as well, Mr  Assistant Speaker Robertson—the ideas
factory of the Labour Party has gone. The ideas factory of  the Labour Party has gone.
Where is it going to get its big ideas from? It  might have to go to Dr Clark. His great
idea was banning Facebook, and we know how popular that was. But that is the
position.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Don’t be so nasty, Simon. It’s  beneath you. You know you love me,
really.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I will be sorry to see Darien Fenton go. I will miss our
little flirtations across the House at question time. I always send a guilty text to my wife
afterwards, telling her I love her, but there you have it.
Then, of course, in that a lternation that David Cunliffe  had between not being sure
about what to say—“You stole our good ideas.”  versus that whole sort of “Look, it’s
terrible and not left wing enough.”—we get the wacky press release from David Shearer
today about home insulation. I do not know what  others think. I have to contend with
David Shearer’s press releases from time to time. From his radio appearances after those
press releases, I just wonder whether he ha s read them. I just wonder whether he has
read them, because the radio appearances do not seem to bear any sort of resemblance to
them. But in this one he says: “The Budget has confirmed that National has virtually
abandoned its programme of insulating cold and damp homes across New Zealand,”.
Well, Mr Shearer, I know it was a stressful time for you last year at Budget time, but
we invested an additional $100 million over 3 years in home insulation across this
country. That means that we are now in a position where we have insulated over
250,000 homes, including 112,000 low-income homes,  and that means that by the time
we have finished the end of our Warm Up  New Zealand: Heat Smart and Warm Up

items.speaker: New Zealand
items.text: Healthy Homes programmes, we will have insulated some $447 million
worth of taxpayer-funded insulated homes, or nearly 300,000 homes. And that is not
good enough for Mr Shearer. He thinks we should have done them all. Well, I just ask
Dr Clark, who is writing notes on this, to tell me how much a policy of doing every
house, which seems to be what Mr Shearer is saying, will cost this country. On this side
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18231
of the House we know that it is managing a growing economy responsibly that allows
us to give the dividends back to families and to do the business for New Zealanders.
This is a responsible Government, working for the people of New Zealand to deliver the
things that we know they want.
Was it not a great families package? Fundamentally, when you think about the
families package and the Budget in total, what does it all sort of mean? Well, I say let us
actually look at the contrast with Austra lia. If you want to know what a Labour-Greens
Government in New Zealand would look like, then look at the Australian Budget. When
Howard left office in 2007, there was no public  debt. Leave it to th e Labor-Greens, and
what a legacy they left Tony Abbott and Mr Hockey to deal with. That is the kind of
David Shearer thinking we have had on home  insulation today. Do not worry about the
money, just promise to do them all. Do not  worry about balancing the books, just say
you will do it and worry about th e money at another time. Bu t we on this side of the
House, through our responsible management, have been able to deliver for families. I
am really proud to be part of a team that  has, through good management, invested more
in families. Really, the fact that families are the first to get the dividends and the
benefits from this growing economy that we are managing is something of a real
pleasure.
Paid parental leave is something that I have had an involvement in. To see us
spending $172 million on that is fantastic for New Zealanders. It is about more and
more. More entitlement—we are moving in two affordable steps from 14 to 18 weeks—
and more eligibility. We are widening it so th at caregivers other than parents, some 800
families more, will receive it on that criteria , and people in less regular work will also
receive more—

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: When will that happen?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: This is not to mention our having done the policy work
that that member over there never did on flexibility of the paid parental leave scheme so
that women, primarily, get the real benefits of  going back to work, attachment to work,
and so on. Just extending the length of paid parental leave in the way that Labour would
want to do, well, frankly, that is lazy, becau se it exacerbates the disparities. Actually,
we have seen from academics in pre-Budget commentary that more important than the
length of entitlement is the targeting, and th at is what we are doi ng. We are effecting a
more modern and diverse set of family arrangements and workplace arrangements.
[Interruption]
They do not like it, because it is true. I know, Mr Assistant Speaker, that you are
about to wind my time up, but I just want to  say, in fairness to  the members opposite
who are retiring, and to one or two of them who should be retiring—not looking at
anyone in particular, Ruth Dyson—that they  were the brains factory of the Labour
Party. As they leave, I do not know who is going to do La bour’s thinking, but on this
side we have done it on paid parental leave.  We are seeing caregivers other than parents
going to get paid parental le ave, as well as grandparents who are working and meet the
criteria, and so on and so forth, and people in  less regular work getting it, and there is
the increased flexibility. This is a Government that is responsibly managing the finances
of this country as they grow, and putting fa milies first. We should all be proud of that
and celebrate that as a country.

items.text: Just before I call the next
