items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: On the topic of retirement, I was
actually in Tauranga not so long ago. The view was expressed to me by members of the
electorate there that they will be very glad when that member Simon Bridges retires. A
number of people said that to me. It wa s not just people who had heard about his
conversations about the Bradford reforms, as  to why power prices were still so high,
where he said “Well, after 15 years they just need a bit more time to bed in.” It was not
that comment that they were complaining about; it was his more recent gaffes.
What that member forgets, though, of cour se, is that people matter—people matter.
He asks how much insulating houses would cost—how much it would cost. He is
always looking for the cost of everythi ng and he understands th e value of nothing—
absolutely nothing. Saving lives is of no consequence. The news I have for that member
is that insulating homes is actually likely to  save costs in our health system. There is
plenty of academic research  out of the University of Otago—an absolutely tip-top
university with an internat ional reputation—that proves th at investment in healthy
housing saves health costs many times over dow n the line. That member would do well
to read some of that researc h, especially with his portfolio responsibilities. But I do not
intend to dwell too long on him, because when he does retire and Rachel Jones takes
over his seat—the excellent, excellent Labour  candidate whom we have in Tauranga,
Rachel Jones—we will see some really good polic y from that part of the country. He is
not universally disliked. [ Interruption] No, no. In fact, I heard Michael Woodhouse
claiming him as his second cousin just the ot her day. So there are a few fans out there.
There are a few fans.
I rise to speak about this Budget here. Mr  Cunliffe has moved a motion for a vote of
no confidence in the Government, which says: “I move, That all wo rds after ‘that’ be
omitted and replaced with: ‘this House has no confidence in a Government that has
failed to put people first; that has widene d gaps, where too many of our children grow
up in poverty; that has failed to provide enough good jobs and has lowered incomes; a
Government that has no vision for our nati on’s long-term wellbeing but is mired in
politics as usual.’ ” That does sum it up. That  does sum it up. Mr Cunliffe has hit the
nail on the head. This is a “f udge-it Budget”. It is a Budget that has fudged its way into
surplus. It has got a finance Minister behind it who has been dotting the i’s and crossing
the t’s, shifting things this way and that, in  order to make sure that his vanity is
preserved in a Budget that just crosses the line.
Of course, we forget too often that Labour produced nine surpluses in its 9 years in
Government, and this is this Government’s very  first surplus in 6 year s. It got there, of
course, by keeping ACC levies $120 million higher than they needed to be, by
disguising $375 million worth of New Zealand Transport Agency spending as a zero-
interest loan, and by spending $560 million less on local infrastructure for the
Canterbury rebuild than it did last year. Th ere is a bunch more fudges in there. We
know there were soft loans to local councils and iwi that ar e listed as a specific fiscal
risk by Treasury. We know that its KiwiSaver auto-enrolment scheme, which cost up to
$290 million, was pushed out for as long as it remains a threat to the Government’s
constructed surplus. We know there are caregiver employment conditions that loom as a
cost to the Government—back-pay relating to equal pay claims and the Minimum Wage
Act. All of these things are swept under the carpet because a surplus was all that this
Government had its eyes on because it had never ever had one before.
This is a Government with the worst economic record in 50 years. You can see why
it was so desperate to get there. But it was at the expense of vision. Labour would have
got there, but we would have got there with a vision for the future. That is the difference
between this side of the H ouse and that side. It had no plan. It is wi dening the gap
between rich and poor, it is wa tching the situation get wors e, it is watching fewer and
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18233
fewer New Zealanders get their first home, a nd those members are content to sit there,
accept their salaries, and do nothing. The La bour Government will be more hands-on.
We will bring down power prices with our NZ  Power plan. We will make sure there are
new houses on the market. We will bring in pr o-growth tax reform in the form of a
capital gains tax. We have a vision for a Ne w Zealand with better jobs and with more
jobs.
Today I want to take a bit of time to speak  about another crazy thing that is wedged
in this Budget document, and that is the cu ts that the Government is hoping to make to
the poison helpline. The 0800 POISON helpline is set to be merged, under the
Government’s current plan, into a combined  helpline with Healthline, Quitline, the
Alcohol Drug Helpline, the National Depressi on Initiative, problem gambling support,
and so on. This is an emergency service. Seconds count. When a child is unconscious,
lying on the floor, convulsing or frothing at the mouth, and a parent picks up the phone
and dials 0800 POISON, they ar e expecting to have expert help. There are toxicologists
on the line immediately, and they are able to  sort the problem. Those who have called
the line have been surveyed, and 90 percent of them said that if they had not got through
on the 0800 POISON line, they would have go ne straight to accident and emergency.
You cannot blame them, but seconds count. The paramedics and the ambulance would
be ringing the 0800 POISON line as well. This is the line that this Government is
proposing to roll in with othe r lines. That could cost live s. It could cost lives. The
National Poisons Centre has operated successfu lly out of Dunedin for 50 years. It is
trusted across the country and it should not be rolled into one line.
The database that supports it is updated c onstantly with product formulas and brand
names that are unique to New Zealand. The people who answer th e phones are expert
toxicologists who update the database. They know their stuff like the back of their hand.
They also know New Zealand place names. They know how far you are from a hospital.
In one of the proposals being looked at, one of the prospective tenders is from
Medibank, an Australian company. It is right  now having conversati ons with the other
helplines, in what looks like a deal behind closed doors, to take over the service. Again,
we are seeing these jobs go off to Australia for a closed-door deal that looks remarkably
like the Skycity deal, where there was one pr ovider that had the inside running, that had
the information on the service, and that was l ooking to bring things together to deliver a
service on behalf of the Government.
You have got to ask why. You have got to ask what is going on there, because it
makes no sense. The poison helpline answers 80  percent of its calls within 20 seconds.
Nowhere else in the world has a poison helpline been integrated, as far as we know,
with other helplines. It is  against the World Health Organization’s best practice
guidelines. Why on earth would we go down th at track? We do not want to move into
the Third World in respect of the emergency services we provide. Why is the Minister
of Health taking us down that track? I have got an online petition. You can sign up. It is
linked to the Labour Party website. It has already surpassed our 2,500 signature target in
2 days. It is gaining signatures rapidly b ecause New Zealanders are worried about their
children. They are worried about the child who swallows some uni dentified pills or
takes something out of the garden shed and who is lying there unc onscious. They know
and they trust that that number on the packet—that 0800 POIS ON number—will be
answered by an expert and that they w ill get immediate help. Why the Government
would want to do without that I do not know.
This Government seems content to select the New Zealand services that will get cut
across the public sector and to let the se rvices provided for every New Zealander run
down whilst the richest 10 percent—the wealthiest 10 percent—get tax breaks and those
in middle New Zealand struggle. They st ruggle. Forty-six percent of middle New
18234 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
Zealanders did not get a wage ri se last year. This is a Govern ment that is content to say
that we have got a rock star  economy. It says that we ha ve got a rock star economy.
Well, those gains are not being shared, and New Zealanders are starting to say “What’s
going on here? Where is Mr Key’s ambition?”. Well, it turns out that that ambition is
for the wealthiest New Zealanders, and for them to take home more and more and more.
Many of the wealthiest New Zealanders are quite happy to share, and I bet that many of
the wealthiest New Zealanders will be keen to see the poison helpline stay, as well.
The Government needs to answer some questions about the poison helpline. The
onus of proof is on the Government. How will the service be improved by having triage
and critical seconds wasted while a desperate parent is on the line trying to explain what
is going on? How will less money be spent if you bring in Medibank or another
provider over the top? The service is nearly half subsidised by the University of Otago.
It will not want to take the risk of produc ing a data bank where it is open to litigation
when the line is run by  another provider. Well, it would be nuts to do so. Why on earth
is the Government proposing to go against World Health  Organization best-practice
guidelines? Why on earth is it wanting to do that? Why is  it wanting to make New
Zealand an outlier by doing away with a worl d-class service? Where is the transparency
in this process?
I urge New Zealand citizens to go to the labour.org.nz website and sign the petition
to save the 0800 POISON number. It is a world- class service. It need s to be preserved.
Questions need to be answer ed by the Minister of Hea lth. In these supplementary
estimates, money is swishing ar ound in relation to these helplines. The Minister needs
to take a call and explain why the Government is doing this to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I am very proud to be associated
with this Government. I would be proud to  vote for it tomorrow, and I am proudly
promoting it in the Hamilton West electorat e. There have been some very fine
contributions to this debate from members on this side of the House, including from
members of our supply and confidence partners. I thank them for highlighting the
important aspects of a Budget that is deliver ing in areas that matter to New Zealanders.
This is a Government that is getting the job done.
Nearly 6 years ago New Zealanders voted  for change. The recession was already
biting. The previous Government had squa ndered the best economic conditions of a
generation. Labour was spending like drunken sa ilors without securi ng the revenue to
fund its commitments. It had encouraged an  explosion in bureaucracy while overseeing
a major decline in the delivery of public services. Treasury was predicting that the
incoming Government would face at least a decade of deficits. So that is why New
Zealanders voted for change. They knew that  the next few years would be difficult.
They were prepared to back a Government th at promised to get its own finances under
control while protecting the vulnerable from the sharp edges of the recession, and that is
what we have done.
One only needs to look at many of the c ountries with which we like to compare
ourselves and those with which we trade— the United Kingdom, the United States of
America, Spain, Portugal, Greece, India,  and the list goes on—t o appreciate the
staggering accomplishments of the John Key - led administration and especially our
excellent Minister of Finance,  the Hon Bill English. As we saw last week, the pain and
the cuts are now really biting across the Tasman as the new Australian Government
attempts to rescue that country from the ra vages and the irresponsibility of the former
Labor-Greens Government. What a grim warni ng that is to all New Zealanders to not
put it all at risk on this side of the Tasm an when they go to the polls on 20 September
this year.
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18235
Earlier this evening I heard some of th e Hon Nick Smith’s contribution to this
debate. He quite rightly made the point that  New Zealand’s level of debt would have
reached bankruptcy levels if the former  Labour Government’s reckless fiscal
mismanagement had continued beyond 2008. So I say to the member for Dunedin
North, David Clark, who barracks across the H ouse regularly about this Government’s
economic record, that he knows, and, more important, his constituents in Dunedin North
know, that this Government ha s rescued the country and its  finances from the worst
Labour Government they have ever seen.
I am very proud of our achievements in get ting the books back into surplus within 5
years, not least because the previous Government delighted in spending all the money it
had and plenty it did not have when it was clear that it was headed for electoral
oblivion. Achieving that feat of  a surplus in half the time that Treasury predicted to the
incoming Government it would take was comme ndable in itself. But given that no one
knew then what devastation lay ahead for th e people of Canterbury and the city of
Christchurch, it is nothing short of remarkable . As others have noted in this debate,
getting back into surplus is important because it gives the Government, and New
Zealanders generally, choices. It means that we can start planning for future debt
repayments and contributions to the Supera nnuation Fund. I and others on this side of
the House are determined to achieve both of those goals, in order to ensure that our
children and their children are not saddle d with an impossible burden that would
encourage many who could to leave our shor es, and cause living standards to plummet
for those who would have to stay behind.
It has been utterly disingenuous to hear  members opposite crying crocodile tears in
this debate about our country ’s indebtedness, while every reasonable person knows that
those same members who were here during th e 9 long years of the Clark administration
are responsible for it. Had the voters not interv ened as decisively as they did in 2008,
the debt projections now would be astronomi cal. In the critical ar eas of managing the
Crown’s finances, this is a Government that  is getting the job done. When it comes to
delivering better public services, which is a major responsibility of any Government and
one of the clear priorities of this one, some demanding targets have been set and met
right across the board, and again we are getting the job done.
In the time remaining I want to focus on some recent announcements that have been
warmly welcomed in Hamilton and elsewhere, I am sure. Prior to Budget day we heard
about the terrific initiatives to deal with this worrying problem of rheumatic fever. This
is an issue that we thought had been dealt with a generation ago and now it has come
back. It is striking at communities right around the country. We have to deal with it and
we have put measures in place to ensure that it can be dealt with. We have seen the new
measures for children who need cochlear impl ants. Again, this is something that those
living in the deaf community have been calling for for a long time. Because of our
responsible fiscal management, we are now in  a position to deal with it. I look forward
to seeing people in my area and elsewhere being able to take advantage of this terrific
initiative. These were the things that peopl e were talking to me about when I was in
Rotorua a couple of weeks ago and last week end in Hamilton at the Women’s Lifestyle
Expo. It is the sort of thing that matters to families.
So, of course, the next thing is to look at how the Budget delivered for our families
and our children. I was pleased to hear Barbara Stewart, my colleague from the Waikato
region, acknowledging the importance of the fr ee doctors visits for children under 13. I
am sure that this is something that is warmly welcomed across the House. I am sure that
we are all pleased to see that it is being delivered. It is part of a $500 million package of
measures to support children and families, and $90 million of that is being spent on
those free doctors visits. There will be $171.8 million allocated to increase paid parental
18236 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
leave to 18 weeks by 2016. We have heard a lot about that issue in recent times. I am
proud to be part of a Government that is delivering on it.
There is the $42.3 million measure to increase the parental tax credit. That was
something introduced by National back in 1999. It helps families with newborn children
who are not on a benefit and who are not receiving paid parental leave.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Say something original. Stop reading your research notes.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: To the member who is chirpi ng at the moment, I would remind
her that many of those people are the ones who used to be called “Mike Moore’s
battlers” and the “Kiwi battlers”. The Labour Party fought for them , but it does not any
more. Now it is National that is delivering.
There is a substantial incr ease to early childhood educat ion. We are seeing results,
with far more children being enrolled in early childhood education. That will benefit
them for a lifetime. We have more th an doubled expenditure on early childhood
education while we have been in office. As the Minister for Social Development talked
about earlier this evening, th at vital $33 million package to help vulnerable children
includes eight new children’s teams around the country. I hope a nd expect to see
something in the Waikato to identify and work  with our at-risk children. We are getting
the job done in really important ways.
Could I close just by payi ng a tribute to budget adviso ry services right around the
country.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: More money.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: In Hamilton, the Hamilton Budgeting Advisory Trust is one of
those budgeting services doing tr emendous work, as my colleague Dr Calder is noting,
with financially vulnerable members of our  community. I meet regularly with that
wonderful team in my city of  Hamilton. I am full of admiration for the work they do. It
is practical, it is compassionate, and it is making a real difference for families.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Effective.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: It is, as Dr Calder says, effective. There is so much I would like
to be able to speak about, but  I am pleased with that $22  million package for the budget
advisory services. I am proud of this Budge t. I return to my theme. This is a
Government that is getting the job done, and I will be proud to campaign on it right
through to 20 September.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next
speaker, this is to advise the House that th is is a split call. The first one will be the
honourable member Gareth Hughes, and he will get the bell with 1 minute to go.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou, kia ora. I know that I am not the ol dest member in the House tonight, but I
know that Budgets are not what they were once upon a time, when all New Zealanders
would tune in on the wireless and hear th e news coming out of Wellington to find out
how it affected them, their family, and thei r community. They are sort of more muted
affairs now, but they still have a huge  impact on our national economy and on
households. I think that Budget 2014 is a great  time to take stock of how our national
economy is doing, but, more important, to take  stock of how that national economy is
working for all New Zealanders.
Budget 2014 was all about the surplus. Bill English has, over 5 years, made this the
only measure of success. It was a test so im portant that he would have sold off the
energy assets and juggled the numbers in the books just to achieve it, which is exactly
what we saw happen. This was always going to be the surplus Budget and, although we
celebrate the increase in free doctors visits  for 5 to 13-year-olds and the small extra
funding for things like comput ers in homes, which are some  good little initiatives, we
also acknowledge that the Greens would have got us to surplus, too. In  fact, in the last
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18237
election we were the only party that took a net fiscal position to the electors of New
Zealand that would have seen a Green Government paying down more debt. So
achieving a surplus was good, but as economists  like to say about surpluses—and it is
important to point out that economists are al so like weather forecasts  in that they are
often wrong. You know, it is the only field where you can win a Nobel Prize disproving
the truth of someone before you. It is an area where th e Treasury analysts and the
economists focus just on the numbers. Well, what we also have to focus on are the real
people.
This year, while people were maybe reading about the surplus in the newspapers, we
also saw that people were struggling. I wa s visiting them in Wellington, in the soup
kitchen, on Monday. We see them sleeping in cars in Canterbury. We see numerous
families to a home in South Auckland. When we talk about the surplus in the Budget,
what does it mean? An economy that work s for all New Zealanders. Right now,
internationally, what we see is that the richest 1 percent have 16 percent of the wealth,
yet the bottom half have only 5 percent of  the wealth. Right now, in National’s New
Zealand, 290,000 Kiwi kids are gr owing up in poverty. It is a travesty that in this land
of ours, which feeds and exports food for 20 m illion people, our kids  are still going to
school without food in their bell ies. At a time when busines s confidence is up, we have
got to ask ourselves whether the economy is  working for all New Zealanders, when we
look back and we reflect that we work some of the longest hours for some of the lowest
wages and pay some of the highest costs of living in the developed world.
As Russel Norman pointed out in his B udget speech, the legacy of this National
Government will be 30 percent of children li ving in poverty, a 50 percent increase in
greenhouse gas emissions, and debt—mountai ns and mountains of debt. When John
Key took that seat in 2008, our net Govern ment debt was around $16 billion. Since then
it has increased to over $61 billion. The interest is being paid by all of us—by our future
generations, and our kids. At a time wh en Bill English is focusing on the Budget
surplus, this election we will be pointing out the other surpluses—the surpluses of
poverty, of inequality, and of  pollution. The only thing that this Government cannot
point to is a surplus in housing or housing ideas and solutions.
In the 20 September lead-up we are quite happy to be talking about the surplus of
inequality and of poverty, but we are also going to be talking about the deficit—the
deficit of ideas, of innovation,  and of leadership, which ar e the things our country is
crying out for. Our Budget shows the crit ical challenges and problems facing New
Zealand into the future. Depending on raw l ogs and milk exports around the world is
not a credible economic strategy. The taxpayer subsidies for the Choruses, the T īwai
Points, the Anadarkos, and the Skycities may he lp the Cabinet club mates, but it is not
helping those real families who are sleeping in cars or where there are many families to
a home.
Our economy is more simplified, and more  dependent on raw commodity exports,
than ever. What it is time fo r is thinking of a future Budge t, a Budget that has a surplus
of hope; a Budget that presses Ctrl-Alt-Delete on National’s failed economic agenda for
the 1 percent and reboots to a richer New Zealand; a Budget that has a surplus of clean
energy, building a clean energy economy and an internet economy, which thrives and
brings in IT businesses to New Zealand with  a second internet cable; and a Budget that
ditches the Government Communications  and Security Bureau Act and the
Telecommunications (Interception Capability an d Security) Act. So this election, while
National is offering a deficit of ideas and a surplus of pollution and inequality, we will
be offering a surplus of hope, real lead ership, a clean economy, and an innovative
economy, protecting our environment and lifting our kids out of poverty. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: Mr Speaker—
18238 Budget Debate 21 May 2014

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Steffan Browning. It is not a race, Mr King.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I note in this Budget,  in the vote for primary
industries, that there seems to be very little extra for biosecurity, and yet consistently we
have new incursions in New Zealand of pests that are costing us hundreds of millions of
dollars. I will point out that through these r ecent years, there have been pests that we
will recognise by name, like wester n flower thrips, guava moths—[ Interruption]—the
National Party, varroa mite, lettuce aphids, tomato and potato psyllid. It has cost a huge
amount to our horticultural industry alrea dy. There is the Hadda beetle, which the
Government gave up on eradicating, and varroa mite, which it gave up on eradicating.
The Greens have a different vision. This Budget has no vision for primary industries
that we can see in there at all. There is cost-cutting all over the place and minimal
increases in any area at all. We would have  smart, green agriculture and we would be
preserving the future for our farming families. We would be using organics more and
more. We would be concerned about climat e change in a real way and in having
resilience in our farming systems—diverse farm ing systems. Biosecurity is integral to
that. It is integral even to agriculture a nd horticulture as we see it right now, today, in
this country.
The Hadda beetle, which the Government gave up on in 2010, is expected to cost
New Zealand $100 million over 20 years. Yes, th e cost of eradication was going to be
expensive—$200 million over 4 years, and that  was why the Government came to that
conclusion—because it let it in in the first place and then did not nip it in the bud. The
painted apple moth cost the Government $65 million, and I suppose that that was a bit
of a fright. Varroa mite cost $20 million, a nd then that eradication was aborted. Then
there are the other ones that have been given up on, like Dutch elm disease, potato
spindle tuber viroid, a leaf miner in euca lyptus, and the lettuce aphid, as I have
mentioned before. The fruit fly incursion has been jumped on quite quickly.
However, what are these pests doing getting in, in the first place? The systems are
letting us down in terms of what is getti ng in. I had a look in the Budget to see where I
could find the figures for an increase in bor der control, and I could not find any. There
is a limited increase—a very limited incr ease—in some money around biosecurity, but
when you put it into real terms there is no real increase at all.
If fruit fly really got going, it would cost $800 million in the Bay of Plenty in the first
year. But there is something else I want to put to members, which is that eradicating
foot-and-mouth would cost $8 bil lion in the first year, if that  got in here. This time last
year the Auditor-General said that we are not foot-and-mouth disease ready; we are not
prepared. Then, on April Fool’s Day this year, the Government came out—yes, on April
Fool’s Day; 1 April 2014—and, through the Mini stry for Primary Industries, said: “We
reckon we’re ready.”
I do not believe that the country is ready because, at the same time, the Government
has let a particular strain of Theileria orient alis, or Ikeda, go loose, and even today in
our newsroom we hear that the big movement of cattle is about to be undertaken and the

items.speaker: Government is saying
items.text: “Look, farmers, try to make sure you don’t share it around.” This
should have been nipped in the bud, and it could have been nipped in the bud if the
Government had used the system it has got, National Animal Identification and Tracing,
and proved that we are foot-and-mouth ready. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: This is just to advise the
House that we have a split call.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It was certainly a blue-letter day for all
provinces in New Zealand on 15 May because of the consistent, reliable, and good
management of this nation’s economy. Low interest rates can never be undervalued
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18239
when you are in the primary industry, nor can low inflation be minimised. Those are the
two evils that were left as a legacy from  the Labour-Greens Government. In fact, when
we look at it, 2014 is a very good time for th e provinces. It is a very good time for the
Kaikōura electorate. I am proud to say that this Friday we will turn the sod on our third
new hospital in 6 years. So the provinces are certainly being looked after well by this
Government.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Only three?

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Only three. However, it is all good news from there, and it gets
better.
When you look across at the Australi an economy, one gets a very clear
understanding of what a Labour-Greens Govern ment leaves as a legacy. What did we
see as a legacy from the last Labour Govern ment? We hear a lot about it. Labour’s last
Budget left this nation with a $4 billion defic it. The last Labour B udget left this nation
with a $4 billion deficit and deficits for the ne xt decade. So from that point of view, it
was pretty good to be on this side of the House, seeing Bill Englis h as the Minister of
Finance give his sixth Budget and having the country back in the black.
One of the standout points was the $500 million that put families at the very heart of
this Budget. When we stop and look at that, it means that, effectively, 400,000 New
Zealanders will benefit from th at family package. I am very proud to see that we have
been able to do that. You get to that space economically only when you have good fiscal
management. So 400,000 people—how is it goi ng to be dished up ? There is $171
million to boost the paid parental leave scheme. That is excellent. There is $42.3 million
as far as the parental tax credit is concer ned. That is something that National introduced
way back in 1999, and it has increased it by e ffectively 50 percent to $220 a week and
extended it to 10 weeks to really balance the equation with regard to parental leave.
Then there is the crowning glory of that  Budget—the $90 million to enable general
practitioners to offer free medical visits  and free prescriptions. Can you believe it?
There will be free medical attention and fr ee prescriptions for pe ople under the age of
13. That has got to be something that we can all be very proud of. It shows you that
families are at the very heart of this G overnment—families. There is $155.7 million to
make sure that we keep working towa rds those goals of getting 98 percent—98
percent—early childhood educat ion participation by our youngsters. Then, of course,
we have got to look at the Ministry of Soci al Development. It ha s really got to grips
with some of the very challenging situations that we see, and is tr ying to bridge those
gaps that obviously from time to time appear with the eight extra Children’s Teams,
which will really start focusing on that. It is my expectation that we will have one of
those in Blenheim, because we are ready and willing to go.
This Government has really se t Marlborough up. It has set Kaik ōura up. It has set
North Canterbury up. We are in particularly good shape and we have got to thank Bill
English and the National-led Government for that, under the stellar leadership of John
Key. There is a lot more I could say about this Budget, but time has got away on me and
I must yield to my fellow member. I look forward to his speech. Thank you.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Kia orana, Mr Assistant Speaker. This is a Budget
that is back in black. If we were to say th at the Budget is red, we  would know that that
is a Budget in debt. We know that the country  knows that if it has a Government that is
red and green, it will have a Budget in debt. I see my co lleague Mr Kris Faafoi over
there. As I listened to his speech about the Budget, I notic ed that he used interesting
words. He used theatrical words. I do realis e that he did train in journalism, but I think
what he did not tell the House, the audience out there, and the nation is that he actually
got an A+ for creative writing. That is right.  He got that for creative writing. So these
18240 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
are the words that he used. He used the word “disgraceful”. He said these words: “It was
disgraceful. It was disgusting. What sort of Budget was this?”.
He went even further. He decided to give an example of a chemist from his
electorate, Mana. He took his beloved leader , David Cunliffe—and he needed to do this
because it is well known that the community does not know him. That is right. It was on
the news. People asked: “Who is David Cun liffe?”. So he is doing his job. He is
winning brownie points. He is taking his leader out so that the community will know
him. He went out. Then he gave this theatri cal story about this chemist and how he saw
the prescriptions on the shelf waiting to be picked up. He said: “How disgraceful that
that has happened.” With his theatrical sk ills and his creative writing he told a
wonderful story. But when you looked in the eyes of that member, you knew that he
was not sincere. Why was he not sincere? I will tell you why. If he had read the Budget,
like everyone reads the Budget, he would know that this is what we are doing for health.
Free drop-ins for sore throat clinics will ex pand the target for dealing with rheumatic
fever to 90,000 children. There is $90 million in the Budget allocated to funding doctors
visits for under-13s, making them free.
That is our voice, but how about we ta ke it from the people out there in the
community? This has got to hurt because this is a little bit of evidence. There was an
interview that was done on 16 Ma y by Martin Johnston that sa ys this: “A child health
expert has hailed the policy to extend free GP visits [as] restoring justice for
children,”—restoring justice for children. That  expert was Diana Lennon, the Auckland
University professor of population health  of children and youth. She expects the
Government’s $30 million a year policy, a surprise announcement in the Budget, will
lead to better management of skin infections by removing the medical clinic cost barrier
faced by many families. That is even the fa milies down in Mana, and it is even the
families who will pick up a prescription at the chemist that Mr Faafoi talked about.
But let us go a bit further. Why? Because those members like to bang the drum about
poverty. They like to talk about South Auckla nd. I am not sure wh ether Mr Hughes has
actually been there. They like to talk about pe ople sleeping in cars. But this is what is
also coming. It is from Dr Nikki Turner of the Child Poverty Action Group. This is
what she says: “It’s really important for families. It takes the pressure off them about
the cost of visiting their GP. It’s important for the people who have to sit at home and
wonder whether they should take th eir sick kids to the doctor or  not. It’s got to be part
of a bigger picture…”. We know that this Budget is delivering for families and for those
in need.
I want to say this. There is all this talk a bout poverty. There is a ll this talk about the
fact of children in need. But I want to say to those members to stop using the people and
their circumstances to make them feel good, because that is  what we are hearing out
there. The communities in M āngere—that is South Auckland, Mr Hughes, OK? In the
South Auckland communities that I work with, the people who come and knock on my
door are faced with two things. It is either choice or circ umstance. This Budget and the
way that we are working as a Government does this—it is truth and love. In other
words, here is the truth and here is the real ity that we want to face, but it is not with
callousness or carelessness, but instead it is with love. We  applaud this Budget. Thank
you.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Tonight there are thousands of
people throughout New Zealand either watc hing Parliament TV or listening to
Parliament on the radio. I acknowledge what my Green colleague said before, that once
upon a time there would have been hundred s and hundreds of thousands of New
Zealanders tuned in tonight to this debate, to listen to the important Budget discussion.
That is not to say that the discussion is not important. It is to say, though, that the power
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18241
of Parliament to communicate to our country has changed. I think that is something
important for us to reflect upon tonight. Parliame nt TV is almost 7 y ears old, and it is a
really important institution in our country. I hope that this Government is not going to
try to destroy it, as it has destroyed public broadcasting in this country.
This is supposed to be an honest debate. Unfortunately, it does not feel like an honest
debate, from listening to some of the comme nts and the speeches tonight from the other
side of the House. This Budget is being framed by this Government as being a Budget
about jobs and a growing economy. I have just got off the phone tonight from a call
from one of the 101 workers in South Ota go who were made redundant yesterday. This
person is part of a group of 180 people who have been made redundant in the last month
from a forest industry enterpri se in South Otago that has f our different plants spread
across four different towns—Mosgiel, Milburn, Milton, and Balclutha. This worker told
me tonight: “It sucks. It sucks what’s happeni ng to us.” He has been working in that
plant for 12 years. He is a good, honest, solid working person, just like the many
hundreds and thousands of good, solid working people who ha ve lost their jobs in
regional New Zealand under this  Government. This is through no fault of his own and
in an industry that should be expanding, gr owing, and thriving, rath er than contracting
and putting people in regional New Zealand out of work.
This person told me tonight that he does not know where his future lies. He has got
three children. They are settled in schools. He may need to leave town to find a job
somewhere else. I would like Government me mbers to get up and tell me tonight what
the future is for him and the other people in  that industry. I would also like the list
member for Dunedin to speak out and stick up for his city and his region, and say where
the job growth is going to come from in that  region. We have just  seen 180 jobs lost
from South Otago in the last month. If that is the sign of a Govern ment that is focused
on growth and jobs, then it is a fairy tale. It is a fairy tale; it is an absolute fairy tale.
One of the important things to note in this debate, though, is that under a Labour
Government the forest industry and the fo rest-processing industry will be a priority,
because we actually have a plan for that indus try, as we do for a number of industries. I
have not seen a plan for any industries under this Government. There is rhetoric—there
is lots of rhetoric. But when it comes to an actual plan for industry development and
growth and actual jobs, where is it? Under a Labour Govern ment, however, the forestry
industry and the forest-processing industry will be a priority.
In a region such as Otago and Southland this makes a huge difference. Our region
contains 11.8 percent of New Zealand’s forest  plantations, which is by far the largest
area in the South Island, a nd it is the second-la rgest in the countr y. But of the $4.5
billion per annum that that industry is worth, half of those exports are raw logs that are
being processed offshore. That is why we ar e seeing 180 jobs go—the latest set of jobs.
Since 2013, 40 sawmills have closed, resulting in the loss of 1,700 jobs across the
country, so I do not think we ha ve seen the last of the demi se of this industry in this
country under this Government. Under a Labour Government it would be very different.
I would also like to address the rhetoric that has been spouted on the other side of the
House that this is a Budget that is focused on health. Well, when you look beneath the
surface, this actually represents a cut, and it certainly does represent a cut in our region.
There is a 2.3 percent cut in real terms; that is what this Budget means in health
funding. When Tony Ryall, the Minister of Health, hyped up the Budget, saying it was
the biggest funding of the health sector to date, he neglected to admit that when you
take into account demographic and popul ation changes, which any responsible
Government would do, it put a massive extra st rain on the health sector and district
health boards.
18242 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
In the Southern District Health Board area, which is the whole of Otago and
Southland, as I understand it from looking at th e Budget figures, it is going backwards.
It is a 0.2 percent cut and it is going to mean extra stra in on the staffing, which is
already under stress; on the services be ing provided to the community; on primary
health care; on the numbers of people who ar e being referred by their specialists to be
getting operations and are not actually ending up on waiting lists; and pressure on the
Dunedin Hospital, which is well out of da te for being upgraded and replaced—extra
strain, essentially, on the whole of the health servic e throughout that whole region.
Again, I say to the list member for Dunedin sitting across the House, who is very busy
doing his work, that this is act ually a critical area for him to  address, and certainly one
that he will be held accountable for in Dunedin.
I would also like to reinforce my support for the petition that my Dunedin colleague
David Clark has put out there tonight to k eep the National Poisons Centre phone line
going. All you have to do is go to the La bour Party website—which is labour.org.nz,
and it is right on the front page; really easy to connect to—and sign that petition. That is
the poison phone line that you ring if you know someone who has been taking the
psychoactive substances and is  suffering the health effect s of that. As I understand it,
because I have stood in this House on numerous occasions, the numbers of people
reporting effects from those substances have  increased extraordinarily in the past
months. To axe that poison phone line would be  disastrous, an absolute backward step,
and it is gobsmacking to understand why that would actually happen.
This is a Budget that takes us backwards. It  is a Budget of inequa lity. It is a Budget
that is not focusing on regional job growth. It is a Budget that is taking us backwards in
terms of our health care. It is not a Budget that any Government could be proud of.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. There is an old
saying that no good deed goes unpunished, and I suspect that that phrase would resonate
with the New Zealand police force at th e moment, which has performed in an
exemplary manner in recent times, in the last several years. The reward is to see its
budget cut yet again. For the fourth or fifth year in a row our police force is being asked
to do more with less. It seems a perverse reward for an organisation that has done
everything this Government has asked of it. It has done a great deal of what the New
Zealand population has asked of it. It continues to be forward-looking and to be creative
in its use of resources, and the reward is to suffer a budget cut. I cannot understand the
logic or the reasoning behind that.
We understand that Minister Tolley is only one  Minister in Cabinet. I believe that
that Minister has done some good things in her portfolios of  policing and corrections,
but, nevertheless, in the police force and, in fact, across the justi ce sector collectively
there has been a significant cut in the available resources. That is a very strange decision
made by this Government.
I give credit and I acknowledge recently  retired Commissioner Marshall, whom I
believe did an excellent job of changing the culture of the police force. He was an
admirable officer. He did an extremely good job of changing the culture of the New
Zealand Police, and that is an extremely br ave ambition. It is an extremely ambitious
objective—to change the culture of an or ganisation to which change does not come
easily or naturally.
I believe that initiatives like Prevention First and th e neighbourhood policing units
are strategies and techniques th at resonate with New Zealande rs. To some extent that is
back to the future. Crime prevention is the be st way to deal with crime and to avoid it
happening. We know that. The Prevention First strategy has been very effective. We
have seen a reduction in some offending. We cannot entirely take credit for that; it is an
21 May 2014 Budget Debate 18243
international phenomenon, some of it related to demographics, to science, to hard
security around premises, and so on.
But the fact is that the police have actual ly risen to the occasion. They have changed
their strategy. They have changed their ta ctics. They have changed their way of
operating, in ways that have b een beneficial and that have served to make our society
and community safer. The reward is that this Budget has taken money away from them
and insisted that yet again they must look to take cuts. You can cut fat. You can cut
flesh. The police are now being asked to cut to the bone. That is perverse, and it is going
to have very unfortunate outcomes.
The president of the Police Association, who is not a fellow given to extreme
language or rhetoric, has said that there is an increasing ri sk of operational failures and
that fear of crime will quickly return wh en the police cannot respond or do not get a
response right. The police have demonstrated that they can make New Zealanders feel
safer and that they can contribute to reducing crime.
The peculiar logic that I am endeavouring to  understand from this Government is to
say that because they have succeeded, we w ill take money away from them. What it is
overlooking is the fact that the Prevention First strategy and the neighbourhood policing
units are people-intensive strategies. Yes,  we know that the police are using new
technologies, and they are using them very well. They are using electronics, they are
using cellphones, they are using GPS system s, and they are using iPads to reduce the
amount of time that officers spend bent over wo rd processors at police stations rather
than being out there providing a face-to-face service to New Zealanders.
These are very people-intensive strate gies. We know that the task of the
neighbourhood police unit, for example, is to create units of officers— a sergeant, and a
number of constables—who will know who the troubled people are in their community.
They will know where the hot spots are in their community. That takes time and
commitment, and it requires good morale.
We heard, and I recall very well, Commissione r Marshall talking a bout the extent to
which a generation ago or even a decade ago young police officers in particular built
their morale from the excitement and the th rill of the chase—ch arging around in cars,
catching people, chasing offende rs down a road and arresting them. That is how they
built their morale. Modern policing, the sort  of policing that our police force now
aspires to do, is a hard gri nd. It lacks some of that ad renalin-fuelled interest and
excitement because the police are seeking to  prevent crime, and you do that by building
relationships within a community, by talk ing to the youth, and by understanding where
the pressure points are in a community. That is people-intensive. It demands a great deal
of time. That is where these Budget cuts are going to show most badly.
I recall having conversations with district  commanders, with senior police officers,
and with officers on the beat, who all agreed that good police morale is critical to the
success of the Prevention First strategy a nd of the forward-looking—shall I say—
modern policing approach, rather than simp ly putting men and women in cars to go out
and chase burglars and offenders  of other sorts. They need to actually engage with the
community. As I said, it is a back to the futu re approach, where we actually treat police
officers as pillars of our community and re spect them as such. That respect comes
through because they engage with the commun ity, with the troubled people, with those
who are damaged, with the youths, and with the offenders.
To the extent that thei r budget is being cut, what sort of a message  is that sending to
those very hard-working men and women? For those men and women with a significant
commitment to a safe community, to limiting harm done on the roads, and to limiting
offending, the message is very clearly that , actually, this Government does not value
those people or the enormous commitment a nd the very difficult and demanding tasks
18244 Budget Debate 21 May 2014
that they undertake on a da ily basis. The cuts  to their budget are saying: “Look, you’ve
done really well and we expect you to do more  with a great deal less.” That is a very
perverse message to send.
I look forward to a time personally when we can cut the police budgets. I certainly
look forward to a time when we can cut the corrections budgets, because we will have
less offending. That time is not now. This Government’s budgeting is the Budget of
parsimony. It is cost cutting. It is penny-pinching in the servi ce of this illusory surplus,
which the Government would have New Zealanders believe it has generated.
This is a very, very dangerous and foolis h place to cut costs—the front-line people
who are out there, on a daily basis, keep ing our communities safe, reducing offending,
and looking to provide service on the roads. The people who serve our communities in a
very difficult and dangerous wa y are getting the message that actually their work is not
respected and it is not valued, because the do llars are not being provided for them to do
that job. The reason they have succeeded is  that they have found efficiencies. For at
least 5 years, and even longer than that, th e police have learnt to do more with less.
They have used technology in a very intelligent way. They have sought to maximise the
amount of good work that ever y individual officer can do in their 8-hour shift, their 10-
hour shift, or their 12-hour sh ift. And their perverse rewa rd is to be told: “Well,
actually, we respect and value you so much, we’re going to make you do even more
with even less.”
This is not the time to be parsimonious. This is not the time to cut costs or cut
corners in terms of policing. Nor is it the time to be reducing th e funding available to
the justice sector more generally. Ther e has been a very good analysis done by
JustSpeak, and I recommend Government me mbers read it through. JustSpeak is the
youth arm of Rethinking Crime and Puni shment—young people with a commitment to
peaceful and safe communities and to na tural justice being done. JustSpeak has
highlighted very well that we have seen ove r the last several year s a chipping away at
the funding available. A justice system can work only if it is properly resourced.
We have seen the debacle of the endeavour to put the courts in a more efficient place.
The eBench has failed badly. The management of that project has fallen over. That is
unfortunate because we know that our courts are overstretched. Justice delayed is justice
denied, and we are not seeing the efficiency  and the streamlining in the court system
that this Government promised. It stood up and said it would make the courts work
better, and it has failed to do that.
We have seen ongoing cuts to legal aid. The most vulnerabl e, the least well-off, and
the people most likely to offend and most lik ely to be offended against are the people
who are going to continue to suffer because of short-term penny-pinching and, as I have
said, because of very misguided, perverse d ecisions that are made that because some
parts of the justice sector are succeedi ng, we will therefore reduce their funding. We
will therefore take money away from them a nd make it even harder for them to achieve
the outcomes that we all aspire for them to achieve.
I give thanks and I do offer our respects to  the police force and those hard-working
people in the justice sector. We look forwar d to a time when thei r activities will be
properly rewarded and resourced. Kia ora.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 21 MAY 2014 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Myanmar—Speaker, House of Nationalities 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House 
that His Excellency U Khin Aung Myint,  Speaker of the Myanmar House of 
Nationalities, is present in th e precincts of the Chamber. I am sure that members would 
wish that he be welcomed and accorded a seat on the left of the Chair. I also 
acknowledge the Speaker’s delegation in the gallery. 
U Khin Aung Myint, accompanied by the Deputy Speaker, entered the Chamber and 
took a seat on the left of the Chair. 
SITTINGS OF THE HOUSE 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Deputy Leader of the House) : In accordance with 
discussions at the Business Committee, I seek leave for the House to suspend for the 
dinner break at the conclusion of the Hon Shane Jones’ valedictory statement today. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Prime Minister—Appointment of GCSB Director, Dotcom Case, and  
Drone Strikes 
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: 
Does he stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Why did he state on 4 April 2013 that the role he played in Ian 
Fletcher’s appointment as head of the G overnment Communications Security Bureau 
(GCSB) was “Only that the State Services  Commissioner came to me”—came to me—
“with the recommendation.”, when in fact he  personally phoned him to encourage him 
to apply for the job? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Because at the time I was asked in the House, that was my 
recollection. At the end of the day, it was my appointment anyway. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Who organised the breakfast meetings on 17 June 2011 and 12 
March 2010 between him and Ian Fletcher at the Stamford Plaza and Hyatt Regency 
respectively? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I cannot be 100 percent sure , but, to the best of my 
recollection, it would be my office. 
Hon David Cunliffe: Given that, to the best of his recollection, his office organised 
both meetings, is it correct that the 17 June breakfast was held 3 days after he signed off 
on the interview panel for the GCSB director ’s position and 3 weeks before the existing 
shortlist of candidates for that  position was scrapped; if so, does he still claim that the 
GCSB role was not discussed with Mr Fletcher at that breakfast? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In answer to the last part of the question, yes. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Was anyone from the Departme nt of Prime Minister and 
Cabinet or his office present at the mee ting held on 14 December 2011 to brief on 
Operation Debut against Mr Kim Dotcom? 
18160 Questions for Oral Answer 21 May 2014 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, no one from my office was. I cannot be sure whether the 
Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet had a representative there. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Does he stand by his statement “We share information in 
isolated cases about New Zealanders with our  partners, and we do that when there’s a 
really good reason to do that .”; if so, what policy govern s when and how the GCSB 
shares that information and whether any limits are placed upon its subsequent use? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes—some, where it is believed to be relevant. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Has the Prime Minister sought  or received any advice on 
whether remote operations such as drone strikes against non-combatants or in non-
declared conflicts are compatible with international law? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. 
Budget 2014—Government Expenditure and Interest Rates 
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance : In 
preparing Budget 2014, what advice did the Government receive on how responsible 
fiscal management will take pressure off interest rates for New Zealand households and 
businesses? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: The Government recognises that interest  rates are the single largest cost on 
families with a mortgage. That is why we are focused very much on keeping rates lower 
for longer—certainly, much lower than the almost 11 percent mortgage rates of 2008. In 
that context, the Budget has struck a very good balance between investing in priority 
areas such as families and children and staying on track for surplus without putting 
undue pressure on interest rates. Last week the Minister of Finan ce released Treasury 
advice showing the impact of increasing the Budget operating allowance. The allowance 
is the amount set aside at each Budget for new policy initiatives, spending, or revenue 
initiatives. This advice confirmed that increasing the allowance to $1.5 billion in Budget 
2015 is around the upper limit before it begins to materially affect interest rates. 
David Bennett : What did Treasury’s advice sa y would be the wider economic 
consequences of significantly higher Government spending? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : That is a very good question, and one that the Opposition 
should listen to carefully. We  all know what those conse quences would be. We saw 
them in 2008 when Government spending in creased sharply. Floating mortgage rates 
reached almost 11 percent, which hurt hous eholds and businesses across the country. 
Treasury advised that in an economy expect ed to be operating at  or above capacity, 
significantly higher spending would lead to a more pronounced  interest rate cycle, push 
the New Zealand dollar higher, and push intere st rates up. This would increase pressure 
on the tradable sector and work against efforts to rebalance the economy and create 
jobs. Treasury said lifting the annual operati ng allowance to $1.5 billion would have an 
official cash rate impact of around 0.15 to 0.3 over 4 years. The Government would still 
meet its objective of reduci ng net Crown debt to 20 pe rcent of GDP by 2019-20. You 
can simply imagine how much higher interest ra tes would be if we sa w the sort of large 
operating allowances we saw under the previous Government. 
David Bennett : Why did the Government seek Tr easury advice about the likely 
impact on interest rates of an increase in the annual operating allowance? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Because interest rates are very important to Kiwi families. 
The Government wanted to modestly increas e spending in priority  areas but remain 
fiscally responsible and not put undue upward pressure on interest rates. This will 
provide options for targeting extra investment to further improve public services, repay 
debt, resume contributions to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and possibly 
make modest tax reductions in future years. However, it is very important that we do 
21 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18161 
not return to the big spending increases of the mid-2000s, whic h, together with a 
doubling of house prices, forced the Reserve Bank to push up th e official cash rate to a 
record 8.25 percent. That is why we sought the advice. 
David Bennett: How does the Government’s planned $1.5 billion annual allowance 
for Budget 2015 compare with allowances up to 2008, and what were the consequences 
of those large previous allowances? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The proposed $1.5 billion annua l operating allowance is a 
very modest one compared with allowances before 2008. As the Mi nister mentioned at 
the Budget lock-up last Thursday, the final year cost of the five Budgets to 2008 
averaged almost $4 billion per Budget. In fa ct, the final year allowance in Budget 2008 
alone was a whopping $7 billion. The impact of that sort of reckless Government 
spending was obvious. Floating mortgage intere st rates were almost 11 percent, the 
economy went into recession ahead of the gl obal financial crisis, exporters were going 
backwards very quickly, and we were left with a $3.9 billion fiscal deficit in 2008-09—
before the global financial crisis and be fore the Canterbury earthquakes—because 
revenue could not support that high spending. We certainly would not want to go back 
to that situation again— 
Hon Trevor Mallard: 2008-09 wasn’t before the GFC. That’s just nonsense. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : It is absolutely correct, Mr Mallard. Y ou should listen 
carefully, because that is why the New Zeal and public will not support your party to 
come back. 
Capital Gains Tax—Investment Properties 
3. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: 
Has he received any report from the Treasur y disproving the analysis from Westpac’s 
chief economist that a proposed  15 percent tax on capital ga ins on investment property 
would have a significant effect on the net pr esent value of resident ial rental property 
investments; if so, will he table that Treasury report? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: Firstly, for the benefit of the member, I note that Westpac advises that its 
absolute clear preference is for a comprehensive capital gains tax on all properties in 
New Zealand. I have not received a report fr om Treasury on the particular proposal the 
member refers to. However, Treasury has a dvised on the expected general effects of 
capital gains taxes over and above the one we actually already have, which applies 
when assets are bought and sold for profit. Again, I should point out that Treasury’s 
preference, if there was to be a capital gain s tax, is that it should be a comprehensive 
one, as well. Anyway, Treasury said that a lthough a capital gains tax would deliver no 
long-term reduction in house prices and “the majority of the effect”— 
Hon David Parker: Oh, rubbish. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: —well, you can disagree with Treasury; we know that you 
do not accept its advice any more—“would be  felt by tenants through higher rents”. So 
the majority of the effect—this is accordi ng to Treasury, which Mr Parker does not 
listen to—would be felt by tena nts through higher rents. Anot her report said that the 
devil is in the detail, and that working out  whether the pros outweigh the cons of a 
capital gains tax “would be a very s ubstantial exercise.” The Inland Revenue 
Department’s view, which was also repor ted by Treasury, was that the practical 
disadvantages were likely to outweigh the advantages. 
Hon David Parker : I seek leave to table the Tr easury report dated 27 September 
2012 on information on a capital gains tax limited to investment housing. 
18162 Questions for Oral Answer 21 May 2014 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The document has now been well described. It is a Treasury 
report dated 27 September 2012. Is there any objection to that Treasury report being 
tabled? There is not. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Hon David Parker : Does he agree with the advice in that Treasury report that the 
taxation of capital gains on investment  housing, excluding the family home, will 
redirect investment into savings and the productive economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I do not have that particul ar quote from the member, but I 
do have the quote—which I suspect is from th e same report—that says that there would 
be no long-term reduction in house prices and th at the majority of the effect would be 
felt by tenants through higher rents. Once again, Treasury ’s preference is for a 
comprehensive capital gains tax on every single New Zealand house. 
Hon David Parker : Does he agree with the advice of Treasury in that same report 
that the taxation of capital gains on investment housing, excluding the family home, will 
“reduce the price of housing and increase affordability of owner-occupied housing;”? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : No, and in that case, any s uggestion that putting a capital 
gains tax on 25 percent or thereabouts of Ne w Zealand housing would have that sort of 
effect is an exaggeration. If you want to see an example of where that has been done and 
where it has not been successful, look at Sydney, Australia. 
Tim Macindoe : What other comments have West pac economists made about an 
additional capital gains tax in New Zealand? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I have seen two other qu ite relevant comments from 
Westpac economists highlighting very signif icant drawbacks of adding an additional 
capital gains tax. The first is that they point out that it is unlikely to happen, because it 
would be complex to administer and, wors e, much of the burden would fall on tenants 
who tend to have low incomes, which is exactly the same advice as received from 
Treasury. The second comment I have seen from Westpac economists is that top-end 
properties rather than low-end properties w ould be less affected by a capital gains tax, 
so price differentials between high-priced houses and low-priced houses would widen. 
That is because investors are less prevalent at the top end of the property market. So it is 
rents at the bottom end of the market that would be most affected. So, once again, the 
Labour Party, in its attempt to fiddle around with the economy, would lift costs on those 
members of society who could least afford that. There are two very good reasons, in 
addition to many others, that an additional capital gains tax is yet another dead-end for 
Mr Parker.  
Hon David Parker: Does he agree with the advice of Treasury in that report that the 
taxation of capital gains on investment  housing, excluding the family home, will 
“reduce the level of foreign borrowing compared to the status quo.”? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: The reality is that we have a capital gains tax on investment 
properties right now. We have tightened rules for loss attributing qualifying companies, 
we have prevented property i nvestors from using rental lo sses to inflate Working for 
Families payments, and we have increased the Inland Revenue Department’s funding to 
target property speculators, and that has b een raising $2.5 billion in additional tax. So 
the Opposition acts like there is not a capital  gains tax on investment properties now, 
and there is. 
Tim Macindoe: What other reports has the Minist er seen from Westpac about the 
New Zealand economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : It is interesting that Mr Parker’s new friends at Westpac 
have been actually considering the nature  of the New Zealand economy after the next 
election. They say that, depending on the out come of the next election, the market 
21 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18163 
implications would be substa ntial. For example, if a cer tain outcome occurred, they 
would see a downturn in domestic demand, a pe riod of slower economic activity due to 
business uncertainty, businesses holding off on  investment and hiring decisions, and 
difficulties for a new Government to keep Government spending in check. It would 
push up interest rates. That is th e Westpac prognosis under a Labour-Greens 
Government. 
Hon David Parker : Why does he not stop the pret ence and admit that National’s 
housing policy has been totally ineffectiv e and adopt Labour’s comprehensive housing 
policy, which addresses both demand and s upply by implementing a capital gains tax, 
excluding the family home, building 100,0 00 affordable houses, and restricting 
purchases by offshore buyers? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : In Mr Parker’s bubble that would make a difference, but, 
actually, they are the policies that some part s of Australia have had for some time, and 
their house prices are higher than New Zealand’s. This Government’s policies of freeing 
up the supply of housing have doubled the num ber of houses being built over the last 3 
years, and those numbers are continuing to climb— 
Phil Twyford: Rubbish! 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : It is absolutely correct. This Government is focused on 
managing growth positively for jobs for Kiwi  builders and Kiwi construction workers, 
not clamping down with yet more taxes to drive the economy back into recession, which 
is the proposal of the Labour Party. 
Tim Macindoe : What other reports has the Mini ster seen opposing an additional 
capital gains tax because of its many drawbacks and problems? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Weirdly, I have seen a very interesting speech to the 
Property Investors Association conference, which was in July 2005. This speech, which 
was unusually good by a Minister, for the standards of the time, noted that the 
Government of the day agreed with a review known as the McLeod Tax Review, which 
concluded that— 
Hon David Cunliffe: Tell us about Rob Muldoon. 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: Be quiet, Mr Cunliffe; I am coming to your punchline. The 
review concluded that the disadvantages of such a tax, such as its complexity and costs, 
outweighed any theoretical benefits. The speaker  at that conference went on to say that 
the Government of the day believed that th e status quo was entirely adequate and that 
any form of new property tax should be off the agenda. That speech was delivered by 
none other than the then Associate Minister of Finance, David Cunliffe. 
Budget 2014—Financial Support for Families 
4. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand 
by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Metiria Turei: When the Prime Minister said that the Budget would focus on young 
families and those vulnerable children who most  need our care, what rationale did he 
use to exclude 60 percent of babies born into poverty from getting the parental tax credit 
payment? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : For a start off, the $500 milli on package aimed at families, 
which includes three of the five elements, includes all New Zealanders. In terms of 
those who are on benefits, there are other wa ys of addressing that, through emergency 
benefits or extra supplementary payments. 
Metiria Turei : I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I was very explicit in my 
question: it asked for the rationale in excl uding children from the parental tax credit. 
That was not addressed by the Prime Minister.

10. JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki)  to the Minister for the Environment : 
How does Budget 2014 help communities and c ouncils manage their local freshwater 
resources? 
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for the Environment) : The Government is 
undertaking significant reforms to better ma nage New Zealand’s freshwater. These 
include a National Policy Statement for Fres hwater Management, a proposed national 
objectives framework, national bottom lines, collaborative  planning processes, and 
better water accounting. In addition, we are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on 
freshwater clean-ups. As part of this, last week in Budget 2014 we announced an 
additional $20 million of new money over the ne xt 4 years to help councils improve the 
way they plan and make decisions about ma naging their local fres hwater resource and 
to help communities restore their local freshwater bodies. 
Jacqui Dean: How will the funding support better decision-making? 
Hon AMY ADAMS: Good decision-making must be backed by robust, high-quality 
information. Funding in the Budget include s $12 million to support water science, 
economics, guidance, and implementation for th e freshwater reforms. This may include 
greater information on the current state of their water bodies and the economic and 
environmental impacts of various water-quality  targets, and improved data collection to 
monitor progress. There is also $3 million that includes support for collaborative 
processes for freshwater management, includi ng the development of tools, guidance, 
and support. We know these processes have th e potential to include a wide range of 
stakeholders in decision making, resulting in stronger, more robust outcomes. A further 
$5 million is targeted to supporting community -led restoration projects through the Te 
Mana o te Wai Fund, announced in partnership with the Māori Party.

Hon HEKIA PARATA (Minister of Education) : Ā, tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Otir ā, 
huri noa i t ō t ātou Whare, t ēnā koutou katoa. Me whakanui t ātou i t ēnei tahua-p ūtea.
